items.abstract: The relevance of this study stems from the continuing conceptual ambiguity surrounding the meaning of circularity in economic activity and the need to distinguish clearly between its conceptual essence, implementation mechanisms, levels of manifestation, and outcomes. The aim of the study is to advance the conceptual foundations of the circularity of economic activity by clarifying the relationships between the key concepts, substantiating its internal structure, identifying its interconnected dimensions, and systematizing its defining characteristics. The study is conceptual in nature and is based on an integrative analysis of the scientific literature, using qualitative content analysis, comparison, grouping, systematization, theoretical synthesis, and structural and logical generalization.The study systematizes the main approaches to interpreting the circular economy and clarifies the relationships between the concepts of the “circular economy”, the “circular approach”, and the “circularity of economic activity”. The circularity of economic activity is proposed to be understood as the degree to which resources, materials, components, and products are actually reused and kept in productive use over an extended period, while preserving their utility and the value already created, substituting primary resources, and maintaining organized recurring flows. The study substantiates the integration of the resource-and-product and value-and-chain approaches and, on this basis, identifies three interconnected dimensions of circularity: the resource-and-product dimension, the economic-and-value dimension, and the production-and-chain dimension. Six defining characteristics of circularity are identified: repeated use, duration of use, substitution of primary resources, value retention, return and exchange, and systemic coherence. items.title: The Circular Economy—A New Resilience Paradigm?
items.abstract: The circular economy (CE) has traditionally been positioned as a central instrument of the sustainability paradigm. Yet escalating geopolitical volatility and supply chain fragility have elevated resilience to a parallel strategic imperative, and the conceptual integration of CE and resilience remains underexplored. This article bridges this gap by reconceptualizing CE as a foundational instrument for (systemic) resilience. We advance eight theoretically grounded propositions specifying how core CE strategies (i.e., narrowing, slowing, and closing loops) can foster resilience across three nested levels: macro (socioeconomic systems), meso (territorial ecosystems and supply chains), and micro (organizations and products). A nested‐level proposition specifies the coupling between these levels and shows that cross‐level cascades may be reinforcing or countervailing. We argue that CE's future value lies in securing long‐term system continuity under exogenous shocks. By positioning CE as an instrument through which a resilience paradigm can be operationalized alongside sustainability, i.e., a paradigmatic evolution rather than a replacement, we offer a theoretical trajectory and research agenda for scholars, practitioners, and policymakers navigating an increasingly volatile global context.

items.title: Strategic Transformation of Enterprise Management in the Context of the Transition to a Circular Economy
items.abstract: The article examines the specifics of the impact of the circular economy conception on the development of small and medium-sized businesses in Ukraine. The main focus is on analyzing the challenges that arise in the process of implementing circular business models, as well as on determining their potential for increasing resource efficiency and ensuring long-term competitiveness of enterprises. Despite the significant number of works on the circular economy, practical mechanisms for adapting the strategic management system of small and medium-sized businesses to the conditions of martial law and postwar reconstruction in Ukraine remain insufficiently covered. The issue of integrating circular tools with digital transformation and the development of territorial communities requires systematic development. The aim of the study is to develop theoretical provisions and scientific and methodological approaches to the strategic transformation of enterprise management in the context of the transition to a circular economy by substantiating modern mechanisms for integrating circular principles into the strategic management system and developing practical recommendations for increasing resource efficiency and competitiveness of enterprises. In studying the dynamics of small and medium-sized enterprises and employment, the authors used methods of scientific generalization, comparative and statistical analysis. To assess the regulatory framework and form strategic directions, methods of institutional and system analysis were used. The key principles of the circular economy are revealed, in particular, preserving the economic value of products, materials and resources throughout the entire life cycle, and the feasibility of their integration into the management system of small and medium-sized enterprises is substantiated. items.title: The circular economy advantage: unpacking the effects of hotel employees' involvement in circular economy initiatives
items.venue: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing from social cognitive theory (SCT), this study explains how active involvement in high value-retention (HVR) circular economy (CE) initiatives leads to increased hotel employees' perceptions of CE facilitating behavior and organizational commitment under the boundary conditions of environmental concerns. Design/methodology/approach A survey with 184 hotel employees involved in CE initiatives was conducted. SPSS v. 31 and Smart PLS-SEM 4 were used to analyze the data. Findings While the direct effect of HVR CE involvement on organizational commitment was not significant, the true value of the model emerges through its indirect mechanism. Specifically, facilitating behavior fully mediated the relationship between HVR CE involvement and organizational commitment. Furthermore, the moderated mediation effect was significant at mean and high levels of individual environmental concerns. Practical implications Practical implications include, but are not limited to, the importance of developing HVR CE initiatives. Hospitality organizations should position employees as core agents of change, supporting them through CE facilitating behaviors and an empowering work environment that enables employees to enact their pro-environmental values. Originality/value This study is among the first to empirically evaluate employees' involvement in HVR CE initiatives within hospitality research. Specifically, the micro-foundational cognitive mechanisms of employees' CE involvement are explained.

items.title: Re-weaving threads for a circular economy: Spatio-temporal dynamics of the textile and clothing sector in Rotterdam
items.abstract: The ambition of achieving a circular economy (CE) brings with it renewed challenges in implementing systemic change in a context reluctant to abandon ‘business as usual’, but in which the urgency to transform linear production patterns into circular ones grows ever stronger. Taking a holistic ecosystem approach to circularising economies, re-localising key supply chain activities offers opportunities, while also challenging the system. This article maps the businesses active in the textile and clothing (T&C) sector in Rotterdam (the Netherlands) between 1996 and 2022 to uncover the geography of the circular T&C supply chain in and around Rotterdam and to find potential hotspots for localised resource flows. The T&C sector offers insights into the potential re-territorialisation of manufacturing supply chains and the spatial distribution of CE in Rotterdam.

items.title: Spatializing the Circular Economy: Firm-Level Evidence and Socio-Demographic Factors within a National Post-Consumer Sneaker Network
items.abstract: Post-consumer footwear constitutes a highly heterogeneous and minimally circular segment of the consumer goods economy. Although the sector has a substantial environmental footprint, empirical research on post-consumer footwear collection and reverse logistics remains limited. This study contributes to circular economy scholarship by showing that post-consumer sneaker collection depends largely on intermediary capacity, territorial coordination, and robust reverse-logistics infrastructure. Using a novel, spatially granular shipment dataset (2024-2025) covering hundreds of U.S. ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs), the analysis examines the spatial organization, temporal dynamics, and persistence of a national post-consumer sneaker collection network managed by Sneaker Impact. By integrating shipment records with American Community Survey data, the research identifies the socio-demographic factors associated with participation in reverse logistics systems. The findings indicate spatial heterogeneity and significant variation in participation frequency, alongside a modest core of recurrently active locations. Aggregate throughput growth mainly coincided with an increase in the number of active ZCTAs, while average shipment activity per active ZCTA changed little, though these patterns remain confounded by unobserved organizational outreach. Community circular participation exhibits modest socio-demographic stratification. Among the variables examined, educational attainment is the strongest and most consistent correlate of shipment activity, while income shows a slight negative association when controlling for educational attainment. However, socio-demographic characteristics explain only a limited share of the variation in shipment activity, suggesting that organizational and infrastructural factors also play an important role in shaping collection performance. items.title: Material Circularity and Waste-Management GHG Emissions of Construction and Demolition Waste in Bangkok: A Dynamic Material Flow Analysis
items.abstract: Construction and demolition waste (CDW) is a major urban material flow whose long-term generation depends on the age structure of the building stock. This study develops an inflow-driven, cohort-based dynamic material flow analysis (dMFA) for Bangkok that integrates reconstructed pre-2004 building cohorts, CDW generation, a system-level Material Circularity Indicator (MCIsys), and waste-management greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting. Six scenarios, representing a business-as-usual baseline and single and combined applications of waste prevention, recycling, and lifetime extension, were evaluated through 2100. Demolition waste dominated the modeled CDW stream, with concrete as the largest urban-mining stream. Total CDW reached a mid-century maximum of 13.8 Mt/yr around 2062, ranging from 12.1 to 14.6 Mt/yr in 2055–2066 across the reconstruction and inflow sensitivity cases. MCIsys increased from 0.128 under the baseline to 0.290 under Circular Routing and 0.313 under Ambitious Circular Economy by 2100. Within the direct waste-management boundary, which excludes avoided virgin-material production, higher recycling increased cumulative GHG emissions by 3–30% over 2025–2100 across all tested inflow cases because of recycling processing and longer transport, whereas lifetime extension lowered them by 9–22% within the horizon by delaying demolition. The MCIsys contrast remained robust under parameter uncertainty, and the GHG increase under circular routing occurred in all paired simulations.

items.title: Toward integrated urban sustainability assessment: a structured review and classification of indicator frameworks and integrated approaches
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Urbanization is a primary driver reshaping global socioeconomic and environmental systems, highlighting the need, particularly in the context of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), to develop robust tools for the evaluation of urban sustainability. This structured literature review of urban sustainability indicators initially identified 419 Scopus® records; screening and supplementary searches yielded 43 sources for the final synthesis, classified into three main categories: i) single and composite indicators, which are flexible but often lack comparability; ii) frameworks based on the SDGs, frequently adopted as classificatory rather than operational assessment tools; iii) approaches based on flows and impacts such as Material Flow Analysis (MFA), Urban Metabolism (UM) and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). Unlike previous reviews, which typically addressed only one methodological perspective, the current study compares these three methodological paradigms, evaluating their integration opportunities, limitations, and operational role. The results highlighted a significant gap between indicator-based and impact-based approaches, while the MFA–LCA integration remains insufficiently developed. Based on literature data, a focused sub-analysis of ten studies highlighted frequent attention to transportation, energy, and construction materials. Given the heterogeneous landscape of urban sustainability tools, the review provides a qualitative decision-support matrix to help urban professionals and policymakers select and combine assessment approaches according to their objectives, data availability, expertise, and implementation capacity. The study contributes by proposing a structured typology of indicators and identifying UM–LCA integration as a promising flow- and impact-assessment component within broader hybrid urban sustainability frameworks.

items.title: SolarEV Cities for deep urban decarbonization: A critical review of integration gaps and transition pathways
items.abstract: Urban decarbonization is essential for meeting global climate goals; however, progress toward integrated low-carbon urban energy systems remains inadequately slow. The SolarEV City Concept integrates rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation with electric vehicles (EVs) as city-scale distributed mobile energy storage, using EV batteries to increase the value and flexibility of urban rooftop PV. Modeling studies suggest that high-penetration PV+EV systems could supply 60–95% of municipal electricity demand under scenarios aligned with future sustainable-city development, but real-world integration remains limited. Despite rapid worldwide growth of both PV and EV markets, bidirectional Vehicle-to-Home/Building (V2H/V2B) and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) applications have advanced unevenly, revealing a persistent PV-EV integration gap. This critical integrative review analyzes this gap using a socio-techno-economic framework encompassing six interdependent dimensions: climate, urban structure, technology, economics, policy, and society, across nine countries: Australia, China, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, and the United States. Cross-national comparison shows that implementation is constrained by fragmented bidirectional-charging standards, immature value-stacking and compensation models, distribution-grid and market-access constraints, regulatory separation between energy and transport sectors, and equity barriers that disproportionately limit access for renters, apartment residents, and lower-income households. items.title: Strategic Allocation of Post-Consumer Textiles across Reuse, Recycling and Value Recovery Pathways
items.abstract: Post-consumer textiles vary considerably in physical condition, fiber composition, remaining product life, recoverable material quality, processing requirements, transportation burden, resale potential, and recycling compatibility. As a result, directing all discarded apparel toward a single recovery strategy may cause unnecessary loss of economic and material value. Effective circular textile management requires systematic decisions regarding whether recovered garments should be reused, repaired, resold, refurbished, repurposed, recycled into fibers, or directed toward other end-of-life pathways. This study develops a strategic allocation framework for directing heterogeneous post-consumer textiles toward circular pathways that maximize value retention while reducing waste. The proposed framework evaluates textile recovery alternatives according to product condition, material composition, remaining useful life, resale demand, repair requirements, recycling yield, processing cost, transportation requirements, recovered-material value, environmental burden, and available recovery capacity. Rather than prioritizing recycling automatically, the framework emphasizes preservation of the highest feasible level of product or material value. A series of simulated textile-recovery networks was developed to represent variations in collection volume, textile quality, fiber mixtures, recovery capacity, transportation distance, resale demand, recycling technology availability, and recovered-material markets. Alternative allocation strategies were evaluated under normal operating conditions as well as scenarios involving sudden collection increases, declining secondary-market demand, recycling-capacity limitations, and changes in processing costs. Performance was assessed through textile diversion from disposal, product reuse rate, material recovery rate, retained economic value, processing requirements, recovery cost, recycling yield, pathway utilization, and overall circularity

items.title: Circular Bioenergy Production from Heavy-Metal-Contaminated Biomass: An Integrated Biorefinery Optimization Approach
items.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CHEMISTRY AND CHEMICAL PROCESSES
items.abstract: The increasing prevalence of heavy-metal-contaminated biomass in industrial, agricultural, and remediation processes poses challenges for the environment and the bioenergy sector. This paper elaborates and analyzes a risk-conscious integrated bio-refinery optimization model for circular bioenergy generation from contaminated biomass, enabling the production of both biodiesel and biogas while accounting for heavy-metal fate and associated environmental risks. System performance was evaluated based on low, moderate, and high levels of contamination (10–1,000 mg·kg⁻¹) using deterministic multi-objective optimization, global sensitivity analysis, Monte Carlo propagation of uncertainty, and multivariate regime classification. Findings indicate that total energy recovery decreased from 13,610 to 6,665 MJ·t⁻¹ biomass with increasing contamination; nevertheless, anaerobic digestion gradually replaced energy production, with a maximum contribution of 75.2 percent to total output at high contamination. Biodiesel production went down to 172.4 to 44.6 kg·t⁻¹, and still, the amount of metals in biodiesel was at a quarter of the previous range, 0.5 mg·kg⁻¹. The fraction of incoming heavy metals immobilized in the digestate exceeded96 percent, and it met regulatory limits for land application in all situations, with compliance rates over 90 percent under stochastic uncertainty. Pareto-optimal solutions have shown obvious trade offs in terms of energy recovery, metal risk index (0.07-0.18), and circularity performance (0.79 0.92). In contrast, principal component and cluster analysis revealed operation regimes influenced by contamination. The investigation introduces a system-level approach and reinvigorates the concept of heavy-metal contamination as a manageable design constraint, offering a significant pathway to sustainable bioenergy recovery from polluted landscapes within the circular bioeconomy.

items.title: Futures, Feedback, and Flexibility: Reimagining Public Sector Management and Evaluation in the Time of Polycrisis
items.abstract: This article examines how evaluative practice can better support public management in an era of “polycrisis” marked by climate breakdown, ecological collapse, conflict, inequality, and democratic erosion. Governments need to manage increasing uncertainty and evaluative practice needs to be repositioned and embedded to support emergent policy and management processes. The article draws on a global futures exercise using the 3 Horizons approach with 39 respondents, combined with literature review, AI-assisted analysis, and four case studies of public sector evaluative systems in South Africa, Brazil, the United Kingdom, and the City of Cape Town.​ Across the cases, findings show that when evaluation is reconfigured as a diverse set of embedded, collaborative practices, it can inform major spending decisions, reframe policy goals to address the polycrisis, and build institutional capability for continuous learning. The article concludes that transforming evaluation from a narrow, compliance-driven function into an agile, futures-linked, and systems-oriented diverse practice is not optional but a precondition for credible public management in the polycrisis, and calls for deliberate changes in incentives, roles, and governance arrangements to institutionalise this shift.​

items.title: A community-based approach to implementing energy access initiatives in low-resource contexts
items.abstract: This article conceptually examines how energy access in low-resource and poverty settings is shaped by interconnected economic, infrastructural, social, and governance determinants, and how decentralised renewable options can respond when implemented through a community-based approach. It reviews conceptual ambiguities of “energy community” and argues that, in marginalised and low-resource contexts, goals are often defined less by market participation than by poverty reduction, productive uses of energy, and social development. Drawing on three community-based initiatives in Mayotte – a “Clean Mobility”, a “Social Housing” and a “Collective Interest” energy community – as practice-based starting points, the paper reflects on participation and empowerment, inclusion and recognition justice, and contextualisation through a socio-ecological systems lens. The conceptual reflection highlights that effective initiatives align technology with everyday practices, build bridging and bonding social capital, and adapt governance, tariffs, and partnerships to local institutions and constraints. The article concludes by outlining cornerstones for designing resilient, equitable grassroots energy communities under conditions of poverty, informality, and climate risk over time.

items.title: A KK-theoretic note on the spectral localiser
items.abstract: We review the construction of the spectral localiser (due to Loring and Schulz-Baldes) from a KK -theoretic perspective. We first give a KK -theoretic argument providing a spectral flow expression for the even or odd index pairing in terms of the “infinite volume” spectral localiser. Our approach towards this first step is more direct, treats the even and odd cases on an equal footing, and has the advantage that the construction of the spectral localiser becomes immediately apparent from the computation of the index pairing via a Kasparov product. In a second step of “spectral truncation”, we then describe how this spectral flow expression can be computed in terms of the signature of the “finite volume” spectral localiser. Throughout, we do not require invertibility of the operator representing the K -homology class, and the even index pairing then obtains an additional contribution coming from the Fredholm index.

items.title: HESS Opinions: Operationalizing sociohydrology from systems thinking to systems doing for sustainable and resilient water management
items.abstract: Sociohydrology has advanced explanations of coupled human-water systems, but its translation into decision support remains uneven. We propose two complementary approaches to move from systems thinking to systems doing: (i) canonical feedback structures, which describe the main components of human-water systems and how they interact and enable comparison across cases while accounting for important local differences; and (ii) critical pathways, which trace how management actions propagate through these components to produce outcomes, including unintended consequences. Drawing on cases such as the levee effect and reservoir effect, these approaches connect system understanding with intervention design, monitoring, and adaptive learning. We then propose a minimal “systems-doing loop” that links the decision setting, feedback mapping, pathway tracing, indicator selection, and iteration, with equity and legitimacy treated as explicit constraints on useful knowledge and acceptable action. This framing complements predictive modelling and integrated water resources management by accounting for potential unintended consequences in decision-making and clarifying what to monitor and revisit as systems change.

items.title: Inclusion in Science: The Social Architecture of Science-Public Relations
items.abstract: Relations between science and publics are tricky affairs. While public participation in science is expanding, it regularly falls short of emancipatory hopes. Claudia Göbel analyzes these tensions as an important feature of contemporary society. She develops an extended model of inclusion in science by bringing science and technology studies, sociology of science and science communication studies into conversation. Popular science audiences and amateur researchers are conceptualized as integral to science, showing how these precarious roles complement professional scientists. The model offers a versatile framework for empirical research and new comparative perspectives on the multiple publics of science and their intricate relations.

items.title: A Data-Driven Sustainable Site Suitability Analysis of Organized Industrial Zones from an SDG Perspective Using a GIS-Based Hybrid Multi-Criteria Analysis Approach
items.abstract: Industrial site selection plays a critical role in shaping regional development trajectories, spatial equity, and long-term sustainability outcomes. However, limited attention has been given to how alternative policy priorities aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) influence spatial suitability patterns. This study develops a GIS-based hybrid multi-criteria decision-making framework integrating SWARA and CoCoSo methods to evaluate the site suitability of the existing Organized Industrial Zones (OIZs) under three alternative policy scenarios: Economically prioritized, environmentally prioritized, and balanced sustainability-oriented structures. A total of 26 criteria linked to SDGs 6–9, 11–13, and 15 are incorporated into the analysis. The results reveal that suitability rankings are highly sensitive to weighting configurations. The economically prioritized scenario reinforces transport accessibility and infrastructure-driven agglomeration advantages, elevating centrally connected districts, while environmentally oriented weighting substantially reshapes spatial outcomes by favoring ecologically resilient areas. The balanced scenario mitigates extreme polarization and produces more stability in rankings. These findings highlight the trade-offs between short-term economic efficiency and long-term environmental sustainability in industrial spatial planning. By explicitly modelling scenario-based policy priorities, the study provides a transparent and replicable decision-support framework that enables planners to simulate alternative development strategies and better align industrial location decisions with SDG-oriented socio-economic planning objectives.

items.title: Organizing for Sustainable Futures: Micro and Macro-institutional Conditions of Transformation: A People-centric Organizational Perspective
items.abstract: This study advances structuration theory by examining the recursive relationship between micro-level agency and macro-institutional conditions in sustainability transformations. Through a mixed-methods research design combining quantitative survey data (n=234) with qualitative interviews (n=42) and comparative case studies (n=6) across multiple sectors, the article presents a people-centric framework that specifies the mechanisms through which individual agency both shapes and is constrained by institutional structures. Statistical analysis demonstrates significant relationships between integration practices and transformation outcomes (β=0.42, p<0.01), with power dynamics moderating this relationship. Qualitative findings reveal distinct transformation pathways across organizational contexts, challenging universal prescriptions for sustainability. The research contributes to theory by articulating how paradox navigation capabilities, power mobilization strategies, and multi-level learning systems mediate between structural conditions and transformation outcomes. For practitioners, these findings demonstrate that successful sustainability transformations require simultaneous attention to institutional environments, power structures, and human capabilities—recognizing that transformation emerges from their ongoing interaction rather than from either dimension alone.

items.title: Art-science collaboration for sustainability challenges: a systematic review of scholarship, sustainability framings, and stakeholder participation
items.abstract: Art-science collaboration (ASC) is increasingly presented as a response to sustainability challenges, yet the literature lacks a clear account of how the field has developed, how sustainability is substantively framed, and who participates. This systematic review synthesises 97 peer-reviewed ASC publications (2002–2024) using mixed quantitative and qualitative analysis organised around three strands. First, we characterise ASC scholarship and practice. The evidence base is rapidly expanding but weakly consolidated. Qualitative case studies dominate, the literature is process-heavy and evaluation-light, and syntheses and outcome-oriented evaluations remain rare. Peer-reviewed knowledge production is concentrated in universities and research institutes in a small number of Global North countries. Multi-media installations are the most frequently reported artistic format, alongside a substantial presence of socially engaged practice. Second, we examine sustainability framings through a triple-bottom-line lens (People, Planet, and Prosperity). Sustainability is most often framed through Planet-related topics. People is commonly implied through engagement and learning aims, while Prosperity is rarely treated as a primary concern. Many sustainability-relevant studies do not use sustainability terminology in titles or abstracts, limiting discoverability in sustainability-oriented syntheses. Third, we analyse stakeholder participation. Thirteen stakeholder types are identified, with a stable core configuration across time and increasing inclusion of policymakers, local communities, and NGOs. Facilitators, media organisations, and private sector actors remain peripheral, and stakeholder co-design of research questions, methods, or evaluation is uncommon. Together, these findings underline that the field would benefit from clearer reporting conventions, greater recognition of non-academic contributors, and stronger cross-community connections. items.title: Policy Instruments Fostering Site Level Application of Circular Practices in Construction
items.abstract: One of the most pursued predicaments in the recent past is the slowness in transmuting circular practices. In the hope of many apparent advantages, construction firms have been attempting to embrace circularity-oriented functions, thus controlling their negativities to the extent possible. However, many of these are futile attempts that have been made ad hoc without having validated policy instruments intact. Only a few studies have taken an overarching approach to address this matter and effectively inculcate circularity at construction sites. This article aims to fill this knowledge gap by introducing a structured outline resulting in 9 policy categories and over 100 policy instruments. Developed from a review of 90 studies selected from the Google Scholar platform and 16 policy documents essentially contributed by eminent research groups, these policy instruments were subsequently validated in a series of 18 semi-structured interviews with experts and industry personnel having international exposure in large-scale construction projects. This study provides over 150 practical examples of scaffolding circularity as a noble cause. Of a practical insight, a fundamental reconfiguration of site operations is deemed indispensable.

items.title: “It is a sham process with participation.” Ten forms of citizen participation for sustainable development in the Norwegian Arctic
items.abstract: Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) requires action at all levels, from local to global, through synergy among all societal actors. Norway shares responsibility for SDG-based sustainable development with local authorities (municipalities and counties). The Planning and Building Act’s purpose clause stipulates that it shall promote sustainable development for the benefit of individuals, society and future generations. Municipal responsibility for sustainable development, when incorporated into planning processes, is complex and requires the inclusion of diverse knowledge holders. Focusing on spatial planning as an instrument for sustainable transformation, this study examined citizen participation practices at the municipal level in the Norwegian Arctic. I conducted semi-structured interviews with 75 residents with very diverse backgrounds. Using inductive thematic analysis, I coded forms of citizen participation, their characteristics, and their links with sustainability and transformation. I further analyzed the forms using Arnstein’s ladder of citizen participation and Fung’s cube of democracy. I identified 10 forms of citizen participation in planning processes. Only two of these give citizens the opportunity to influence decisions, but only on matters less relevant to sustainability. A link to sustainability and transformation is prominent in all forms. Citizens emphasize the importance of focusing on climate adaptation, nature conservation, and local values. Local authorities see green industry, power plants, and the economy as fundamental. Lay citizens, some politicians, and some planners believe these are destructive to local sustainability values, which are strongly linked to the importance of nature in people's lives. Overall, the current practice of participation in planning processes in my sample of municipalities in the Norwegian Arctic lacks genuine cooperation, fails to incorporate local knowledge, and hardly leads to citizens’ influence

items.title: Envisioning transition pathways for a sustainable meat and protein supply system in Japan: A Research through Design approach
items.abstract: The transition toward sustainable protein supply is constrained by consumer, supply-side, and policy barriers that are often studied separately, leaving unclear how a cross-domain lock-in diagnosis can inform multilevel intervention pathways. In Japan, small, dispersed farmland and imported-feed dependence intersect with established expectations of price and convenience. This exploratory case study examined Japan’s meat and protein supply system through a Research through Design approach integrating the multi-level perspective and Transition Design. Interviews with 21 participants and a co-creation workshop were used to structure current problems, envision desirable futures, and backcast potential interventions. The diagnosis showed how regulative, normative, and cognitive rules mutually reinforce these structural and cultural constraints. The research team synthesized participant outputs into three contrasting scenarios: pasture-raised lean beef, localized circular communities, and food-printer technology. Cross-scenario comparison yielded two provisional design principles: creating experiential proximity, which makes unfamiliar transition options tangible through situated experience, and culturally situated value translation, which connects sustainability values with meanings embedded in existing food cultures. The principles were instantiated differently and combined with pathway-specific system and governance components, including grading standards and sales channels, interorganizational coordination, and food law, labeling, and safety standards. The contribution lies in translating fragmented actor perspectives and a cross-domain lock-in diagnosis into a future-oriented intervention portfolio while making the interpretive steps traceable. The resulting principles and configurations provide testable propositions for comparative research and future pilot studies.

items.title: Digital and Intelligent Technologies for Construction and Demolition Waste Sorting: A Systematic Mapping Review of Research Maturity, Circularity Outcomes, and Industry Gaps
items.abstract: Construction and demolition waste (CDW) sorting is increasingly supported by digital and intelligent technologies, yet their functional coverage, maturity, circular economy (CE) contribution and alignment with industrial practice remain fragmented. This review systematically mapped the field using a PRISMA-based search, with 396 publications forming the broader bibliometric corpus. Within this corpus, 204 publications were retained for the scoped review, comprising 185 primary technical studies and 19 review articles. An illustrative ZenRobotics/Kuljetusrinki case was examined separately within a case-bounded academic-industry comparison. Artificial intelligence, computer vision, and sensing dominated the technical literature, particularly for identification, classification, localisation, and segmentation, while fewer studies progressed to robotic handling, physical separation, and integrated system functions. Among the 185 primary technical studies, validation remained concentrated at lower maturity levels, with 54.1% at laboratory maturity, 6.5% testing fully realistic CDW conditions, 18.9% reporting external or independent validation, and 3.2% reporting industrial deployment. Although 94.1% of these studies had a direct CE link, specific CE and sustainability outcome-related evidence such as recovered material quality, reuse, and landfill diversion was reported less consistently than technical performance. The case-bounded comparison showed that several capabilities investigated separately across the academic literature were integrated within the selected operational case, while independently verified operational and CE outcomes remained limited. These findings highlight the need for robust, integrated and operationally validated CDW sorting systems that connect emerging technologies with measurable recovery, material quality and circular outcomes under practical operating conditions.

items.title: Building blocks of localized storm tracks: revisiting asymmetries between the NH and SH in storm track strength
items.abstract: An intermediate-complexity moist general circulation model is used to investigate the forcing of localized storm tracks by land–sea contrast, horizontal gradients in ocean heat uptake, planetary albedo, and topography. The additivity of the response to these building blocks is investigated. Consistent with previous work focusing on stationary waves, the storm track patterns and strength are not simply the linear additive sum of the response to each surface inhomogeneity. As observed on Earth, the SH storm tracks are stronger than those in the NH, and also stronger over ocean basins than over continents. In this model, the most important building block for this asymmetry is land–sea contrast, however, there is substantial non-additivity both in the regional structure and also the hemispheric asymmetry. An energy budget perspective offers some insight on the causes of the non-additivity, and highlights how the net impact of each building block on outgoing longwave radiation is dependent on the existence of the others. Relatively small changes in oceanic heat transport from the Southern Ocean to the North Atlantic have a pronounced impact on the individual terms making up the energy budget, however there is substantial cancellation between these terms leading to a small impact on the NH vs. SH asymmetry in storm track strength. The detailed structure of albedo has a weak impact on the NH vs. SH asymmetry due to substantial cancellation between the changes in individual terms making up the energy budget, even though the albedo profile has a large impact on the overall transient eddy activity in each hemisphere.

items.title: Digital Twins in AEC: Gemini Principles, ISO 19650 Information Management, Lifecycle Decisions, Cybersecurity, Interoperability, and Circular Economy
items.abstract: This chapter examines the rapidly evolving role of Digital Twins in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction industry, emphasizing their integration with Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence, ISO 19650 information management, and Industry 5.0 principles. Digital Twins, continuously updated through Building Information Management, IoT sensing, and AI analytics enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and lifecycle optimization. The chapter highlights foundational frameworks such as the Gemini Principles, ISO 23247, and human-in-the-loop approaches that ensure transparency, trust, and explainability in Digital Twin-driven decisions. Critical challengesincluding cybersecurity vulnerabilities, semantic interoperability, and ethical governanceare addressed through zero-trust architectures, ontology-based data models, explainable Artificial Intelligence, and blockchain-enabled auditability. The chapter further explores how Digital Twins support sustainability and the circular economy via material passports, carbon tracking, and resource-efficient lifecycle strategies. Case studies demonstrate measurable benefits in safety, energy performance, and predictive analytics, positioning Digital Twins as central to human-centric, resilient, and sustainable Construction 6.0 ecosystems.

items.title: Building Consensus Among Intensive Care Nurses on the Scope of Practice for Registered Nurses Deployed to Intensive Care During Surge Events: A Real‐Time Delphi Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Disaster events that overwhelm health system capacity often require the deployment of nurses from non-critical care clinical areas to supplement the specialist intensive care workforce. However, the role of deployed registered nurses in intensive care is poorly defined and without clear role boundaries, experienced intensive care nurses often bear disproportionate supervisory burdens, and deployed staff may assume clinical responsibilities for which they are inadequately prepared. Developing a scope of practice for deployed nurses is essential for safe, effective surge responses. AIM: To achieve expert consensus on the scope of practice of deployed registered nurses in a surged intensive care unit. STUDY DESIGN: A Real-Time Delphi study was conducted using a web-based platform. A 65-item survey was administered to a panel of experienced Australian intensive care nurses and educators with expertise in training and/or supervising nurses deployed to intensive care during surge events. Participants rated activities that could potentially be undertaken by deployed registered nurses in a surged intensive care setting using a 5-point Likert scale across two dimensions: appropriateness for delegation and importance within a tiered nursing model. Consensus was defined a priori as ≥ 70% agreement. Free-text comments were analysed thematically. RESULTS: Fifteen expert panellists completed the survey. Of the 69 items assessed, 33 reached consensus and were retained as constituting the scope of practice for registered nurses deployed to intensive care. Consensus items spanned neurological observation, basic cardiovascular monitoring, gastrointestinal care, fluid balance documentation, and essential nursing cares. No consensus was reached for mechanical ventilation, non-invasive ventilation or renal replacement therapy. items.title: Coordination without Hegemony: RCEP and the Political Economy of Multipolar Regionalism in Asia
items.venue: European Journal of East Asian Studies
items.abstract: Multipolarity is usually treated as a shift in the distribution of capabilities, yet its practical consequence is institutional: who writes the rules, and with what domestic consent. This article asks how cooperation is organised when no power can impose order, taking the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership ( RCEP ) as its case. An integrative review with theory-building purpose maps the Scopus literatures on multipolarity and the RCEP , synthesises a purposive pool of 36 studies, and anchors it against the treaty text and accounts of the negotiation. The synthesis supports reading the agreement as coordination without a hegemonic orchestrator: procedural leadership by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations steered the negotiation, while broad coverage with calibrated obligation preserves autonomy. Domestic authorisation is hypothesised, not shown, to be the binding constraint on deepening, with stated refutation conditions. The Multipolarity Governance Triangle organises these trade-offs as a heuristic and specifies indicators for testing it.

items.title: The Activist’s Guide to the Decentralized Social Universe: A Framework for Exploring How Decentralized Social Networks Can Support Collective Action
items.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
items.abstract: The overreaches of mainstream social media platforms have been extensively reported and studied. For activist communities, these platforms pose risks of surveillance, censorship, or erasure. Decentralized social networks (DSNs) serve as alternative online spaces that appear to prioritize values such as user privacy, free speech, and community control. However, the decentralized ecosystem is vast and complex, making it difficult for communities to understand how to best use these platforms for their organizing aims. We address this gap by proposing a conceptual framework for navigating the DSN landscape that defines core activist community needs—minimal overhead, community building and reach, on- and offline safety, and operational sustainability—and links them to concrete platform affordances such as resource efficiency, interoperability, and data ownership. We apply the framework to (1) evaluate and compare the sociotechnical tradeoffs of two contemporary DSNs (Mastodon and Bluesky), (2) understand broader community configurations that emerge across different DSN infrastructures and their implications for collective action, and (3) explore how two distinct activist communities facing infrastructural and political constraints might use the framework to find platforms that align with their needs. We conclude by reflecting on the theoretical promises of DSNs and the structural conditions that shape and constrain participation across them.

items.title: A comprehensive mapping review of participatory autism research over a 22-year period
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Participatory research, which involves community members as partners rather than merely research subjects, has gained prominence in autism research. However, the extent and nature of participatory approaches across the field remain unclear. METHODS: We conducted a mapping review of autism research reporting community involvement, searching six databases. We coded who was involved, at what level, and in which research activities, and examined factors associated with participation. RESULTS: We identified 382 studies published between 2001 and 2023, with 95% published in the past decade. Two-thirds (67%) involved Autistic people, though one-third claiming to be "participatory" excluded them entirely. The most common participation level was consulting (31%), with community-led (5%) and community-controlled (1%) research remaining rare. Community involvement concentrated in study design (73%) rather than analysis (33%) or dissemination (29%). Participatory research was heavily concentrated in Western countries (USA, UK, Australia, Canada: 86%), applied research areas, and qualitative studies. Deeper participation was associated with identity-first language use and publication in journals with clear community-centered agendas. CONCLUSIONS: While participatory language is increasingly becoming the norm in autism research, genuine power-sharing between researchers and community members is still a rare occurrence. Most participatory research operates at consultative levels, with academic researchers retaining primary decision-making authority. Moving toward authentic participation requires systemic changes to funding structures, institutional policies, and epistemic hierarchies that determine whose knowledge counts.

items.title: A Scoping Review of Queer Health and Well-Being Technology Research
items.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
items.abstract: Technology has and will continue to have a significant impact on queer people’s health and well-being; however, it is not guaranteed that these implementations lead to meaningful advancements. Through a scoping review of 69 queer health technology papers in the ACM Digital Library, we review who queer health and well-being research has centered, what health topics have been targeted, and how technology has been used to address them. Our results identify trends in health foci and intervention implementation strategies, revealing opportunities for upstream efforts that work across individual, community, and structural levels. We therefore argue for greater attention towards structural constructions of queer health and well-being, specific and intentional groupings when developing interventions, and four commitments for designing and carrying out technology-enabled health interventions: commitments to holistic constructions of problem spaces, leverage points, and unintended harms; to reflexive practices for challenging assumptions; to accountability to community needs and flourishing; and to expansion towards situated and relational understandings of health. This work culminates in a framework and research agenda for queer health technology that provides guidance for future interventions.

items.title: Exploring animal production futures in the Nordics through efficiency, sufficiency, and consistency: towards integrated sustainability and resilience
items.abstract: The sustainability aspects of animal production are complex, and aligning multiple objectives related to it is challenging. Public discussion related to animal agriculture is strongly dualistic: Prevailing strategies for more sustainable animal production are mainly aiming at increasing the efficiency of production processes. At the same time, others are criticising the consumption of animal-derived foods, and these two extremes, efficiency and sufficiency, hardly understand each other. An emerging strategy, consistency, which in the agricultural context is close to agroecology and regenerative agriculture, emphasises the integration of animal agriculture into the socio-ecological environment. Consistency also addresses dimensions undercommunicated by efficiency and sufficiency, such as food security. In this conceptual article these strategic approaches to sustainability are identified, reflected against socio-environmental and agronomic literature, and critically examined from a Nordic perspective. Each of these strategies provide different solutions for improving the sustainability of animal agriculture. It is argued that to successfully reorient animal agriculture towards a sustainable and resilient future, efficiency, sufficiency, and consistency strategies should be considered as mutually complementary.

items.title: Does Materials Reuse Strategy Facilitate European Polycotton Circularity? System Dynamic Drivers in the Innovation Ecosystems
items.abstract: This study examines the multi-stakeholder complexity and intra-supply chain limitations that supply chain management entails while analysing circular textile transitions and polycotton reuse. Using a participatory design approach, it combines expert insights into a causality matrix with causal loop diagrams (CLD) to map cause-and-effect relationships. The findings claim that a better understanding of the circularity drivers and their interconnections is reached by applying the innovation ecosystems perspective around the eight key drivers of the Polycotton circular transition in Europe. Our research also shows that circular innovation ecosystems can link previously disconnected sectors such as clothing, waste management, biochemical industries, and construction. The empirical settings depicted in the polycotton case conclude an insufficient emphasis on workforce training and consumer awareness as a critical gap in EU policy, recommending increased political investment in these areas to support large-scale polycotton reuse and achieve broader circularity. items.title: Dissolution, Reconfiguration and Formation: Decarbonisation Effects on Regional Industrial Interpath Dynamics
items.venue: Tijdschrift voor Economische en Sociale Geografie
items.abstract: Decarbonising mature industries is crucial for achieving overall carbon neutrality. This article provides an interpath dynamics perspective on how mature industries' decarbonisation paths affect interconnected industries via three key interpath transformation dynamics: interpath dissolution, reconfiguration and formation. Based on 19 semi‐structured interviews with industry representatives in Germany, this article illustrates how the exchange and utilisation of secondary resources in the steel and cement sector change in times of transformation. Findings reveal that individual industries' decarbonisation strategies can be closely interwoven with other regional industries' development paths. From this backdrop, technology change can directly affect existing industrial regional configurations, challenge existing or create novel inter‐industry linkages with variegated outcomes across regions. The concept of interpath dynamics provides a comprehensive perspective to identify challenges and opportunities of decarbonisation processes for industrial regions.

items.title: Simulation Model of a Waste Loop Based on The Closed Loop Logistics Method for Food Waste Management in The Free Nutritious Meal (MBG) Program in Bandung City
items.venue: Journal Research of Social Science Economics and Management
items.abstract: Food waste generated by Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meal (Makan Bergizi Gratis [MBG]) Program presents an environmental and logistical challenge, particularly in urban areas with limited waste-processing capacity. This study aimed to formulate a Waste Loop model based on closed-loop logistics for managing food waste generated by Nutrition Fulfillment Service Units (Satuan Pelayanan Pemenuhan Gizi [SPPGs]) in Bandung City. A qualitative approach supported by empirical measurements and a field perception survey was employed. Organic waste generation was measured over five consecutive working days at three purposively selected SPPGs. Questionnaires were administered to 77 operational personnel, while interviews and observations were conducted to identify workflow processes, infrastructure constraints, and institutional readiness.The three SPPGs generated 940.07 kg of organic waste, with an average generation rate of 188.01 kg per day. Plate waste accounted for 64.92% of total organic waste, while food preparation residues accounted for 35.08%; vegetables represented the largest waste component. Respondents identified limited processing facilities and the absence of reverse logistics procedures as major barriers, despite strong support for circular waste management practices. The resulting causal loop diagram connected organic waste management with black soldier fly larvae bioconversion through two reinforcing pathways: vegetable cultivation using larval residue and poultry production using larval biomass. The proposed model provides a conceptual basis for reducing landfill disposal, recovering resource value, and strengthening circular food supply chain resilience within the MBG Program.

items.title: Water management and the circular economy: a critical analysis of the emergence of a dominant paradigm
items.venue: International Journal of Water Resources Development
items.abstract: The circular economy framework has become a popular paradigm framing interventions in the water sector. The promise is to sustain economic growth while decreasing the water footprint of societies. This paper goes beyond the discursive association between the circular economy and the water cycle that dominates the literature. It unpacks the contradictions that exist when confronting the ‘neat’ principles of the circular economy to the ‘unruliness’ of water flows and practices. We call for the adoption of a grounded approach to assess the scope for the circular economy framework to support sustainable and just water management.

items.title: Cognitive barriers to circular intellectual capital: exploring the role of stakeholder biases and inertia in the textile ecosystem
items.abstract: Purpose This study explores whether and how stakeholders' cognitive biases hinder the development and mobilisation of circular intellectual capital during the transition toward the circular economy (CE). It also explores how psychological barriers shape collaborative dynamics, knowledge sharing, and long-term investment, thereby slowing the adoption of circular practices within a textile ecosystem. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative inductive research design was adopted. Twenty-six semi-structured interviews were conducted with managers from textile firms, associations, and consortia engaged in CE initiatives. Data were analysed using the Gioia methodology to identify recurring cognitive mechanisms that affect stakeholder behaviour and circular decision-making. Findings The analysis reveals that cognitive biases generate self-reinforcing loops of resistance that limit experimentation, inter-organisational collaboration, and investment in long-term circular strategies. Organisational inertia, short-term financial logics, and distorted sustainability narratives lock human and structural capital into linear mindsets, while the externalisation of responsibility erodes relational capital, weakening collective accountability and coordination across the textile ecosystem. Originality/value This paper offers an empirical investigation of the psychological and behavioural dimensions of decision-making in the circular economy. It contributes to the CE literature by conceptualising cognitive biases as key barriers to stakeholder collaboration and by providing actionable recommendations for managers and policymakers to overcome these biases and accelerate circular transitions.

items.title: Transition vers une économie circulaire : une étude de cas longitudinale de gouvernance régionale
items.abstract: Cet article étudie le positionnement dans le processus de transition sociétale d’une Région française chargée de la gouvernance de transition de son territoire vers une économie circulaire (TVEC). Elle fait face à trois paradoxes relevés dans la littérature pluridisciplinaire : imbrication dans un régime qui résiste, pilotage d’une transition imprévisible, et promotion de réseaux auto-organisés émergents. L’étude longitudinale de l’élaboration, avec 150 participants, et du lancement de la mise en œuvre d’un cas de plan Régional de TVEC montre des contournements plutôt que des résolutions de ces paradoxes. Des pistes de recherche sont ouvertes autour de deux spécificités françaises identifiées dans cette gouvernance : la TVEC envisagée comme moteur de développement territorial et l’incompatible conjugaison entre les rôles de décideur-financeur et d’acteur intermédiaire. Il en résulte une invitation aux acteurs de TVEC à se rassembler, dans des arènes distinctes du régime, pour expérimenter en recherche-action une méta-gouvernance de TVEC.

items.title: The role of community developers in facilitating citizen-based monitoring and strengthening public accountability in South Africa's public sector
items.abstract: Citizen-based monitoring (CBM) has emerged as an important mechanism for strengthening public accountability and improving service delivery in developing countries. While existing scholarship has primarily focused on citizens, civil society organisations, and government institutions, it has paid limited attention to the intermediary actors who facilitate monitoring processes at the community level. This study examines the role of community developers in facilitating CBM and strengthening public accountability in South Africa's public sector. Using a qualitative research design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 community developers involved in CBM initiatives. The findings reveal that community developers play critical intermediary roles by mobilising citizen participation, translating governance processes and monitoring frameworks into accessible information, mediating interactions between communities and public institutions, and sustaining monitoring activities over time. However, their effectiveness is constrained by limited institutional support, resource constraints, weak coordination, and inadequate feedback mechanisms. The study contributes to participatory governance and accountability scholarship by demonstrating that effective CBM depends not only on citizen participation but also on intermediary actors who facilitate engagement and connect citizen-generated evidence to decision-making processes. The study recommends formally recognising community developers within CBM frameworks, strengthening institutional support, and institutionalising responsive feedback mechanisms.

items.title: From barriers to bundles: a risk-policy appraisal of alternative marine fuels
items.abstract: The transition to alternative marine fuels is often framed through fuel choice decisions, technical feasibility, or specific policy measures such as pricing, subsidies, standards, and training. Less attention has been given to governance at the port-shipping interface, where fuel availability, bunkering infrastructure, vessel deployment, safety readiness, investment timing, and sufficient demand must align under uncertainty. A comparative governance appraisal is therefore needed to identify which systemic risks warrant priority and which policy responses remain robust across stakeholder perspectives and transition horizons. This study addresses this need through an integrated risk-policy appraisal of the alternative-fuel transition. The analysis combines single-round structured fuzzy expert elicitation, descriptive rating-dispersion analysis, stakeholder-survey triangulation, and selected contextual indicators. Systemic risks are assessed to the year 2040, while policy instruments and 63 functionally feasible policy portfolios are evaluated for 2030 and 2040 under port-oriented and shipowner-oriented conditions. The findings suggest that transition fragility does not stem from a single hurdle but from interacting fuel supply constraints, fuel price volatility, policy instability, safety disruption, stranded asset exposure, and port–fleet misalignment. Under the salience dispersion screening rule, safety disruption and port-fleet misalignment emerge as the clearest relative fragility hotspots. A carbon levy shows the strongest robustness profile among the evaluated individual instruments, but the results do not support a pricing-only approach. Within the evaluated set, the preferred portfolio combines a carbon levy, CAPEX subsidy, standardisation/codes, and training/competence schemes. The study contributes a transparent comparative governance screening framework, linking risk salience, rating dispersion, instrument robustness, and portfolio risk coverage under uncer

items.title: Perumusan Mekanisme Hak Veto untuk Perlindungan Hak Konstitusional Masyarakat Hukum Adat dalam Proyek Strategis Nasional Sektor Pariwisata
items.venue: Jurnal Ilmu Hukum Humaniora dan Politik
items.abstract: Pariwisata telah menjadi salah satu instrumen strategis dalam pembangunan nasional Indonesia, sementara pengembangan Proyek Strategis Nasional sektor pariwisata berpotensi menimbulkan konflik konstitusional yang melibatkan masyarakat hukum adat dan wilayah adatnya. Meskipun kerangka konstitusional Indonesia telah mengakui masyarakat hukum adat beserta hak-hak tradisionalnya, kerangka hukum yang berlaku belum menyediakan mekanisme kelembagaan yang mampu mentransformasikan pengakuan tersebut menjadi perlindungan hukum yang efektif ketika kepentingan masyarakat hukum adat berhadapan dengan proyek pembangunan strategis. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis kelemahan konstitusional dan regulatif dalam perlindungan hak masyarakat hukum adat serta merumuskan mekanisme hak veto sebagai instrumen perlindungan konstitusional dalam pelaksanaan Proyek Strategis Nasional sektor pariwisata. Penelitian ini menggunakan penelitian hukum normatif dengan pendekatan peraturan perundang-undangan, konseptual, kasus, dan perbandingan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa mekanisme partisipasi yang tersedia masih bersifat konsultatif dan prosedural pada umumnya serta belum memberikan konsekuensi hukum yang menentukan terhadap persetujuan masyarakat hukum adat dalam keputusan akhir pemerintah dan keberlanjutan suatu proyek. Penelitian ini merumuskan mekanisme hak veto yang bersifat proporsional, dengan batasan substantif dan prosedural serta jaminan kelembagaan dan pengawasan yudisial. Kebaruan penelitian ini terletak pada perumusan desain kelembagaan yang mentransformasikan pengakuan konstitusional masyarakat hukum adat menjadi mekanisme perlindungan hukum yang dapat ditegakkan dalam pengambilan keputusan pembangunan melalui kerangka ius constituendum.

items.title: Catholic Religious Traditions as Heuristic Resources for Energy Transition: Integrating Material Flow, Desire Formation, and Sustainability Governance
items.abstract: This conceptual and interpretive article asks how historically distinct Catholic religious traditions can illuminate socio-spiritual dimensions of contemporary energy transition and how those insights can be synthesized without treating the traditions as a single movement or as direct policy blueprints. Using comparative historical–theological analysis of selected foundational texts, institutional documents, and historical scholarship, the study examines Benedictine and Cistercian approaches to material organization, Franciscan accounts of poverty and sufficiency, and Dominican and Jesuit resources for normative and adaptive governance. It proposes a Triadic Socio-Spiritual Framework comprising Material Flow, Desire Formation, and System Governance. The framework is an analytical construction rather than a historically observed integrated system. It complements—not replaces—established research on socio-technical transitions, demand-side mitigation, energy justice, and religious agency. The article also distinguishes normative ideals from historical performance, acknowledging tensions involving landholding, commerce, labor, resource use, and institutional power. It concludes that selected Catholic traditions can function as critical heuristic resources when their principles are translated into pluralistic, democratic, and justice-sensitive policy mechanisms rather than transferred as religious disciplines. The framework offers conceptual propositions and scope conditions for subsequent historical and empirical testing.

items.title: Sustainable Resource Cycles and Functional Reproduction of Resilience in Circular Economy Transformation
items.abstract: Background. Despite the development of the circular economy, approaches remain limited to assessing resource flow closure, not covering adaptability, resistance, or the restorability of functions. This highlights the need to study the mechanisms that maintain the continuity of the Functional Reproductive Viability (FRV) of socio-economic systems under poly-crisis conditions and to establish the prerequisites for their long-term viability in the circular economy. Purpose. This study substantiates the concept of the functional reproductive viability of socio-economic systems and develops the Circular Economy Resilience Loop (CERL) model to assess the ability of circular systems to maintain continuity of functioning under poly-crisis conditions. Findings. A conceptual FRV-based approach is proposed to ensure the continuous reproduction of its viability by maintaining, adapting, and reconfiguring resource cycles. A conceptual and analytical CERL model has been developed to reflect the logic of transforming resource circulation into a continuous process of functional resilience reproduction. An integrative methodological approach to assessing the FRV of circular systems is proposed based on six dimensions: resource circularity, functional stability, adaptive flexibility, recovery capacity, resistance to shocks, and resilience potential. Pilot calculations of the integral index of functional reproductive viability for 2021–2024 were performed using publicly available statistical data on resource, production, and adaptive and regenerative characteristics. The results showed a sharp decrease in the value of the integral index IFRV of Ukraine to 0.372–0.377 in 2022 (low viability) with subsequent gradual recovery to 0.475–0.488 in 2023 and 0.515–0.542 in 2024, which confirms the analytical suitability of the proposed methodology for assessing the resilience dynamics of cyclical socio-economic systems amidst a polycrisis. items.title: Closing the loop: digital nomads in coliving spaces and their influence on the urban circular economy in Brazil
items.venue: Journal of Science and Technology Policy Management
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to investigate how international digital nomads and Brazilian professionals working globally remotely, residing in coliving and coworking communities, influence the demand, perceived value and diffusion of circular economy practices in their urban environments. Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design (QUAL→QUANT) was adopted in two Brazilian urban case studies: São Paulo and Florianópolis. The qualitative phase comprised semistructured interviews (n = 22), focus groups with coliving managers (n = 2) and circular business entrepreneurs (n = 2), as well as netnographic analysis. The quantitative phase consisted of a survey (n = 387) with partial least squares structural equation modeling to test eight hypotheses based on the theory of planned behavior and the literature on social norms. Findings Social integration in coliving communities is positively associated with the intention of circular consumption, with the effect fully mediated by descriptive and injunctive procircular norms. Easy access to information about local circular services positively moderates the conversion of intention into actual behavior. Qualitative evidence reveals that the community acts as a curator of sustainable options and that convenience is a critical factor for adherence to circular practices. Originality/value To the best of the author’s knowledge, this is the first study to systematically connect the literatures of digital nomadism and urban circular economy in the context of the Global South, proposing digital nomads as potential agents of socio-ecological transition and coliving communities as diffusion nodes in circular ecosystems.

items.title: GOVERNING INFORMALITY : Eviction, Recognition, and Legal Ambiguity in Kampung Akuarium, Jakarta
items.venue: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
items.abstract: Informal settlements in Jakarta have long been governed through cycles of tolerance, eviction, and selective recognition. Rather than resulting from the absence of planning, informality is often produced through spatial regulations, legal ambiguity, and political intervention. This article examines Kampung Akuarium, a settlement in North Jakarta, to explore how informality is governed through planning instruments and political change. The study combines an overlay analysis of Jakarta's spatial planning documents from 2005, 2014, and 2022 with satellite imagery and a review of news media and policy archives. The findings trace how Kampung Akuarium was alternately erased from planning maps, criminalized through redevelopment agendas, and later partially recognized through state intervention. Eviction under the Basuki Purnama administration functioned as a political assertion of legality rather than a resolution of land‐use conflict. The subsequent shift toward in‐situ redevelopment under the Anies Baswedan administration reconfigured informality into a negotiated condition. Spatial planning documents played a central role in institutionalizing legal ambiguity, enabling flexible governance while sustaining residents’ precarity. The article argues that conflicts over informal settlements are central to remaking urban citizenship, exposing colonial and postcolonial logics of dispossession while opening spaces to renegotiate tenure, design, and belonging through fragile, contested forms of co‐production.

items.title: Evolving motivations for participation in community-based conservation: A relational perspective
items.abstract: Successful outcomes of community-based conservation, both ecological and social, rely on local actors being motivated to engage at the outset of the programme and to sustain their motivation over time. Using semi-structured interviews, we explore the motivations of 22 community Conservation Officers who have participated in marine turtle conservation in Tanzania for more than two decades. We focus on factors that motivated initial participation, as well as those that contributed to sustaining their participation over the past 20 years. Our study reveals the intricate dynamics of motivational processes, including the influence of values, identities, autonomy, agency, and power, which are shaped by relationships between nature, people, and place. With these findings, we challenge dominant assumptions about economic motivations and highlight the risk of over-reliance on monetary incentives to drive participation in community-based conservation.

items.title: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC)‑enabled whole‑building semantic optimisation and query‑driven decision‑support workflow for low‑carbon and circular smart construction
items.abstract: Material choices fixed early in design determine much of a building’s embodied carbon and how much of its material can later be recovered, but the data needed to weigh the two are usually held in separate tools. To bring them together, a deterministic process was implemented that reads Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) data, enumerates whole-building material scenarios, filters them for Pareto dominance, answers controlled semantic queries, and packages the results as prompt text for optional downstream interpretation. One buildingSMART reference IFC model yielded seven valid components, and 150 wall-floor-roof material configurations were evaluated on that basis. Twelve configurations were non-dominated: six low-carbon-oriented configurations, in which timber systems predominate, and six circularity-oriented configurations built on aluminium-roof systems. The same candidates were returned under all five Building Circularity Score (BCS) weighting schemes (12/12 overlap with the equal-weight baseline), and the classification of 0 balanced, 6 low-carbon-oriented, and 6 circularity-oriented scenarios held across nine threshold combinations. In a scenario-based Monte Carlo check, every one of the 12 baseline candidates stayed non-dominated in at least 83.2% of 1000 sampled runs under the stated assumptions. The full 150-configuration case took approximately 0.79 s, of which pairwise Pareto filtering accounted for approximately 0.023 s. Within this single test case, IFC-derived quantities were sufficient for a reproducible environmental ranking, and the outputs are candidate scenarios for prototype-stage decision support, not complete design prescriptions. External validation, additional IFC models, engineering feasibility checks, and deployment beyond the prototype are left to future work.

items.title: Digital technologies and circular economy innovations: evidence from manufacturing firms in Emilia-Romagna and Veneto
items.abstract: This paper investigates the role of firm-level investments in specific digital technologies (DTs) in shaping the propensity to introduce circular economy innovations (CEIs), and on the intensity of CEIs. We further differentiate CEIs according to the core principles of the circular economy, namely, reduction, recycling, and reuse (3R). Moving beyond treating digitalization as a homogeneous aggregate, we apply multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) to firm-level adoption patterns and identify a core bundle of jointly adopted technologies comprising the Internet of Things, Big Data, Cloud Computing, 3D Printing, and Cybersecurity. Firms adopting this bundle exhibit stronger CEI outcomes than those adopting other technologies in isolation, indicating that complementarities among DTs amplify their enabling role. Industrial robotics retains an independent positive effect, whereas artificial intelligence shows no significant association. We further document that the enabling effect of DT on CEI is more pronounced in urban and intermediate regions, while it holds across both high- and low-GHG-emission industries. Our findings remain robust across a range of additional specifications and tests addressing potential endogeneity concerns.

items.title: Corporate Social Resposibility dan Ekonomi Sirkular Untuk Pemberdayaan penyintas TBC di Gresik: Perspektif Maqashid Syariah Jasser Auda
items.venue: Jurnal Asy-Syarikah Jurnal Lembaga Keuangan Ekonomi dan Bisnis Islam
items.abstract: Tuberkulosis (TBC) tidak hanya berdampak pada kesehatan, tetapi juga menurunkan produktivitas dan pendapatan penyintas selama pengobatan. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis penerapan ekonomi sirkular dalam program Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) PT Smelting bersama Human Initiative untuk pemberdayaan ekonomi penyintas TBC di Kabupaten Gresik, meliputi persiapan, pelaksanaan, monitoring dan evaluasi, kendala, serta dampaknya. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif deskriptif melalui wawancara, observasi, dan dokumentasi. Sebanyak 11 informan dipilih secara purposive, terdiri atas satu karyawan PT Smelting, satu karyawan Human Initiative, dua penyintas TBC, empat penerima manfaat, dan tiga warga sekitar. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan penerapan ekonomi sirkular melalui peternakan ayam Elba, pemanfaatan sumber daya lokal, pengolahan limbah ternak menjadi kompos, dan skema buy-back hasil produksi. Berdasarkan keterangan informan, program berkontribusi terhadap tambahan pendapatan, peningkatan akses modal dan pengetahuan, partisipasi ekonomi, serta kemampuan sebagian penerima manfaat melanjutkan usaha secara mandiri. Kendala meliputi keterbatasan lahan, kualitas bibit, pakan, pendampingan teknis, serta koordinasi dan distribusi.
