items.title: The #chatsafe Youth Participation Model: Evaluating Participatory Workshops Involving Young People in the Design of Suicide Prevention Initiatives
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: #chatsafe is a programme aiming to empower young people to communicate safely on social media about self-harm and suicide. This study aimed to assess the feasibility, acceptability, safety, and impact associated with attending a #chatsafe participatory workshop, using the #chatsafe Youth Participation Model. The workshops aimed to educate young people on safe communication practices and gather their insights to inform new #chatsafe social media intervention content. METHODS: Quantitative data were collected in a pre- and post-workshop survey using bespoke items measuring perceived feasibility, acceptability, and safety of the workshops, and self-efficacy in communicating online about suicide. Qualitative data were collected during the workshop (via participant feedback, field notes, audio recordings, and facilitator debriefing notes) and in open-text responses in the post-workshop survey. RESULTS: Nine workshops were held with 107 participants (age M = 19.7 years, SD = 2.7 years). Two thirds (64.5%) reported lifetime suicidal thoughts. Eighty-seven (81.3%) completed both the pre- and post-workshop survey. Feedback was positive, with 94.3% of participants reporting satisfaction with the workshop, 96.5% reported enjoying the workshop, and no adverse events were recorded. There was a significant increase in confidence when communicating online about suicide following participation in a #chatsafe workshop, z = -5.99, p < 0.001. Workshop insights informed two national Australian #chatsafe Instagram campaigns, that reached 950,000 young people and 818,000 young people respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The #chatsafe workshops were highly feasible, acceptable, safe, and led to young people feeling better equipped to communicate safely online about suicide. items.title: Regenerative business models in B Corps: seven multi-level criteria for identification, drivers of transition, and a maturity trajectory
items.abstract: The body of literature on regenerative business models is growing rapidly. Nevertheless, three significant gaps remain unresolved: no operational criteria distinguish regenerative enterprises from sustainable firms; the drivers enabling transition toward regeneration remain poorly understood; and only a few frameworks explain how regenerative practices develop within organizations. Together, these gaps hinder coherent understanding of regenerative enterprises. This research aims to address these gaps through an exploratory qualitative study based on multiple case studies of Italian B Corps. Following a multi-stage selection process, seven B Corps with regenerative characteristics were selected for in-depth analysis. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using an abductive approach and the Gioia methodology. The findings reveal that visionary leadership, organizational culture, and authentic purpose are the most significant drivers of regenerative transition, whereas regulatory and market pressures play a comparatively marginal role. This result diverges from the prevailing assumptions in the circular economy literature. The contribution of the paper is fourfold. First, it adapts the analytical logic of the Multi-Level Perspective (MLP) to the regeneration domain, providing an integrative framework that links individual, organizational, and institutional dimensions. Second, it develops and validates seven multi-level operational criteria distinguishing regenerative enterprises from advanced sustainability-oriented firms. Third, it identifies and organizes the main drivers of regenerative transition within a multilevel framework. Fourth, it introduces regenerative maturity as an emerging evolutionary path inferred from cross-case patterns among pioneering regenerative firms. Finally, the paper outlines several operational guidelines for managers and policymakers seeking to promote systemic regenerative transitions.

items.title: Logistics Processes as Enablers in the Transition to a Circular Economy: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Background: Logistics plays a fundamental role in enabling the Circular Economy (CE), yet existing research has predominantly emphasized reverse logistics (RL) activities, providing limited understanding of how individual logistics processes contribute to different circular strategies. This study examines how logistics processes enable the implementation of R-strategies across supply chains. Methods: Following the PRISMA protocol, a qualitative content analysis was conducted on 116 peer-reviewed studies, classifying the literature according to nine logistics processes and ten R-strategies (R0–R9). Results: The findings show that research is heavily concentrated on Reverse and Circular Logistics, particularly return, collection, repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing, recycling, and value recovery activities. Reuse (R3), Recycle (R8), and Reduce (R2) are the most frequently addressed strategies, whereas Refuse (R0) and Rethink (R1) are comparatively less represented in the reviewed corpus. Conclusions: This review proposes a framework linking logistics processes with R-strategies and highlights the need to extend attention beyond end-of-life recovery toward preventive logistics capable of avoiding waste generation and preserving resource value across product life cycles. The findings should be interpreted in light of the restricted search strategy, which may have excluded studies using alternative terminology for circularity and logistics.

items.title: Circular Economy Regulatory Frameworks as Catalysts for Regional Integration and Sustainable Development in the Andean Community
items.abstract: This study examines the regulatory frameworks for reverse logistics and circular economy in the four countries of the Andean Community: Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. Methodologically, it adopts a mixed descriptive-exploratory approach; it employs content analysis of official sources and a quantitative assessment of compliance indicators, organized into comparative matrices. The official sources come from national legislative repositories, environmental ministries' institutional websites, and regulatory databases in the four countries. The findings highlight a gradient of institutional maturity. Colombia leads with 15 active instruments and full coverage of Extended Producer Responsibility, although it recycles only 16.9% of its municipal waste. Peru is growing rapidly in the area of electronic waste, and Ecuador combines a pioneering constitutional framework with low traceability. Bolivia lags the furthest behind. This research helps demonstrate that an abundance of regulations does not guarantee effective circularity. The results serve to guide regulatory harmonization, the design of verifiable schemes, and regional technical cooperation as pathways to bridge the gap between regulation and results.

items.title: Data governance, business strategy, and sustainability practices: exploratory employee-perception evidence from a single pulp and paper corporate group
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how data governance (DG) contributes to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) integration by strengthening data accountability, the reliability of ESG-related information, and strategic alignment. Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV), it investigates the relationships among DG, Business Strategy (BS), and sustainability practices and principles (SPP) within a single pulp and paper organisation. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a bounded single-organisation employee survey design based on non-probabilistic convenience sampling. Survey data were collected from 103 valid respondents within one pulp and paper corporate group and analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling to examine perceived associations among DG, BS, and SPP. The analysis was complemented by contextual information on the organisation's DG model and its integration with operational excellence to support ESG objectives. Findings Within the studied organisation, the results suggest positive direct and indirect associations among DG, BS, and SPP. The indirect association through BS is statistically significant and consistent with partial mediation, suggesting that BS may play an alignment role between DG and SPP. The findings provide exploratory, context-specific evidence that respondents perceive DG as associated with the organisational embedding of ESG principles when aligned with BS, particularly through the reliability, traceability, and strategic use of ESG-related information. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by its focus on a single industry and cross-sectional design, which may affect generalisability. Future research should explore longitudinal approaches and extend the model to other sectors. items.title: Sustainable Recycling of Excavated Soil Waste into Unfired Bricks: Mechanical and Microstructural Performance
items.abstract: Although soil stabilization has been widely studied, the mechanical behaviour and microstructural characteristics of unfired bricks produced from excavated soil waste have received limited systematic investigation, particularly across soils with different properties and stabilizer combinations. This study investigates the feasibility of producing unfired bricks from four excavated soils using cement, lime, and fly ash stabilization. Mechanical performance was evaluated through unconfined compressive strength tests and supported by microstructural observations. The 28-day UCS reached approximately 0.4–0.6 MPa for silty clay, 1.0–2.0 MPa for silt, and 0.8–1.6 MPa for silty sand when cement was the primary stabilizer. A simplified model was further developed to predict the strength performance based on soil properties and stabilizer composition. The results indicate that stabilization effectiveness strongly depends on soil characteristics, and different stabilizer combinations show different advantages for various soil conditions. Furthermore, life-cycle assessment and economic evaluation demonstrate that the proposed unfired bricks can reduce environmental impacts compared with conventional fired clay bricks by eliminating the high-temperature firing process and utilizing waste soil as a resource. The unfired brick showed a GWP of 332–394 kg CO2-eq/m3, compared with 503–721 kg CO2-eq/m3 for fired clay bricks. This study provides a practical approach for converting excavated soil waste into sustainable construction materials and supports the development of low-carbon and circular construction practices.

items.title: Business Competition and Institutional Regulation in Explaining MSME Sustainability: Evidence from Strategic Resources and Practices
items.venue: Business Innovation Management and Entrepreneurship Journal (BIMANTARA)
items.abstract: Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) play a critical role in economic growth and job creation, yet achieving long-term sustainability remains challenging in increasingly competitive business environments. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Institutional Theory, this study examines the effects of digital marketing, circular economy practices, credit facilities, inclusive partnerships, distribution strategy, pricing strategy, and innovation strategy on business competition and MSME sustainability, with business competition as a mediating variable and institutional regulation as a moderating variable. A quantitative research design using a survey was employed to collect data from 250 MSME owners and managers in East Java, Indonesia. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that circular economy practices, distribution strategy, and pricing strategy significantly affect business competition. Circular economy practices, inclusive partnerships, pricing strategy, and institutional regulation have significant positive effects on MSME sustainability. Business competition has a significant negative effect on MSME sustainability, suggesting that intense competitive pressure may weaken long-term business performance. In contrast, digital marketing, credit facilities, and innovation strategy have no significant effects on either business competition or MSME sustainability, while the moderating effect of institutional regulation on the relationship between business competition and MSME sustainability is not significant. Business competition also does not significantly mediate the relationships between the predictor variables and MSME sustainability. items.title: Pathways to sustainable business model transformation: corporate governance, strategic leadership and business strategy
items.abstract: Purpose In today’s rapidly evolving business environment, firms face increasing pressure to adopt sustainable practices, with the circular economy (CE) model emerging as a transformative pathway toward environmental and economic resilience. This study aims to investigate the role of governance mechanisms, particularly board and chief executive officer (CEO) dynamics, in enhancing CE performance among manufacturing firms in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. In addition, it examines the moderating role of business strategy in the relationship between governance mechanisms and CE performance, with a focus on innovation, resource efficiency and operational sustainability. Design/methodology/approach The analysis uses panel data from 6,929 firm-year observations and applies dynamic panel estimation techniques, including the system generalized method of moments, to assess the effects of governance, leadership and strategy on CE performance. To strengthen causal inference and ensure robustness, this study incorporates lagged variables, two-stage least squares, propensity score matching and generalized least squares. Findings The results show that board interlock, independence, expertise, CEO foreign experience and external roles significantly enhance CE performance, while concentrated ownership and long CEO tenure constrain it. Business strategy acts as both a direct driver of CE adoption and a moderator that amplifies governance and leadership effects. Heterogeneity across industries reveals that governance plays a stronger role in resource-intensive sectors such as energy and chemicals, while consumer-driven sectors such as food and beverages are shaped more by market pressures and regulatory demands. items.title: Operationalizing Circular Hospitality: An Integrative Review and Governance-Ready 5D Management Framework
items.abstract: Circular-economy research in hospitality has expanded from isolated waste-reduction practices to questions of procurement, digital measurement, stakeholder participation, and organizational change. Yet the available evidence remains difficult for hotel managers to convert into a governed investment portfolio: published reviews classify practices and barriers, while implementation decisions require owners, baselines, decision gates, auditable indicators, and feedback routines. An integrative review was therefore conducted to connect circular-hospitality evidence with management and governance mechanisms. The synthesis began from an established bibliometric map of 71 hospitality publications (2018–2024), audited its principal references and claims against publisher and DOI metadata, and incorporated peer-reviewed studies published through August 2026 that materially extended evidence on food systems, furniture and procurement, digital leadership, institutional pressures, and human participation. Sources were coded by operational domain, decision level, actor, information requirement, barrier, and outcome. Four mutually dependent governance functions emerged: strategic direction, knowledge mobilization, process control, and portfolio integration. On this basis, the article develops a five-stage 5D framework—Diagnose, Design, Deploy, Digitize, and Demonstrate—and specifies deliverables, decision gates, responsibilities, and denominator-aligned indicators for each stage. The resulting model shifts circularity from a catalogue of environmental initiatives to a repeatable management system. Its contribution is conceptual and translational rather than causal: it offers a testable architecture for hotel groups, independent properties, and destination partnerships, while identifying where longitudinal validation, common measurement rules, and evidence from emerging economies remain necessary.

items.title: Tersendatnya kebijakan food estate: evaluasi logic model atas kesenjangan implementasi berjenjang
items.abstract: Indonesia's food estate programme has been studied mainly from legal, political-ecological and agronomic perspectives, leaving unexplained where along the policy's causal chain public investment fails to become food security. This study evaluates the food estate policy in Central Kalimantan Province and identifies the points and mechanisms at which the input–activity–output–outcome chain breaks down. A theory-driven qualitative evaluation with a post-positivist stance was applied, using the logic model as the analytical frame. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with purposively selected key informants (provincial and district officials, sub-district heads, extension workers, field supervisors and farmers in Kapuas Regency), field observation and document analysis, and were analysed through open, axial and selective coding with source and method triangulation. The findings reveal a cascading implementation gap. Despite a 2025 budget of IDR 5.1 trillion, only 43 of 156 (27.6%) agricultural machinery units delivered to the province were operational; each extension worker served at least eight farmer groups, twice the ideal ratio; average rice productivity (2–3.5 t/ha) remained below the provincial (3.8 t/ha) and national (5.2 t/ha) averages; the cassava component produced almost nothing; and farm-gate prices exceeded the government purchase price by only 3.9%, a margin eroded by rising production costs. Theoretically, the study introduces the concept of a cascading implementation gap and extends logic-model evaluation into a diagnostic tool by explaining, through implementation and high-modernism theories, why top-down inputs fail to translate into outcomes on fragile peatlands. Practically, it calls for land-suitability-based, participatory and phased intensification instead of massive extensification.

items.title: Towards inclusive age-friendly communities: A scoping review of diversity and representation in global initiatives
items.abstract: While calls for meaningful inclusion of diverse and socially excluded older populations in age-friendly urban planning initiatives have increased, little is known about how these groups are actually involved in shaping such programmes, and what mechanisms are effective in enabling their inclusion. The aim of this article is to present the findings of a scoping review on how effectively age-friendly urban planning includes socially excluded older populations, including the key strategies employed and the challenges and enablers encountered. Searches yielded 10,857 records, and, together with grey literature screening, resulted in Eight studies meeting the inclusion criteria. The review documents a range of participatory approaches, such as co-design workshops, graphic facilitation, advisory panels, peer research and intergenerational collaboration, that aim to involve older adults in meaningful ways. These approaches target promoting trust and empowerment and offer more equitable representation in age-friendly planning. However, despite promising practices, most efforts were limited in scale, short-term in nature and lacked integration into decision-making systems. These initiatives point to the potential of inclusive planning, but with current impacts remaining uneven and limited. We call for more sustained and embedded forms of participation that support rethinking how inclusion is defined, operationalised and structurally supported in age-friendly planning processes.

items.title: The perspectives on space circular economy
items.abstract: The circular economy is gaining momentum among the space community since the rise of the new space era stresses the linearity of the industry. Spacecraft are made, launched, used, left in orbit, as debris, or deorbited, with most of their material dispersed in the atmosphere. It is crucial to understand the reasons why this momentum exists to build adequate answers. The state of the art of the space industry and its challenges determine the core drivers of the space circular economy, which shape its definition and objectives. Several space actors are starting to consider the space circular economy and are building on their own space circular economy perspective. Analyzing those perspectives permits the determination of core principles, objectives, and strategies investigated. They have the potential to build a commonly adopted and used framework necessary to successfully implement a long-term space circular economy. This paper aims to define core drivers for space circular economy from the space industry’s state of the art. Moreover, it investigates the perspectives on space circular economy of different space actors to compare them and extract core strategies. A parallel with circular concepts for Earth application is conducted using the R-strategy framework. The overall objective of this research is to propose a potential, commonly understood, and adopted space circular economy framework.

items.title: From Fragmented Environmental Labels to Integrated Logics and Operational Structures in Community Development
items.abstract: The proliferation of environmental-community labels has expanded the vocabulary of urban environmental discourse while obscuring a more consequential question: do these labels represent distinct environmental models, or differentiated configurations within a shared operational field? This study examines that question and considers whether such a structure can support environmental decision-making beyond predefined label selection. Using a bounded comparative conceptual synthesis of 177 documents, 33 Qualified Approach Scopes were organized into 14 Analytical Approach Groups, examined through 7 Core Operational Components, and related to 4 Environmental Logic Families defined by environmental success criteria. The results reveal differentiated configurations within a shared operational field: approaches recurrently mobilize common operational domains, but neither label identity nor component presence determines a single environmental purpose or achieved outcome. Cross-linked component–purpose relationships further show that the same operational mechanism can serve different environmental ends depending on the mechanism, boundary, and criterion of success. The resulting Integrated Translation Architecture supports purpose-led environmental decision-making by allowing environmental purpose to define the decision entry point before relevant mechanisms and approach configurations are identified. The framework provides analytical traceability rather than ranking, causal validation, or city-specific optimization.

items.title: Public Perceptions of Personal Data Spaces for Citizen-Centered Health Data Governance in Belgium: Cross-Sectional Survey
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Personal Data Spaces (PDSs) are promoted as infrastructures that strengthen citizen participation in health data governance through transparency and individual control. However, empirical evidence on citizens’ views of PDSs remains limited. This study examined how citizens evaluate We Are, a proposed citizen-centered PDS model in Flanders, Belgium, including overall support, preferences for control and transparency, acceptance of different data types and uses, and factors associated with support. Methods: An online survey was conducted among 1041 adults aged 18–79 years in Flanders using quotas for gender, age, education, province, and urbanization. Participants evaluated the We Are model and completed measures concerning reasons for support, control and transparency, storage of medical and lifestyle data, and data sharing across purposes and recipient types. Data were analyzed using t-tests, linear regression, and mixed models with repeated measures. Results: We Are evaluations were ambivalent but slightly positive (M = 2.51 on a 1–4 scale) and did not differ significantly from the scale midpoint. Sociodemographic characteristics explained little variance in support (R2 = 0.033), whereas adding understanding and psychographic factors increased variance to R2 = 0.238. Respondents valued control more than transparency and were more willing to store medical than lifestyle data (Δ = 0.380, p < 0.001). Willingness to share data was higher for both personal and public non-commercial uses than for public commercial uses, whereas personal commercial uses were rated lower. Private recipients were associated with lower willingness to share than public recipients. Conclusions: Support for PDSs was conditional and related more strongly to understanding and psychographic factors than to sociodemographic characteristics. items.title: Metric Selection Framework: A Method for Optimizing Multidimensional Value Assessment of Resource Recovery Systems
items.venue: Annual Review of Environment and Resources
items.abstract: This article introduces the metric selection framework (MSF), developed as part of the CVORR+ methodology. CVORR+ is a systems-based evaluation toolkit designed to support complex sustainability assessment and decision-making. Within CVORR+, the MSF translates system analysis into decision-oriented, multidimensional metrics for monitoring, assessment, and evaluation of progress toward sustainability targets. Grounded in a value-focused decision-making approach, the framework combines expert elicitation with stakeholder engagement to ensure that metrics are system grounded, context specific, and practically relevant. Applied to England's plastic packaging system, the MSF reveals systemic inefficiencies, identifies leverage points for intervention, and informs policy design to support systemic value recovery. The case study demonstrates the heuristic and practical value of the MSF in capturing interdependencies across environmental, economic, social, and technical domains. Future developments will streamline the translation from system conceptualization to metric development, ensuring that metrics are responsive to long-term monitoring and policy-making, remain aligned with technological and regulatory shifts, and enhance the robustness and transferability of CVORR+.

items.title: Circular Economy Financial Performance: Sustainability (ESGUI), and Tourism Uncertainty (TUI)
items.abstract: Although circular economy investments are seen as an important tool for achieving the SDGs, studies that examine the different sources of uncertainty affecting these investments within a nonlinear framework remain limited. The current literature largely focuses only on traditional uncertainty indices such as EPU, GPR, and pandemic‐related uncertainty. This study fills this gap in literature by including, for the first time in the circular economy literature, two newly developed uncertainty indices, the ESG‐related sustainability uncertainty indices (ESGUI) and the Tourism Uncertainty Index (TUI), alongside traditional uncertainty indicators, and examining their associations with circular economy financial performance. In this study, wavelet power spectrum (WPS), wavelet quantile regression (WQR), wavelet quantile‐on‐quantile regression (WQQR), and Baruník–Křehlík frequency‐domain connectedness (BKFSC) methods were used. The findings show that the relationships between uncertainty and circular economy financial performance differ across investment horizons and market regimes. WQQR results show that the relationships between ESGUI and TUI and circular economy financial performance are nonlinear and vary by market regime. Similarly, the relationships between EPU, GPR, PNDMC, the S&P 500, and circular economy financial performance also differ by market conditions. These findings highlight the importance of considering different sources of uncertainty and general market conditions together when evaluating circular economy financial performance.

items.abstract: ABSTRAKKerusakan wilayah pesisir di Indonesia makin parah dikarenakan beragam faktor di antaranya ‎penebangan, reklamasi, maupun pencemaran. Indonesia telah memiliki Undang-Undang (UU) No. ‎‎32 Tahun 2009 tentang Perlindungan dan Pengelolaan Lingkungan Hidup serta UU No. 27 Tahun 2007 ‎terkait Pengelolaan Wilayah Pesisir dan Pulau-Pulau Kecil. Meskipun ada undang-undang, masih ‎banyak kendala untuk mengelola wilayah pesisir dengan melibatkan masyarakat. Studi ini hendak ‎memahami seberapa efektif kebijakan hukum lingkungan dan apa saja yang mendukung atau ‎menghambat pengelolaan wilayah pesisir bersama masyarakat. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode ‎hukum empiris dengan mempelajari kasus dan menganalisis data dari observasi, wawancara, dan ‎dokumen. Data tersebut kemudian dianalisis dengan cara tematik menggunakan bantuan NVivo. ‎Temuan studi memperlihatkan bahwasanya efektivitas kebijakan sangatlah bergantung dari partisipasi ‎masyarakat, kekuatan lembaga lokal, keselarasan hukum formal dengan pranata adat, kemampuan ‎penegakan hukum, serta dukungan ekonomi dari masyarakat. Di sisi lain, tumpang tindih kewenangan, ‎kurangnya koordinasi antarlembaga, tekanan dari investasi, kapasitas masyarakat yang rendah, dan ‎perubahan iklim menjadi beberapa hal yang menghambat efektivitas pengelolaan pesisir. Dari ‎penemuan tersebut, studi merumuskan model integrase hukum-komunitas adaptif. Model ini ‎mengaitkan beberapa hal, yakni regulasi formal, pranata adat, kelembagaan lokal, dan penguatan ‎ekonomi dalam satu kerangka tata kelola. Model ini menempatkan negara tidak hanya sebagai ‎regulator, tetapi juga sebagai fasilitator yang memperkuat kapasitas masyarakat dan mengintegrasikan ‎norma hukum formal dengan hukum yang hidup dalam masyarakat. Model tersebut diharapkan dapat ‎mendukung pengelolaan wilayah pesisir yang lebih partisipatif, adaptif, dan berkelanjutan‎.Kata kunci: hukum lingkungan; kearifan lokal; partisipasi masyarakat; pengelolaan berbasis masyarakat; wilayah pesi

items.title: Developing a maturity model for circular economy transitions: A firm-level artifact grounded in design science
items.abstract: Many firms facing major regulatory, resource, and market challenges are increasingly under pressure to adopt circular economy practices, yet they lack integrated and empirically validated tools to evaluate their circular maturity in a systemic and actionable way. To fill this gap, our study developed the Circular Maturity Tool (CMT), an artifact that assesses firms' circular capabilities and guides capability development across successive stages. Using a design science (DS) approach, we conceptualize circular maturity as a capability comprising interdependent organizational dimensions that the CMT integrates in a staged architecture. Following a full DS cycle, the CMT is grounded in a systematic literature review and 54 interviews, that we then refined through expert-based alpha testing, and subsequently tested in a multi-method beta evaluation. Guided by the Design Science Validity Framework, the evaluation confirmed the CMT's structural integrity and contextual robustness and revealed positive associations between maturity scores and the adoption of circular resource strategies. The study contributes to science by specifying an integrated developmental logic that links organizational dimensions, maturity levels, and operationalized capabilities, and by demonstrating how DS supports rigorous artifact development and evaluation. In practice, the CMT helps firms assess their circular maturity, identify capability gaps, benchmark progress, and prioritize capability development; to date, it has been applied in nearly 3000 assessments across more than 900 firms.

items.title: Increasing Circular Practices to Achieve Competitive and Financial Outcomes Among SMEs in the Sustainability Age
items.abstract: This study assesses the financial sustainability (FS) of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Malaysian context and explores the possibility of the use of CE as a tool to bridge the financial sustainability gap between national sustainability goals and financial realities for SMEs. The paper is based on Circular Economy (CE) theory and is contextualized by Resource Dependency Theory (RDT) and discusses how the processes of environmental scanning (ES), resource recycling (RR) and integration into the circular resource chain (CRC) affect FS, which is mediated by green innovation (GI) and moderated by competitive advantage (CA). In this study, PLS-SEM analysis of 309 manufacturing and service sector SMEs found that ES, RR, and CRC had significant effects on GI, explaining 55.2% of the variance. The results indicate that CA positively moderates the ES → GI relationship, while negatively moderating the RR → GI and CRC → GI relationships. This unanticipated phenomenon is referred to as ‘success-induced rigidity’: the more competitive firms can ease up and invest less in improving their operational circularity. The results confirmed the three moderation hypotheses (H11-H13), including the H11 and H13 negative moderation results. Overall, financial stability, which is positively influenced by green innovation, significantly mediates the relationship between ES and FS and between CRC and FS (H8–H10). The model has good explanatory power and predictive power (R² = 66.6% and Q² = 0.627 for FS). The research is valuable because it treats financial stability as a business outcome for SMEs, covers RDT and CE theory, and treats competitive advantage as a counterintuitive moderating variable. The results show that (in the real world) green innovation is needed in the sector and that some policy support is required to support and facilitate SMEs’ circular transitions.

items.title: Exploring public actors’ beliefs about behavioural change for the mobility transition and their expectations for transdisciplinary collaborations
items.venue: GAIA - Ecological Perspectives for Science and Society
items.abstract: Politics and public administration are key actors when it comes to the implementation of behaviour change policies for sustainable mobility. We explore their beliefs on the matter and their expectations for transdisciplinary cooperations with scientific actors.Policy measures are central to shaping individual mobility behaviour, and a coherent policy approach is essential to advance sustainable transport transitions. While research provides extensive insights into the malleability of mobility behaviour, little is known about what policymakers and administrators know about behaviour change. This study addresses the gap through qualitative interviews with 13 political and administrative actors in Berlin and Brandenburg, combining Sabatier's Advocacy Coalition Framework from 1988 and Michie and colleagues' Behaviour Change Wheel . We explore who public actors view as their allies for the transition, and their expectations for collaboration with scientific actors. Our findings indicate that public actors possess substantial knowledge of behavioural change measures, many of which align with the Behaviour Change Wheel . Yet, their beliefs about mobility behaviour change vary in sophistication, and systematic links between assumptions and interventions are lacking. Public actors tend to view civil society as a key ally. Understanding their specific expectations for cooperation with scientific actors strengthens transdisciplinary research processes.

items.title: Dual exclusion: Mobility poverty and democratic representation in participatory governance
items.venue: GAIA - Ecological Perspectives for Science and Society
items.abstract: Those with the fewest mobility options are often the least heard in decisions about mobility. We call this “dual exclusion”: mobility poverty and democratic underrepresentation are co-constituted and mutually reinforcing, obstructing a sustainable mobility transformation. We show how participation formats can be redesigned to break this cycle.Vulnerable populations often face exclusion from democratic processes in the context of sustainable mobility transformations. We introduce the notion of “dual exclusion” to capture how barriers to political articulation and everyday mobility reinforce each other to obstruct democratic representation in citizen deliberations on mobility policy. Drawing on democratic representation theory and intersectionality, we redefine participatory formats as requiring proactive inclusion. Through qualitative interviews, we explore prevailing representation practices, identify structural limits, and derive design principles for participation formats capable of overcoming dual exclusion. The paper offers practice-oriented recommendations linking participatory governance and democratic theory to disrupt cycles of social exclusion and mobility poverty.

items.title: The sense and sensibility of the circular material use rate: a case study of EU's key circularity indicator
items.abstract: The Circular Material Use Rate (CMUR) has become a flagship indicator for monitoring progress towards a circular economy in the European Union. Promising in its conceptual simplicity, CMUR is widely employed in policy evaluations, international comparisons, and national target-setting. Yet despite its prominence, the indicator has been subject to limited empirical scrutiny. This paper examines the performance and interpretive validity of CMUR through a case study of Iceland, an economy characterized by high levels of imported materials, large-scale aluminum production, high percentage of renewable energy, significant biomass flows, and substantial domestic extraction of rock, sand and gravel. Based on a calculation of Iceland’s CMUR for 2024 and six policy-relevant scenarios—those being transport-related fossil fuel phase-out, increased recycling of household waste, food-waste reduction, material-efficiency measures in cement use, sufficiency scenarios for electronics and textiles, and all measures combined—the analysis shows that CMUR exhibits limited responsiveness to core circular economy interventions in this particular case. In some scenarios, such as food-waste prevention, CMUR decreases when environmental performance improves. The paper identifies one main structural reason for this behavior: the overwhelming dominance of a few inert and/or structurally non-circular materials in domestic consumption. To address this, the paper explores a contextualization of CMUR by modifying the boundary conditions for those materials. The findings highlight the importance of contextual interpretation when CMUR is used to evaluate circular performance and to inform policy. The analysis further suggests that similar interpretive challenges may arise in other European economies with comparable material-flow structures.

items.title: Layers of Time: The Conservation of Cultural Heritage and Architecture
items.abstract: Cultural heritage represents the collective memory of societies, reflecting the values, knowledge, traditions, and experiences that have shaped the built environment over time. Layers of Time: The Conservation of Cultural Heritage and Architecture brings together diverse academic perspectives on the conservation, interpretation, and sustainable management of cultural heritage. The title reflects the multiple historical, cultural, social, and architectural layers embedded in the built environment; understanding these layers requires approaches that move beyond the physical preservation of buildings to consider authenticity, collective memory, cultural identity, social values, and the evolving relationship between heritage and contemporary life. The chapters address a broad range of themes, including architectural conservation, adaptive reuse, the sustainability of historic environments, heritage policies and practices, modern architectural heritage, archaeological sites, contemporary architectural interventions, and the relationship between cultural heritage and urban development. By bringing together theoretical discussions and practice-oriented research, the volume shows that conservation is not simply about preserving what remains of the past, but about recognising cultural significance, negotiating change responsibly, and ensuring that heritage continues to contribute to the lives of present and future generations. It is intended for architects, academics, conservation professionals, students, and policymakers.

items.title: Blind Spots in Circular Economy Data Infrastructure for Sustainable Textile Management: End-of-Life Textile Products in Trade Statistics
items.abstract: Sustainable textile management and circular supply chains depend on shared product classifications that make used products visible. This paper investigates whether the Harmonized System (HS), which underpins trade statistics and the EU textile extended producer responsibility (EPR) scope, can distinguish used textile products from new ones. All 152 headings of HS Section XI, along with five associated headings, are graded on a four-level end-of-life resolution scale based on the HS legal notes. Coverage is measured with 450,872 UN Comtrade records for 2013–2023, using a validated procedure for missing and misreported weights, and Eurostat data for the EU market. Carpets, other made-up articles, and technical textile articles have no used or waste code, so their used forms are declared as new goods. They accounted for 26.5% of finished textile exports in 2023 (bootstrap 95% interval 22.7–35.3%; 20.3–39.7% under alternative boundary definitions) and 29% of the EU market by mass (13% by value), and they lie outside the EU textile EPR scope. These shares locate a classification gap rather than measure unrecorded waste. Removing records without usable weights converts a 37% increase under the recovery headings into a 6% decline. The gap limits the monitoring of reuse, recycling, and used-textile exports, the coverage of EPR financing, and the tracking of Sustainable Development Goal 12. Combined Nomenclature subdivisions, digital product passport data, and transparent treatment of incomplete records could close it and support resource-efficient, accountable textile value chains.

items.title: Purpose, scale and power: expanding the role of community benefits for the energy transition
items.abstract: The energy transition is neither proceeding as rapidly, nor as widely, as required to meet global climate policy goals. Moreover, the energy transition is under pressure due to rising far right political movements which frame the economic shifts required as a threat to livelihoods. One strategy for generating support for renewable energy development has been the distribution of “benefits” by project proponents. In this critical review, we explore the literature on benefit sharing in distinct contexts: energy projects, urban infrastructure and the extractive industry. Reading the literature through a theoretical lens that centres community engagement, power relations and social provisioning economic theory, we argue that prevailing approaches to benefit sharing for the energy transition are too narrow. We propose three changes that constitute a new point of departure for benefit sharing in the energy transition. First, we expand the scale of benefit sharing from project to recognise that the scale of the energy transition impacts not only the immediate and local area but the economy as a whole. This demands that we query not only the scale, but also the objective of benefit sharing. Existing benefit sharing practice often adopts a compensatory aim. We argue instead that the purpose of benefit sharing, should be broad-based, redistributive and prioritise agency for community parties. This reorientation demands that “the community” be actively and consciously constructed, rather than assumed. Finally, community parties must be properly resourced to participate in the process - financially, organisationally and through regulatory structures – to support their bargaining power.

items.title: Circular Economy in the Built Environment: A Systematic Literature Review 2005–2025
items.abstract: The circular economy (CE) offers a viable pathway for advancing sustainable development in the built environment (BE) due to its potential to reduce waste, resource extraction, and environmental impacts. This study conducts a systematic literature review (2005–2025) to examine CE research through a unifying analytical perspective across the micro, meso, and macro levels of the BE and their integration with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It applies a sequential two‐stage design combining science mapping and critical content analysis. Findings show that existing research in the field remains conceptually fragmented across the three levels. CE‐SDG linkages remain generic and rarely operationalised within the BE. Seven cross‐level enabling mechanisms including life‐cycle analysis, circular design strategies, circular business models, circularity assessment, digital technologies, stakeholders collaboration, and integration with the SDGs, emerge as the connective tissue linking levels together. Building on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual framework that operationalises cross‐level linkages to support CE implementation in the BE. The framework offers a diagnostic tool that practitioners and policymakers can use to identify level‐specific characteristics, cross‐level relationships, enabling mechanisms, and remaining gaps. The study contributes to the existing knowledge by providing an integrative approach and recommendations for future CE research, policy, and implementation in the BE.

items.title: Circular Economy, Waste Minimization and Resource Efficiency in Nigeria
items.abstract: Nigeria’s growing waste generation and inefficient resource utilization pose significant challenges to environmental sustainability and economic resilience. This study examines the role of circular economy practices in promoting waste minimization and resource efficiency in Nigeria using a mixed-methods research design. Quantitative data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 398 respondents drawn from manufacturing firms, waste management agencies, and environmental regulatory institutions, while qualitative insights were obtained from semi-structured interviews with 15 key informants across the same sectors. Descriptive statistics and regression analysis were employed to test two hypotheses, complemented by thematic analysis of interview data. The findings reveal that circular economy practices have a significant positive effect on waste minimization (β = 0.621, p < 0.05) and resource efficiency (β = 0.584, p < 0.05). Qualitative evidence further shows that recycling, material reuse, and recovery initiatives reduce landfill disposal, improve material productivity, and lower operational costs, although their effectiveness is constrained by weak policy enforcement, limited financing, and inadequate technical capacity. Anchored on ecological modernization theory and the resource-based view, the study concludes that a transition from linear to circular production systems is essential for achieving sustainable development in Nigeria. The study recommends strengthening regulatory frameworks, investing in circular infrastructure, and integrating informal sector actors to scale circular economy implementation.

items.title: Collective place leadership: lessons from culture
items.abstract: This paper explores the contribution of culture to place leadership. Adopting a relational approach to place, and using placemaking as a theoretical bridge between place and the cultural sector, it analyses three examples which brought local voices into place leadership through cultural policy and practice. The case studies highlight how people shape places from the periphery of formal leadership structures, and demonstrate how developing effective place leadership through cultural practice means nurturing these distributed knowledges and practices. This has significant implications for scholarly understandings of place leadership, and for the ways in which policymakers seek to incorporate local identities and voices within governance practices. The paper concludes that leadership capacity must be seen as constitutive of how place is actively negotiated, if place-based policy initiatives are to truly reflect local context and serve the collective good.

items.title: From centralised artificial intelligence to democratic systems: African Union-aligned pathways for economic justice and the right to development
items.abstract: Four decades after the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development (DRtD), artificial intelligence (AI) is being deployed across Africa’s financial services, digital identity systems, public administration and cross-border trade. Prevailing models of AI governance, however, are highly centralised concentrating data ownership, algorithmic control and economic value in a small number of predominantly external actors. This chapter pursues three objectives. First, it examines how centralised AI governance undermines the right to development (RtD) by weakening democratic accountability, limiting public participation and reinforcing structural inequality. Second, it establishes the RtD, as recognised in the DRtD and article 22 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, as the normative foundation for AI governance in Africa, and clarifies the chapter’s conception of economic justice. Third, it develops an African Union (AU)-aligned framework for democratic AI governance. Drawing on doctrinal analysis of African and international instruments, including Agenda 2063, the AU Digital Transformation Strategy, the AU Continental AI Strategy and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Protocol on Digital Trade, the chapter finds that existing approaches prioritises efficiency and innovation over participation, accountability and distributive justice. It proposes a framework built on participatory algorithmic impact assessments, independent oversight, digital sovereignty and regional harmonisation, and argues that democratic AI governance is a precondition for, rather than an obstacle to, the realisation of the RtD in Africa.

items.title: Community Participation in Environmental Health Improvement: Developing a Sustainable Rural Sanitation Model for Southeastern Nigeria
authors: Phd Rev. Fr. Polycarp Chibueze Nworie
items.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science
items.abstract: Environmental health challenges associated with inadequate sanitation remain significant obstacles to sustainable rural development in Nigeria. Although sanitation interventions have increasingly emphasised community mobilisation, behavioural change and improved access to sanitation facilities, persistent deficiencies suggest that sustainable improvement requires stronger integration of community participation, appropriate infrastructure, institutional responsibility, financing, monitoring and long-term maintenance. This article develops a Community-Integrated Rural Sanitation Model (CIRSM) for rural communities in Southeastern Nigeria, with Ndubia, Ebonyi State, serving as the contextual reference. A qualitative, practice-oriented conceptual design was adopted. Documentary sources were selected for their relevance to community participation, rural sanitation, environmental health, institutional accountability, sanitation infrastructure and sustainability. The materials were examined thematically and synthesised through a staged framework-development process linking identified sanitation problems, stakeholder responsibilities, implementation mechanisms and measurable indicators. CIRSM comprises six interconnected components: participatory sanitation assessment; joint planning and allocation of responsibilities; environmental-health education; appropriate infrastructure and technical support; monitoring and accountability; and periodic review, adaptation and sustainability. Unlike approaches centred predominantly on community triggering and behavioural mobilisation, CIRSM conceptualises sustainable sanitation as a coordinated socio-technical and institutional process in which community ownership operates alongside public investment, professional expertise, equitable financing, infrastructure maintenance and accountable governance. items.title: Infrastructuring Arrival: Envisioning the Migration-Integration Nexus Beyond Crisis
items.abstract: Based on extensive ethnographic research across diverse European contexts, this volume repositions migrants’ arrival not as an exception or a crisis, but as a constitutive condition of contemporary societies. The lively, interactive processes through which newcomers, together with a wide range of actors, rebuild and transform the socio-material settings in which they arrive and carve out their future belonging, are captured in the concept of ‘arrival infrastructuring’. By foregrounding the everyday agency in arrival infrastructuring, this volume proposes a ‘minor integrations’ framework that re-embeds the contested term ‘integration’ within an alternative discourse of world-building, in the process closely attending to the structural forces that limit and channel such agency. The ‘minor’ in ‘minor integrations’ highlights the continuous work of arrival infrastructuring in our contemporary migration societies: the everyday practices of socialising and social reproduction through which future belonging is created, and the urban fabric maintained, repaired and transformed. Infrastructuring Arrival is a companion volume to the Integration Otherwise Inspiration Kit. While the latter offers practical guidance for practitioners, policymakers and community builders, this book develops a deeper conceptual and analytical understanding of arrival infrastructuring.

items.title: Intersectoral Linkages in Kazakhstan’s Energy Sector: A Comparative Leontief Analysis
items.venue: Eurasian Journal of Economic and Business Studies
items.abstract: The intensive utilization of production resources in Kazakhstan’s energy sector and the increase in interdependence between industries make it particularly important to assess the stability and efficiency of the economic system structure. In particular, the coal, petroleum, natural gas and electric power industries constitute the main energy base of the national economy and reflect the interconnection between industries. Therefore, the analysis of intersectoral relationships and structural transformation in the energy sector has become the main direction of modern economic research. In addition, changes in the flow of resources within the energy system directly affect the long-term stability and efficiency of the economy. The purpose of this research is to use a comparative Leontief input-output analysis to examine changes in intersectoral relationships within Kazakhstan’s energy sector and evaluate structural transformations from 2020 to 2024. The methodological basis of this research is a comparative input-output analysis based on the Leontief inter-industry equilibrium framework. This study uses the official statistics of the Republic of Kazakhstan for 2020-2024, including production indicators of the energy sector and intersectoral intermediate consumption data. The analysis is based on a reduced four-sector input-output framework representing the main energy industries of Kazakhstan (coal, oil, natural gas, and electricity), rather than the complete national input-output table. In addition, the intermediate consumption matrix ( Z t ), the technical coefficient matrix ( A t ), the Leontief inverse matrix (( I − A t ) − 1), and backward linkage (BL) and forward linkage (FL) indicators were calculated. The findings reveal that moderate structural adjustments occurred within Kazakhstan’s energy system during 2020-2024. items.title: Assessment of leached heavy metals from construction and demolition waste
items.abstract: Construction and Demolition Waste (CDW) presents significant environmental concerns due to heavy metals leaching into soils and groundwater. This study examines the concentrations and spatial migration patterns of heavy metals leached from CDW at a construction site in Kumasi, Ghana. Samples of CDW and underlying soil were collected and analyzed for heavy metals, including lead (Pb), arsenic (As), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), manganese (Mn), and cadmium (Cd). The study finds that the CDW mainly consists of sand, which helps leachate move easily. Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation and Radial Basis Function (RBF) neural network modeling were used to predict the spread of contaminants vertically and horizontally. Results show that Cu, Zn, and Mn have higher mobility, while Pb and As tend to stay localized. The mobility raises environmental risks such as soil degradation and threats to plant and microbial life. The study recommends regulatory reforms, sustainable construction practices, and chemical stabilization to reduce the environmental impacts of CDW leachates.

items.title: Evaluating Post-Hoc Explainable AI Methods for a Multitask-CNN in Sensor-Based Quality Monitoring of Comminuted Construction and Demolition Waste
items.abstract: There is a lack of comparative XAI evaluations for sensor-based quality monitoring (SBQM) appli-cations in the context of construction and demolition waste (CDW) management. Moreover, such studies are generally oriented towards classification architectures and tasks. To address these gaps, we compared the faithfulness, stability and localization of three common post-hoc XAI evaluation methods, namely Grad-CAM, LIME and SHAP. These post-hoc methods were implemented into a multitask-CNN, i.e. CDW-MT-CNN, containing an identical classification and regression head architecture. No single method excels on all aspects: only Grad-CAM is fast and stable enough for near-real-time monitoring (10 ms/instance) but suffers from its large receptive field limitation, impacting its faithfulness and localization. LIME and SHAP are faithful and localize well but have limited stability and their computational overhead (180–600 ms/instance) renders them unsuitable for the near-real-time application. Further research in the directions of correlation studies between explanation and predictive quality, a detailed sensitivity study of the hyperparameters for LIME and SHAP, explainability evaluations of advanced gradient-based methods that mitigate the large receptive field limitation, and a detailed per-image runtime and energy consumption study on representative recycling plant hardware would further contribute to responsible deployment of XAI in SBQM for CDW management.

items.title: Circularity for Whom? Selective Social Sustainability in the Just Circular Economy
items.abstract: Circularity is often framed as a bridge paradigm supporting sustainability transitions — but a bridge to where, and for whom? Drawing on qualitative analysis of twelve circular bioeconomy business models in Argentina, this Perspective examines their social practices against the five justice dimensions of the just circular economy (JCE). The analysis shows that social sustainability was neither completely absent nor comprehensively incorporated. Concrete achievements in employment, livelihoods, and formal protection coexisted with weaker integration of shared decision-making, territorial knowledge, long-term organisational autonomy, and the distribution of burdens within circular systems. We conceptualise this recurrent but non-uniform pattern as selective social sustainability. The concept explains how organisational, evaluative, and governance arrangements make certain social concerns more visible, actionable, and enduring than others, without presuming deliberate exclusion or a single organisational cause. Its central contribution is to complement the JCE’s normative benchmark with a diagnostic lens for identifying why genuine social advances do not necessarily develop into integrated just circular transitions.

items.title: THE CIRCULAR ECONOMY, A FACTOR OF TERRITORIAL DEVELOPMENT: AN ANALYSIS OF WASTE RECOVERY VALUE CHAINS IN KOUDOUGOU (BURKINA FASO)
items.venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
items.abstract: The circular economy model stands in contrast to the traditional linear model, which is based in part on the systematic disposal of waste in landfill, with its associated environmental impacts. Against a backdrop of dwindling natural resources and environmental crises, the circular economy paradigm is emerging as a catalyst for fostering and driving innovative practices that are environmentally friendly and promote sustainable development. This article aims to analyse the socio-economic opportunities arising from waste recovery in the medium-sized town of Koudougou. The methodology is based on a qualitative approach, combining literature review, direct observations and field surveys. The surveys enabled qualitative data to be collected from 39 stakeholders in the waste value chain between September 2023 and February 2024. The results reveal the emergence of informal waste recovery sectors through salvage, reuse, recycling and composting. Although these circular economy activities generate jobs and contribute to regional development, their potential remains hampered by a lack of regulation and support. Effective involvement by local authorities, through the structuring of these sectors and the training of stakeholders, is essential to ensure the long-term sustainability of this local circular economy.

items.title: Reconfiguring Production, Governance and Territorial Value Creation through Circular Economy: Institutional Pathways for an Ecological and Solidarity-Based Transition
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between the circular economy, ecological transition and solidarity-based development by bringing together contributions from sustainability studies, transition theory, social economy research and environmental governance. The literature shows that circularity cannot be reduced to recycling or resource recovery, since its transformative potential depends on changes in production systems, consumption practices, organizational models, institutions and territorial governance. Particular attention is given to circular business models, community energy, circular cities, cooperatives, social enterprises and just-transition policies. The review indicates that environmental improvements do not automatically generate social inclusion or equitable development. Their contribution depends on ownership structures, participation, employment conditions, distribution of economic value and access to decision-making. Cooperatives, social enterprises and community-based organizations may therefore provide institutional arrangements through which ecological objectives can be combined with territorial value creation and social participation. The paper argues that a solidarity-oriented ecological transition requires coordinated public policies linking resource efficiency with democratic governance, local economic development and distributive justice. Circular economy policies should consequently be assessed through environmental, economic, social and institutional criteria rather than through material-flow indicators alone.

items.title: Barriers to Manufactured Sand Adoption in India’s Construction Industry: a STEEPLE-based Assessment for Advancing Circular Economy and Sustainable Resource Management
Circular Ecosystem‐Orchestrating Leadership: Microfoundations of Ecosystem‐Related Dynamic Capabilities for a Circular Economy Transition
items.abstract: The transition to a circular economy (CE) increasingly depends on circular ecosystems: networks of autonomous yet interdependent actors that must coordinate material, information, and value flows to narrow, slow, and close resource loops. This creates a governance problem: Circularity requires orchestration, yet no single actor can impose coordination hierarchically. Combining an integrative review of peer‐reviewed articles at the intersection of CE, dynamic capabilities (DCs), and leadership research with theory synthesis, we introduce Circular Ecosystem‐Orchestrating Leadership (CEOL): an actor‐level, boundary‐spanning leadership capability that helps convert coordination barriers into governance outputs. We theorize three mechanisms: (1) narrative bridging translates divergent circularity meanings into shared interpretive frames; (2) platform convening creates credible multilateral commitments for coordinated investment; and (3) institutional entrepreneurship produces legitimate rule adaptation across public and private arenas. Each mechanism has a primary pathway to collective sensing, seizing, or reconfiguring respectively, but the mechanisms interact laterally and are recursively reshaped by the collective capabilities they support. Through these governance outputs, CEOL microfounds ecosystem‐level DCs. The framework advances CE leadership research beyond firm‐level adoption, extends DC theory by specifying governance‐mediated microfoundations of collective capabilities, and reframes circular ecosystem governance as a contested, territorially conditioned achievement vulnerable to narrative capture, platform capture or exclusion, and regulatory capture.

items.title: The Built Environment
items.abstract: This chapter summarizes current knowledge on climate-related risks affecting the built environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East (EMME) region to identify possible pathways to address the climate crisis with coordinated action at a regional level. Urban vulnerability stems from a combination of climate exposure, geographic and morphological features, and limited adaptive capacity influenced by social and economic conditions. Rapid urbanization, unplanned development, and rising energy demand exacerbate greenhouse gas emissions, intensifying the region's exposure to climate impacts. The complexity of the built environment that encompasses buildings, infrastructure, and urban systems necessitates localized strategies for climate adaptation. Cities, as economic and innovation hubs, are critical to achieving global goals such as the Paris Agreement and the United Nations 2030 Agenda. However, limited resources often constrain local authorities' ability to implement effective measures. Despite emerging adaptation actions across EMME urban areas, progress remains uneven. High-quality, locally relevant data are urgently needed to inform robust vulnerability assessments and guide sustainable urban transformation. As cities continue to grow – they are projected to host 70 percent of the global population by 2050 – their capacity to respond to climate change will be crucial to safeguarding both regional development and global economic stability.

items.title: Modelling the circular economy–renewable integration nexus: a cross-national empirical analysis of smart-technology adoption, territorial CO₂ emissions, and the material footprint
items.abstract: Climate neutrality relies on two levers usually examined separately: circular-economy (CE) practices and renewable integration. Drawing on ecological modernization theory and the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC), we regress per-capita carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions in 20 European Union member states over 2014–2023 ( N = 200) on the circular material use (CMU) rate and the renewable energy (REN) share, with smart-technology adoption [ST; internet penetration and research and development (R&D) intensity] as a moderator. The pooled ordinary least squares (OLS), two-way fixed-effects (FE), and random-effects models use cluster-robust standard errors and a wild cluster bootstrap. A 1-percentage-point rise in the renewable energy share is associated with approximately 0.9% lower per-capita emissions in the baseline FE model ( p = 0.095) and 0.95% in the moderated model ( p = 0.030; bootstrap p = 0.048). CMU has no significant unconditional association with emissions in the levels models, and income exhibits concave curvature, although the implied EKC turning point lies above the sample maximum. The CMU × ST interaction is positive and significant ( β = 0.0065, p = 0.009; bootstrap p = 0.033) and is robust across all 20 leave-one-country-out subsamples: the circularity–emissions slope becomes less favourable as adoption rises, with the estimated interaction coefficient larger for internet diffusion than for R&D intensity, although the two estimates cannot be statistically distinguished. Because no conditional slope is individually significant, this association is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, a digital-rebound mechanism. For the material footprint outcome, the CMU coefficient is negative, and the interaction changes sign, but neither is significant, so the pattern is specific to production-based CO₂ accounting.

items.title: A Multi-Dimensional Approach to Orange Peel Waste Management in the Circular Economy Perspective
items.abstract: This study develops an integrated circular economy assessment framework for valorizing orange peel waste (OPW), applied to a biocomposite production process for additive manufacturing and comparatively evaluated against anaerobic digestion, incineration, and animal feed pathways. The methodology combines three sequential steps: (i) a Holistic Diagnosis (HD), supported by Systemic Design and META-SWOT/C-DE analyses, to map material and energy flows, stakeholder relations, and territorial dynamics; (ii) a cradle-to-gate Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) to quantify environmental impacts of pelletized biocomposite production; and (iii) a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) integrated with circular economy indicators based on the 9R framework to compare alternative OPW valorization options. Results demonstrate that agricultural waste valorization requires a systemic and multidisciplinary approach, where technological efficiency is integrated with environmental and contextual dimensions. The analysis highlights key leverage points—such as multi-stream waste valorization and renewable energy integration—while identifying structural constraints related to seasonality, biopolymer costs, and scalability. Environmental findings confirm that substituting virgin materials with agri-food residues reduces impacts, particularly by avoiding disposal and lowering resource depletion. Sensitivity analyses further underline the importance of low-carbon electricity mixes and increased OPW incorporation to support decarbonization and long-term circular transition pathways in agro-industrial systems.

items.title: Development of a Mechanism for the Transition of the Regional Economic System to a Circular Economy
items.abstract: Purpose. To provide a statistical justification for differentiated circular economy transition strategies across Russian regions and to develop a mechanism linking the territorial profile of a region to the selection of a management strategy, priority measures, and project selection criteria. Materials and methods. The empirical dataset covers 85 regions of the Russian Federation and includes comparable data for 2021 2023. The study draws on official statistics from the Federal State Statistics Service and the Unified Interdepartmental Information and Statistical System. The A–G typology was constructed before the environmental and energy characteristics were calculated and was used as an external stratification framework. Medians and structural shares were calculated, together with Spearman’s rank and Pearson’s correlation coefficients. Differences in energy-related indexes were tested using the Kruskal–Wallis test and effect-size measures. The methodological framework of the mechanism comprises four components: the integral readiness R, the weakest mandatory block B, the potential effect P, and the data quality D. Unavailable direct indexes of the final use of secondary resources were not replaced with assumed values. Results. The median environmental stress index across the seven types of regional economic systems ranges from 0.365 to 0.562, while median air pollutant emissions from stationary sources ranges from 17.9 to 374.1 kg per capita. Types B and D, comprising 26 of the 85 regions, account for 66.2% of the emissions recorded in the sample and 60.4% of environmental protection expenditure. The correlation of emissions and expenditure is ρ = 0.854 according to Spearman’s coefficient and r = 0.844 according to Pearson’s coefficient; for the specific values ρ = 0.851 (p < 0.001). items.title: Development of a small batch flexible station for packaging waste sorting in circular economy applications
items.abstract: Introduction: Efficient packaging waste sorting is an important requirement for implementing circular economy strategies, yet many automated sorting solutions are designed for large-scale, high-throughput recycling facilities and are not well suited to small-batch industrial environments characterized by limited waste volumes, frequent material changes, and the need for rapid system reconfiguration. Methods: This paper presents the design, implementation, and laboratory validation of a modular collaborative robotic workstation for small-batch packaging waste sorting. The proposed system integrates a collaborative robot, RGB-D vision system, conveyor-based material flow, and a ROS2-based control architecture within a unified perception-decision-manipulation framework. The perception pipeline combines class-agnostic segmentation using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with lightweight MobileNetV2-based classification for material recognition and is extended with optional modules for geometric reasoning and damage assessment. The proposed architecture reduces dependence on task-specific segmentation training and provides semantic information relevant to grasp planning, safety-aware task allocation, and human-robot collaboration. Results: The workstation was validated under controlled laboratory conditions using three representative packaging waste categories: plastic bottles, aluminium cans, and Tetra Pak containers. The SAM + MobileNetV2 perception pipeline achieved an accuracy of 0.93, precision of 0.93, recall of 0.92, and F1-score of 0.92. System-level experiments demonstrated successful integration of RGB-D object localization, conveyor tracking, camera-to-robot coordinate transformation, and robotic pick-and-place execution. In contrast to conventional high-throughput sorting systems, the proposed workstation emphasizes modularity, flexibility, and collaborative operation for small-batch industrial packaging waste streams.
