items.title: From Resource Circulation to Sustainable Value Creation
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationships among circular economy, green innovation and sustainable production systems through a structured review of recent academic contributions. It considers circular economy as a systemic approach to resource circulation, value retention and business-model transformation, while recognizing that circularity cannot be considered equivalent to sustainability without evaluating its environmental, economic and social outcomes. The review further examines green innovation as a mechanism through which firms translate environmental pressures, technological capabilities, organizational resources and institutional incentives into cleaner products, processes and managerial practices. Particular attention is given to the influence of regulation, stakeholder pressure, knowledge management, digitalization and organizational capabilities on environmental innovation and corporate performance. The final part addresses sustainable manufacturing, Industry 4.0 and sustainable supply-chain management, emphasizing the growing convergence between technological modernization, circular production, environmental management and interorganizational coordination. The reviewed literature suggests that sustainable production depends less on isolated environmental practices than on the integration of technological, organizational and institutional mechanisms across product life cycles and supply networks. Digital technologies can strengthen traceability, resource efficiency and circular material flows, but their contribution remains conditional on managerial capabilities, sustainability-oriented operations and appropriate governance arrangements. Overall, the paper highlights the need for integrated production strategies capable of combining circularity, innovation, supply-chain coordination and multidimensional performance measurement

items.title: Additive remanufacturing strategies for increased sustainability and resilience
items.abstract: Additive remanufacturing strategies for increased sustainability and resilience This article explores how advanced additive remanufacturing feedstock can increase sustainable material use and resilience of society. Remanufacturing is considered a primary value retention process when applied to industrial products for economic reasons. This is already established and well known for many automotive parts, mobile phones or ink cartridges, to name a few examples. The traditional definition of remanufacturing is that a product, or part, is returned to like-new, same-as- when-new, or better-than-when-new condition. This can be done through repair, refurbishment, or upgrading. However, remanufacturing can also be considered essential to the circular economy and sustainability (1) since it contributes to reduced resource use and resilience in supply crises.

items.title: Life cycle assessment for disposal of polypropylene food packaging plastic waste
Conclusion
items.abstract: This concluding chapter synthesises the central arguments of the book and positions circular fashion as both a structural necessity and an operational direction for the future of the industry. As environmental pressures, material constraints, technological developments, and European regulatory frameworks continue reshaping fashion, the chapter argues that the industry is entering a broader systemic transition affecting design, production, sourcing, education, and long-term product management. The chapter reframes design as a system-level practice influencing material flows, traceability, durability, repairability, recovery potential, and long term value retention. Circularity is presented not as a single strategy or compliance exercise, but as a broader shift in how responsibility, creativity, and operational decision-making are understood across the fashion system. The conclusion further emphasises that regulation alone cannot transform the industry without implementation, collaboration, education, and organisational adaptation. Ultimately, the chapter positions progress, accountability, and collective direction as essential to reshaping how fashion products are designed, used, valued, and managed over time.

items.title: Constrained Dense Correspondence Graphs for Robust Structure-from-Motion Targeting Endoscopic Videos
items.abstract: Reconstructing complete 3D geometry from monocular clinical endoscopic videos is challenging due to weak texture, repetitive tissue patterns, and severe illumination artifacts. Although emerging dense matching methods exhibit improved resilience to textureless regions, they often produce abundant spurious correspondences across non-overlapping views, which corrupts the correspondence graph and cause structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines to fail. In this work, we propose a framework for the construction of dense correspondence graph that leverages explicit temporal locality, parallax-driven geometric constraints, and loop- closure revisiting to enable reliable SfM for monocular endoscopic videos. Instead of exhaustively connecting all frame pairs, the approach effectively suppresses invalid inter- frame correspondences while preserving essential long-range geometric relations critical for stable reconstruction. Combined with illumination-aware masking and SfM initialization adapted to endoscopy, the proposed framework achieves substantial improvements in registration robustness and reconstruction completeness for both phantom and real clinical datasets.

items.title: MOSM-SLAM: lightweight OSM-aided monocular SLAM via geometric structure association
A Spatiotemporal Consistency-Enhanced Tightly Coupled LiDAR-Visual-Inertial SLAM Method for Complex Degraded Environments
items.abstract: Tightly coupled LiDAR-visual-inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (simultaneous localization and mapping, SLAM) systems are prone to observation distortion, weak state observability, and cumulative drift under weak-texture conditions, dynamic illumination, geometric degradation, multisensor time asynchrony, and long-term operation. To address these issues, we propose a spatiotemporal consistency enhancement method. The method is built upon the sequentially updated Error-State Iterated Kalman Filter (ESIKF) framework of FAST-LIVO2. First, using the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) clock as the unified reference, the LiDAR-IMU and Camera-IMU time offsets are jointly estimated online, and the estimates are fed back to point-cloud motion compensation and image reprojection. Second, through joint parameterization of vignetting, exposure time, and the camera response function, pixel intensity is inversely mapped to scene irradiance, while scale normalization and physical feasibility constraints are introduced to improve the identifiability of photometric parameters. Third, a LiDAR health indicator is established from the spectrum of a scale-normalized Hessian matrix, and direction-selective kinematic virtual observations are introduced under degeneration when motion is in a steady state and the innovation passes the gating threshold. Finally, low-frequency loop-closure constraints are generated using a ring-sector descriptor, rotation-invariant matching, and point-cloud geometric verification, while small-residual gating and progressive correction are adopted to reduce violation of the small-error assumption of ESIKF. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves an overall RMSE of 0.379 m on the self-built visual and geometric degradation datasets; on the building-corridor loop-closure sequence, the average ATE decreases from 0.188 m with FAST-LIVO2 to 0.080 m; and in the unified ablation experiment, the average RMSE of the full system decreases fr

items.title: DESIGNING SUSTAINABLE BUSINESS MODELS FOR RURAL GREEN BIOREFINERIES: VALUE CREATION, STAKEHOLDER INTEGRATION AND BIOMASS VALORISATION
items.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
items.abstract: This article examines the design of sustainable business models for rural green biorefineries, focusing on value creation, stakeholder integration, biomass valorisation and supply-chain configuration. A conceptual framework is developed by combining the Business Model Canvas with sustainable and triple-layer business model perspectives. Four alternative configurations are discussed: centralized, decentralized wet fractionation, on-farm processing and hybrid models. The analysis demonstrates that the suitability of each configuration depends on biomass availability, transport requirements, processing capacity, stakeholder capabilities, market access and territorial conditions. Biomass valorisation and product diversification are identified as important mechanisms for improving resource efficiency, revenue resilience and local value retention. The study also emphasizes the importance of coordinated stakeholder relationships, transparent value distribution and appropriate governance arrangements. The proposed framework provides a basis for assessing and designing context-specific business models that can support rural development and the transition towards a circular bioeconomy.

items.title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning
items.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.

items.title: UpDown-SC: Gravity-Canonicalized Dual-Envelope Scan Context for Indoor LiDAR Place Recognition
items.abstract: LiDAR place recognition is a key front end for loop closure and global relocalization, yet indoor retrieval remains difficult when attitude or sensor mounting height changes between mapping and query sessions. Scan Context stores the maximum height in each polar cell; indoors, broad ceilings can suppress the lower and mid-level geometry that distinguishes adjacent rooms and corridors. We present UpDown-SC, a training-free polar descriptor that first canonicalizes gravity and then represents two complementary surfaces: the upper envelope of lower/middle structures and the lower envelope of overhead structures. Their physical split is estimated once from a cell-balanced map height distribution and reused by every query. A mask-aware, non-uniform two-channel distance retains discriminative lower-level evidence while limiting sensitivity to its cross-session variation, without treating unobserved cells as zero-height measurements. Conventional Scan Context shortlisting and circular yaw alignment are retained, so retrieved hypotheses directly initialize geometric verification. Experiments across repeated indoor sessions, mounting-height changes, mixed outdoor-to-indoor trajectories, and an outdoor transfer sequence show more reliable first-choice retrieval on the indoor and mounting-height-varied sessions. A paired test finds a significant gain over Scan Context on the in-house sessions. UpDown-SC also gives the best or second-best F1max and AUPR under threshold-based acceptance while retaining a lightweight CPU front end. Continuous replay confirms that the retrieved hypotheses support metric prior-map localization. Code and evaluation artifacts: https://github.com/jiejie567/updown-sc.

items.title: Large language model agents in watershed environmental response: a hypothesis-and-theory framework for the cognitive orchestration layer
items.abstract: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

items.title: Online sea-ice mapping for shipborne polar navigation via hybrid feature matching and sliding-window filtering
Return on AI (RoAI): A framework for assessing AI investments in the marketing organization
items.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing as firms increasingly delegate activities and decisions previously performed by marketers to AI systems. As AI assumes a greater role in market-facing decisions, understanding the value firms realize from these investments becomes increasingly important. Building on marketing accountability and resource-based theory, we develop a Return on AI (RoAI) framework that conceptualizes AI investment through the people, processes, and capabilities that enable its deployment and governance. RoAI evaluates incremental benefit while accounting for value retention, evidence durability, and the full costs of deployment over time. The framework identifies a distinctive consequence of delegated judgment, wherein AI can improve current performance while reducing the experiential practice through which marketers develop and maintain the judgment required to evaluate and redirect the AI solution. This mechanism helps explain heterogeneity in AI returns across firms and over time. We develop seven testable predictions and an agenda for research on creating, appropriating, and sustaining value from AI.

items.title: Reactor geometry as a high-dimensional design variable: Representation, evaluation, and closed-loop design
items.abstract: Reactor performance emerges from the coupled effects of kinetics, catalyst properties, operating conditions, transport phenomena, and reactor geometry. Among these factors, geometry is the central spatial design variable because the arrangement of flow paths, heat transfer surfaces, and catalytic interfaces governs how these effects are expressed across the reactor domain. However, design methodologies have long fixed geometry early and optimised it over a narrow parametric range. This contribution argues that an important limitation of current reactor design practice is structural: when geometry is confined to a small set of parameters, evaluated sequentially, and disconnected from manufacturing, the accessible design space is small by construction. The problem is therefore reformulated by treating reactor geometry as a high-dimensional design variable whose representation, evaluation, and physical realisation form three interdependent axes of a geometry-centric framework. Within this formulation, approaches usually treated separately emerge as instances of a common geometry-performance mapping, while additive manufacturing enters directly as a constraint that defines which geometries are physically realisable. The framework is operationalised through explicit integration criteria and applied diagnostically to published reactor design workflows. The analysis shows that the components required for a fully closed design loop are individually operational but have not yet been coupled within a single iterative system in which measurements from fabricated geometries update the geometry generation model itself. The remaining challenges (high-dimensional representation, evaluation cost, data-efficient learning, realised geometry characterisation, and manufacturing loop closure) define a research agenda toward autonomous reactor design capable of exploring architectures beyond conventional parametric families.

items.title: Exact memory requirements for retaining path irreversibility in finite Markov systems
items.abstract: Coarse-graining can preserve a dynamical task while losing the irreversibility of a realized trajectory. We study the additional information that must remain after labeled jumps have been read and discarded, so that the accumulated path log-likelihood ratio can be reconstructed exactly and updated under subsequent inputs. For a fixed product of homogeneous three-state rings with positive rational rates and a uniform stationary initial law, this question reduces to an integer-current coding problem. Given the total jump count m, and no other history-dependent side information, the exact number of required output classes is C_E(m) = |E S_d(m)|, where E is the prime-exponent matrix of the rate ratios and S_d(m) is the reachable current set. If r = rank_Q E, the minimum additional fixed-length code uses r log₂(m+1) + O_E(1) bits. A recursive counter representation attains this leading term. For two rationally independent logarithmic affinities, we construct an exact recursive code for the (m+1)² classes. Established relative-entropy identities place these results within coarse-grained stochastic thermodynamics and separate realized-value retention from preservation of mean dissipation or fluctuation statistics. The bounds concern a conditional representation with a symbolic output; event-count storage, working space, model constants, and physical implementation costs are separate. Exact finite checks support the constructions but do not replace the proofs. This item contains the preprint PDF and a reproducibility archive with manuscript sources, unchanged finite-check code, expected outputs, and verification instructions.

items.title: Interactive Genetic Algorithm for Narrative-Driven VR Scene Layout Optimization
items.venue: Frontiers in artificial intelligence and applications
items.abstract: The integration of large-scale models and intelligent algorithms into virtual reality (VR) visualization of magical realism literature - including intelligent VR film and television production and AIGC-driven VR gaming-has not only redefined the representational paradigms of literary imagery but also sparked significant scholarly discourse on the interplay between technological empowerment and humanistic aesthetics. This study employs the VR scene generation of Not in This Lifetime [1], a science fiction work by the corresponding author, as a research case to develop a comprehensive algorithmic framework that integrates multimodal perception, aesthetic principles, and narrative logic to propose a full-chain framework for VR scene layout generation. This work proposes an interactive genetic algorithm-based optimization method for large-scale 3D building cluster layout as its core innovation. Following the “text-feature-model-layout” pipeline, it analyzes algorithm-driven aesthetic evolution, the tension between technical rationality and artistic expression, and humanistic value retention in immersive scenarios. A multi-objective fitness function integrating visual saliency, aesthetic norms, narrative logic and functional constraints is established. Validated on ten literary scenes, the proposed method exceeds baseline schemes in narrative consistency, aesthetic performance and 3D layout constraint adaptation. It achieves an NFMR of 89.7% (37.58% higher than GA) and a 7.86 aesthetic score, with 30-participant tests confirming its validity in literary immersive visualization. Combined with narrative constraints and dynamic feedback, the system balances computation efficiency and artistic expression, delivering a robust technical paradigm for cross-media adaptation of literature and VR interactive contents.

items.title: The symbiotic loop: Integrating community resilience, carbon negativity, and economic anti-fragility in tourism design
items.abstract: Objective: Tourism destinations face compounding geopolitical, climatic, and market shocks; however, destination management, carbon mitigation, and local economic development are still governed as separate domains. This fragmentation leaves communities exposed and detaches offsets from the visitor activity that causes emissions. This study introduces the Symbiotic Ecosystem View (SEV). This framework treats the destination as a regenerative socio-ecological loop built on four pillars: systemic mutual dependence, symbiotic orchestration, algorithmic co-evolution, and regenerative adaptation. Methodology: A hybrid system dynamics (SD) and agent-based model (ABM) of a coastal island destination archetype, with 80 operator agents and 600 household agents, was stress-tested over 120 months under a 50% arrival collapse, a localized climate event, and a compound shock, against a baseline of isolated operators—analysis combined 1,000 Monte Carlo replications per scenario, a threshold map, and Sobol variance decomposition. Results: Under arrival shock, the SEV configuration limited the loss of community capital to under 3% and recovered within 19 months, whereas the baseline never regained its pre-shock level. Anti-fragility emerged only as a lagged property, visible seven years after the shock, when revenue pooling exceeded a threshold that increased with baseline value retention. In-destination emissions became net-negative within four years, but long-haul aviation remained positive at full boundary. Value/Contribution: The SEV offers a testable and replicable architecture that unites community, carbon, and economic outcomes in one feedback structure. Implications: Destination managers should favor pooled reserves and local capability building over short-horizon recovery targets and state the boundaries of any carbon claim.

items.title: Reducing Systemic Development Risk Through Distributed Technology Adoption
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Modern developing economies face escalating systemic risk due to the structural fragility of centralized, hub‑and‑spoke infrastructure. As the monograph states, “a shock to a single central node triggers catastrophic systemic failure across all interconnected economic sectors”. Empirical network physics show that compromising 8.5% of critical nodes precipitates discontinuous percolation collapse, while centralized grids impose 3.9–4.8% GDP annual outage penalties across regions such as Sub‑Saharan Africa and South Asia. The work demonstrates that distributed mesh architectures—spanning energy, water, agro‑logistics, manufacturing, healthcare, communications, and urban utilities—halt failure contagion, restore services 15× faster after disasters, and deliver stable, low‑cost operations. Islandable solar microgrids maintain 92% power availability during cyclone landfall, compared to total macro‑grid collapse, enabled by Wright’s Law cost deflation in LFP storage and PV modules. Decentralized membrane bioreactors reduce non‑revenue water losses from 48.5% to 4.2%, restoring potable supply within 48 hours after hydrological shocks. Solar cold‑chain hubs cut post‑harvest spoilage from 45% to under 6%, doubling smallholder income and stabilizing food systems under climate and fertilizer shocks. Localized additive manufacturing compresses industrial spare‑part lead times from 16 weeks to under 12 hours, eliminating chokepoint fragility and preserving $18.4B in foreign exchange reserves through domestic value retention. Distributed health systems equipped with point‑of‑care molecular diagnostics restrict epidemic dispersion radiuses by 85%, while solar‑powered clinics preserve 98% of vaccine stocks during grid failures. Urban resilience is achieved through polycentric spatial planning and circular poly‑utility loops, reducing municipal capex by 59%, attenuating extreme heat by 6.4°C, and preserving over 350 labor hours per worker annually under severe wet‑bulb conditions. items.title: The Economics of Development Under Accelerating Technological Change
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: The monograph argues that accelerating global technology deflation—across compute, storage, solar photovoltaics, batteries, AI, and digital infrastructure—is fundamentally rewriting the pathways through which developing economies achieve prosperity. The traditional development ladder, built on labor‑intensive export manufacturing, has collapsed due to premature deindustrialization and the rise of industrial robotics in advanced economies. As the document states, “the traditional industrial escalator is permanently broken… modern low- and middle-income countries are seeing manufacturing employment peak below 14% at incomes under $3,800.” In its place, a new modular, capital‑saving development paradigm is emerging. The text highlights that “modular technological capital delivers immediate economic returns with zero gestation delay,” enabling latecomer nations to bypass the debt‑heavy megaproject model. The monograph identifies four flagship pillars of this new development architecture: Modern Tradable Services & TFP Without Smokestacks Digital services—software, data engineering, remote professional work—are now the fastest‑growing export category for emerging economies, with domestic value retention of 65–85%. AI tools amplify productivity and enable millions of workers to participate directly in global labor markets. Zero‑Marginal‑Cost Clean Energy Systems Solar and wind LCOE deflation allows economies to decouple growth from fossil fuel imports. Distributed microgrids stabilize FX reserves, eliminate blackout‑driven productivity losses, and provide predictable industrial power. Human Capital Acceleration via AI & Adaptive EdTech A 99.8% collapse in AI inference costs enables personalized tutoring at near‑zero marginal cost. Learning velocity increases 3–4×, and vocational training cycles compress from years to months, unlocking rapid workforce modernization. Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) as State Capacity Open‑protocol identity, payments, and data rails reduc

items.title: Separated by Physics: A Permanent Space Settlement Measured Against 1776
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Settlement advocates invoke the American frontier and the New World as precedents for a polity beyond Earth; the 1776 analogy is the strongest form of that claim, and it has not been tested against what it requires. This paper defines seven criteria for a governance rupture (C1-C7) with explicit thresholds, codes 1776, twenty-four comparison cases chosen by a stated rule and the prospective settlement against them from the cited literature, measures the structural preconditions of 1775 against the gate variables of a companion governance model, and traces three continuities: the corporate charter, the information revolution and the Roman legal grammar of property and authority. A permanent settlement beyond cislunar space would be the first polity whose separation from its founding States is set by physics and engineered survival: light time that rules out real-time government from Earth, together with survival dependence on engineered life support (C7). C7 is a definitional criterion chosen to capture that condition, which no terrestrial case can meet by construction; it is not a coding result. The testable claim is that the condition produces a distinct governance pathway, and §11 states the observations that would refute it. Measured against 1776, the reference rupture, such a settlement could reach the same magnitude only by meeting the four general criteria C1-C4 after it exists. items.title: Circular Economy in the Reuse of Electronic Components Recovered from Printed Circuit Board Waste: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Introduction: The growing generation of waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) and the potential value of printed circuit boards (PCBs) reinforce the need for recovery strategies aligned with the circular economy. Methodology: A Systematic Literature Review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020. The search was performed in Google Scholar between 1 and 8 August 2026, considering publications from 2012 to 2025 in Portuguese, Spanish, and English. Fifty records were identified and, after screening, eligibility assessment, and relevance analysis, 25 studies were included and qualitatively synthesized. Results: Thematic analysis showed a predominance of studies on circular economy, urban mining, and the transition to circular models (32%), followed by reverse logistics and WEEE management (20%), PCB material recycling and recovery (16%), and reuse, remanufacturing, and recovery (16%). The remaining studies addressed environmental impacts, management and operational support (12%) and public policy/PNRS (4%). Conclusions: The reviewed literature confirms the potential of WEEE and PCBs as secondary sources of materials and components. The main gap identified was the limited integration of disassembly, characterization, functional testing, classification, and direct component reuse. The development and validation of standardized procedures is therefore recommended.

items.title: Review of Nanotechnology-assisted E Waste Valorisation for Circular Economy Applications: Precious Metal Recovery and E-Plastic Upcycling
items.abstract: The escalating production of electronic waste is a major environmental and resource management problem globally. However, electronic waste is also a source of precious metals and polymeric materials, which can be recovered through circular economy approaches. In this review, recent progress in nanotechnology enabled approaches for electronic waste valorisation, including precious metal recovery and E plastic upcycling, is discussed. The use of magnetic nanoparticles, graphene nanomaterials, metal organic frameworks and nanocatalysts for selective metal extraction is presented, as well as novel methods for transforming E plastics into pyrolytic oils, carbon nanotubes and other high value added materials. It underlines the potential of these technologies to improve resource efficiency, mitigate environmental impacts and contribute to the development of sustainable urban mining. Major challenges such as scalability, economic viability and environmental safety will be discussed, as well as interesting avenues for the future potential integration of green nanotechnology and circular economy principles in sustainable electronic waste management.

items.title: Planning for circular urban metabolism: Intertwining skills and spatial transformation for manufacturing transition in Padua and Venice, Italy
items.abstract: The shift from a linear to a circular economic structure needs a new urban metabolism that minimizes waste and the use of raw materials and energy. However, a city’s potential for circularity is contingent upon its manufacturing path-dependency, both from an economic and spatial perspective. The research looks at two Italian industrial areas—Padua and Venice—and proceeds to investigate the recent dynamics of their manufacturing spatial distribution at the “transect” level scale. Using a mixed-method approach that combines morphological-spatial analysis, urban planning assessment, and quantitative labor and waste data, the study investigates how manufacturing industries contribute to circular transitions and how planning policies can support or hinder this process. Findings show that technological manufacturing, supported by technical skills and green jobs, drives circular performance through waste prevention and recycling. Industrial diversification and firm relatedness further enable symbiotic material flows. However, both cities reveal a persistent misalignment between emerging circular dynamics and existing zoning frameworks. While Padua has begun adopting mixed-use zoning, planning strategies in both areas remain fragmented and reactive. The paper calls for more integrated, circularity-oriented spatial planning that mobilizes skills and proximity as key territorial resources.

items.title: Closing the Loop on Electronic Waste: Circular Economy Strategies for Sustainable E-Waste Management, Resource Recovery, and Hardware Repurposing in the Digital Age
items.abstract: In recent times, technological advancements in ICT have contributed immensely to the increasing production of e-waste, which is regarded as one of the fastest growing waste streams globally. In this chapter, a critical analysis will be provided on how circular economy approaches can be used to ensure sustainable e-waste management through resource recovery, recycling, and hardware repurposing in the digital era. Qualitative inter-disciplinary review of the literature that includes scientific sources, international documents, government policies, and industrial publications on e-waste are associated with health and environmental impacts of e-waste. The chapter will also address some circular economy solutions such as repair, reuse, refurbishment, remanufacturing, and repurposing to prolong the lifespan of e-products, as well as urban mining/resource recovery for recovering valuable secondary raw materials. Furthermore, the chapter will address policy actions that include Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and Right to Repair (R2R).

items.title: Housing-service conditions and urban mining potential of single residential buildings: insights from material stock–flow analysis in the Philippines
items.abstract: Single residential buildings (SRBs) are a major component of housing, yet their material stocks and flows remain insufficiently quantified in data-scarce countries. This study applies a bottom-up dynamic material stock–flow analysis that integrates material intensities derived from construction documents, statistical data, and remote-sensing datasets for the Philippines from 2008 to 2023. Results show that the estimated annual inflows increased from 19 million metric tons (Mt) in 2009 to 34 Mt in 2023, while the estimated outflows increased from 4.7 to 5.6 Mt. Cumulative inflows and outflows reached 383 and 76 Mt, respectively, resulting in approximately 5921 Mt of in-use stock in 2023. In-use stocks were dominated by mineral- and masonry-based materials. Regional indicators also show that housing-service conditions of SRBs are multidimensional, reflecting distinct aspects of material concentration, population, dwelling-scale accumulation, and active occupancy, while stock-based urban mining assessment identified concrete, masonry materials, and metals as priority streams.

From Bioregional Territories to Regenerative Practices: Plant-based Material Application in Lithuania’s Construction Sector
items.abstract: The conversation between project lead and curator Martynas Germanavičius, architect and researcher Eglė Kliučinskaitė, urbanist Paulius Kliučininkas, and material researcher Gabrielė Šimkutė captures their ongoing work at Architektūros fondas.In recent years, as part of the Circular Design Innovation Alliance, they have developed an interest in the application of bio-based materials and methods to architectural practice and how they could contribute to the circular economy.It was explored through the workshop series »Altering Matter« and in the recently published research titled »Decompose to Grow-Towards Regenerative Architecture«.The conversation ref lects the knowledge and experience they have gained through both analytical research and hands-on practice.In particular, with a focus on how regional and territorial dimensions are fundamentally linked to architectural design questions, when working with local materials and practices.Martynas Germanavičius: Looking back at the first two editions of the Altering Matter workshops, we were looking more into materiality aspects.The 2023 edition, titled Urban Materials and Their Trajectories, focused on reuse and urban mining, while the 2024 edition, titled Decompose to Grow, explored the combination of materials from biosphere and technosphere.In the most recent edition in 2025, Altering Matter: towards regenerative practices, the workshop was much more informed by our ongoing research and attempt to define a more systemic methodological design approach, from research and material scouting to hands-on experimentation and building.As this approach was new to us, it was very inspirational to work with experienced colleagues such as Clara Kernreuter from Atelier LUMA, who introduced bioregional mapping methods developed within their practice, From Bioregional Territories to Regenerative Practices A conversation on Plant-based Material Application in Lithuania' s Construction Sector

items.title: THE EL-RAKHAWI THEORY OF SYMBIOTIC URBAN INTELLIGENCE AND REGENERATIVE INDUSTRIAL ECOSYSTEMS From Self-Healing Cities to the Sovereign Cognitive State A Unified Framework Integrating Regenerative Urban Metabolism, Digital Immune Systems, and Living Industrial Twins for the Next Generation of Sustainable Smart Nations
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: The El-Rakhawi Theory of Symbiotic Urban Intelligence and Regenerative Industrial Ecosystems (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23192881) integrates urban metabolism, sovereign digital governance, and precision manufacturing into a unified self-healing national ecosystem. Three pillars: (1) Regenerative Urban Metabolism with genetically engineered Bio-CCUS microorganisms featuring adaptive carbon absorption efficiency, transforming ports into carbon-negative hubs through waste heat valorization and circular water systems; (2) Sovereign Cognitive State Architecture with a Digital Immune System employing predictive AI, quantum-resistant communications, homomorphic encryption, and Federated Learning to ensure absolute industrial data sovereignty while enabling system-wide optimization; (3) Living Industrial Twins synchronized with urban infrastructure via Federated Learning, achieving zero-waste production and demand-responsive energy management. Introduces the Symbiotic Urban-Industrial Resilience Index (SUIRI) and Regenerative ROI metric (>1.0 within 7-10 years) as novel evaluation frameworks. Integrates organically with the El-Rakhawi Corpus on Quantum-Cognitive Convergence, Bio-Silicon Synergy, Cosmic Digital Sovereignty, and Symbiotic Bio-Intelligence. items.title: A Deep Learning and Digital Twin Framework for Automated Crack Detection and Maintenance-Oriented Condition Assessment of Industrial Buildings
items.abstract: The maintenance of industrial buildings is essential to ensure the operability, safety, and efficiency of these facilities, which are key pillars of the industrial sector. Proper maintenance management has a direct impact on productivity and the continuity of operational processes. However, managing the maintenance of these built assets pose significant challenges, particularly in terms of efficiency in inspection, diagnosis, and the planning of corrective and preventive activities, requiring substantial investment to preserve functionality and prevent disruptions. To address these challenges, this paper presents the development of an intelligent system for advanced damage diagnosis in industrial buildings. The system integrates the MIVES multi-criteria decision-making methodology to objectively assess the structural condition of built assets, incorporating complementary technologies: drones for inspection; artificial intelligence (AI) for data analysis and automatic damage detection; extended reality (XR) for the relocalisation of previously captured environments and the spatial positioning of identified damage; and radiance fields (such as 3D Gaussian Splatting) for 3D scene reconstruction and digital twin generation. A prototype workflow for damage detection was developed by training deep-learning algorithms trained on field images of pathologies in industrial built assets and generating digital twins of the facility using photogrammetry techniques and 3D Gaussian Splatting. This workflow supports the detection and visualization of potential pathologies and provides the data necessary for their objective assessment within the MIVES-base condition condition-assessment framework. These developments are integrated into an application that allows managers and asset owners to access and track inspection information through structured damage records, spatial localization, and digital visualization tools that support maintenance planning and decision-making.

items.title: Raw materials and recycling
items.abstract: This chapter explores the central role of raw materials and recycling in achieving sustainable development within the framework of the UN 2030 Agenda, with particular reference to Sustainable Development Goal 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). After introducing the fundamental concepts of primary and secondary raw materials, urban mining, resource efficiency, and circular economy, it analyzes global and European trends in raw material extraction, demand, and consumption. Particular attention is given to critical and strategic raw materials and their relevance for the green and digital transitions and the associated supply risks and policy responses developed at the European level. The chapter addresses waste management and recycling, discussing waste generation patterns, management hierarchies, and regulatory targets, and it then examines the structure of the recycling process, including advanced physical, mechanical, and sensor-based separation technologies. By linking material flows, policy frameworks, and technological solutions, the chapter highlights how recycling and circular strategies represent key enablers for long-term environmental sustainability, economic resilience, and climate neutrality.

items.title: Recovery of Critical Raw Materials from extractive waste supported by AI algorithms within a geodata framework
items.abstract: The European Union’s dependence on extra-EU imports for Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) poses significant risks to strategic industries. Secondary resources, particularly extractive waste from abandoned mining sites, represent an underexploited opportunity to enhance supply security and circular economy objectives. This paper presents the URBES (Urban Mining and Extractive Waste Information System) project, an intelligent platform designed to integrate mineralogical, geochemical, and urban-resource datasets within a geodata framework for the systematic inventory, organisation, and preliminary screening of CRM-bearing secondary deposits in Italy. The datasets are developed in accordance with INSPIRE and M4EU standards and their extension within the mineral resources domain. This framework enables the application of artificial intelligence and machine-learning techniques to support data integration, information retrieval, and the prioritisation of secondary resources for further investigation, in line with the objectives of the Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252), thereby providing a unified information framework for scientific research, environmental management, and policy implementation.

items.title: Calcium looping for post-combustion CO2 capture using sorbents derived from incineration ashes
Heavy Metal Contamination of Coal Mining Tailing Dumps: A Case Study of the Petrila Mining Site, Jiu Valley, Romania
items.abstract: The increasing demand for metals and the depletion of primary mineral resources have led to a growing interest in alternative sources of raw materials. In this context, mining waste deposits are increasingly considered as potential secondary resources within the concept of urban mining and the circular economy. Historical mining activities have generated large quantities of waste rock that can contain significant concentrations of valuable metals. The Petrila mine tailings dump, located in the Jiu Valley coal basin (Hunedoara County, Romania), includes such a deposit, where millions of tons of mining waste have accumulated over decades of mining. The tailings dump occupies an area of approximately 225,201 m² and constitutes an important anthropogenic deposit with potential resource value. The objective of this study was to characterize the chemical composition of residual materials from the tailings dumps of the Petrila mine and to evaluate their potential as secondary resources for metal recovery potential, in urban mining zone. Sampling was carried out at several locations in the tailings heap, at depths of approximately 30 cm , 50 cm and 70 cm, to investigate the distribution of metals within the deposit of tailing dumps. Elemental concentrations were determined using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP - OES). In addition, X - ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis was performed to determine the majority oxide composition of the samples and to support the geochemical characterization of the tailings material. XRF analyses show that the tailings material is dominated by silicate phases, with SiO ₂ concentrations ranging from approximately 42 to 65 wt % and Al₂O₃ concentrations ranging from approximately 15 to 24 wt %. Iron oxides are also significant, with Fe₂O₃ values reaching up to about 17% by weight, while TiO₂ concentrations range between about 1.2 and 2.4% by weight. Urban metabolic performance and spatiotemporal evolution in central Beijing: a community-scale emergy accounting study
items.abstract: Introduction Urban areas are central to resource consumption and carbon emissions, yet community-scale metabolic mechanisms remain underexplored, particularly when green-space ecosystem services are incorporated into emergy accounting. Methods Taking the 305.8 km 2 central area of Beijing as a case and communities as analytical units, this study develops a community-scale emergy accounting framework for 2011, 2014, 2017, and 2020. Green-space carbon sequestration and oxygen release are included as explicit output emergy. Results Emergy per area (EPA) was high and spatially uneven. Emergy per capita (EPP) was higher in 2020 than in 2011 in most communities, and its spatial disparities narrowed. The emergy yield ratio (EYR) remained below 1. The environmental loading ratio (ELR) rose from mostly 3-10 in 2011 to above 10 in many communities by 2020, and the environmental sustainability index (ESI) remained below 1. Within this accounting framework, expanding green space within community boundaries can only marginally improve the direct accounted output emergy and cannot raise ESI above 1; the limiting factor is the renewable fraction of external supporting flows. With only four observation years, these temporal changes cannot be attributed to specific policies as opposed to interannual fluctuations. Discussion Differentiated community governance should prioritize energy-efficiency retrofits and circular economy pilots in low-EYR areas, functional green infrastructure in high-ELR areas, and, more fundamentally, an increase in the renewable fraction of external supporting flows. The study advances community-scale urban metabolism accounting for SDG 11 while highlighting boundary, data, and methodological limitations.

items.title: Unmodified Kraft lignin and humic acids as biowaste-derived sorbents for selective gold and palladium uptake from acidic e-waste leachates
items.abstract: The management of waste electrical and electronic equipment (e-waste) is a major challenge and an opportunity to recover critical raw materials and precious metals from printed circuit boards (PCBs). Herein, we propose unmodified, low-cost biowastes as sustainable sorbents to recover gold and palladium from HCl-based hydrometallurgical PCB leachates. Kraft lignin (KL), a pulp and paper by-product, and humic acids (VV) from municipal compost were selected as representative industrial and urban aromatic waste streams. Metal uptake was investigated across HCl concentrations (0.0001–1 M) and temperatures (25–70 °C) to identify optimal conditions and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Both materials captured and reduced noble metal ions without prior chemical modification, while showing negligible Cu 2+ uptake in model Au-Cu and Pd-Cu systems, with selectivity exceeding 99.9%. FT-IR, TEM and XRD analyses provided evidence of interactions of metal ions with oxygen-containing functional groups and metallic nanocluster formation, particularly Au 0 . The results highlighted the role of pH- and temperature-dependent structural reorganization of biowastes (BWs) in governing metal uptake. These biosorbents were also tested in real, strongly acidic e-waste hydrometallurgical leachates from PCB components and automotive catalytic converters, demonstrating their ability to capture noble metals in complex multimetallic matrices. Furthermore, thermal treatment of the metal-loaded biowastes at 650 °C yielded solid residues containing crystalline metallic gold (Au 0 ) and palladium oxide (PdO), providing a preliminary demonstration of metal recovery without any intermediate chemical elution step. This study provides a proof of concept for integrating biowaste valorisation and precious-metal recovery within a circular-economy framework for urban mining.

items.title: Economic succession: an ecology-informed diagnostic framework for sustainable urban transformation
items.abstract: Cities around the world face the difficult task of transforming their economies to decarbonize, use resources more efficiently, strengthen resilience, and broaden access to opportunity. Yet a transition that progresses in one city may stall in another, and urban economics offers limited practical guidance for explaining why. To address this gap, this Conceptual Analysis develops urban economic succession as a middle-range framework for ordered but non-deterministic change in an urban economy's portfolio of activities. It translates the causal architecture of ecological succession into six economically observable components: opportunity availability, access to potential activities, local capability fit, interactions among activities, historical legacies and feedback, and extra-local connectivity. The framework brings together insights from sectoral transition, urban scaling, relatedness, economic complexity, production networks, and urban metabolism, while distinguishing changes in economic composition from judgments about what counts as sustainable. Five falsifiable propositions and a seven-step diagnostic workflow show how it can identify different barriers to green industrial diversification, circular production, low-carbon buildings, resilience, and other sustainable transformations. The framework does not treat cities as biological ecosystems, assume that urban economies follow a universal sequence, or equate greater internal cycling with greater sustainability. Instead, it offers a comparative research program for identifying recurrent transition pathways, explaining why cities depart from them, and matching interventions to the specific constraints operating in particular city-regions.

items.title: Assessment of adhesion and durability of laminated safety glass made from end-of-life float glass
items.abstract: As part of urban mining initiatives aimed at reducing waste, CO 2 emissions and the extraction of raw materials, the demand for sustainable resource recovery and repurposing of construction materials is growing. With many European buildings due to be renovated to meet current energy standards, recovering insulating glass units (IGUs) presents a valuable opportunity to reclaim significant amounts of glass panes while reducing environmental impact of glass facades. However, the outer surfaces of IGUs are especially exposed to environmental influences, such as weathering and mechanical impacts, which may introduce surface defects or changes to the glass surface composition, such as corrosion. These phenomena may affect the processability and remanufacturing processes. This study evaluates the feasibility of producing laminated safety glass (LSG) from reclaimed insulating glass units (IGUs). First the surface roughness is analyzed to evaluate environmental exposure of the glass surfaces. Next, laminated glass, with a new PVB interlayer, is manufactured using two configurations of the glass surfaces, primarily with the reclaimed glass, to determine the effect of natural aging, positioning, and combinations on its adhesion performance tested under temperature and humidity conditions in accordance with EN ISO 12543-4, as well as under mechanical loads in the pummel tests. Comparative tests are also conducted with LSG made entirely from new glass. The results demonstrate the possibility of producing standard-compliant LSG from reclaimed float glass.

items.title: METABOLISMO URBANO Y MATERIALES EN LA CONSTRUCCIÓN DE VIVIENDA: Un estudio en tres ciudades intermedias de Colombia
items.venue: Seminario Internacional de Investigación en Urbanismo (SIIU)
items.abstract: Housing construction is one of the main activities generating environmental impacts, due to the high consumption of materials and CO2 emissions. This study analyzes the urban metabolism in three intermediate Colombian cities, evaluating the flows of materials most used in construction and their environmental effects. It is hypothesized that it is possible to identify patterns in the use of materials to optimize their management and mitigate negative impacts. The study considered the period 2015–2020 and selected urban expansion areas through cartographic analysis and specific criteria. The dwellings were classified according to the homogeneity of their materials and structural complexity. A census was conducted in homogeneous dwellings and an adapted ecological sampling in heterogeneous ones. Through field visits, apparent materials and their sources of origin were identified, complemented with Life Cycle Analysis to evaluate CO2 emissions. The results show that reinforced concrete, fired brick and glass predominate in construction, varying according to the type of housing. These findings allow us to formulate strategies to reduce impacts and promote urban sustainability.

items.title: The value of impurity. The second life of WEEE-derived yttrium in the pharmaceutical industry
items.abstract: Among the strategic raw materials supporting today's digital and energy transition, rare earth elements (REE) pose increasing geopolitical and industrial-economic challenges. Urban mining offers a promising alternative, although the high energy costs associated with recycling remain a significant obstacle. This paper investigates the technical feasibility and economic viability of processes for obtaining secondary materials of lower purity. As an illustrative case study, we analysed the recovery of triflate-yttrium from a mixture of e-waste containing yttrium oxide at varying concentrations; the resulting material can be used in pharmaceutical applications. The study evaluates the economic efficiency and recycling effectiveness, achieving medium-to-high purities under economically viable conditions. These results demonstrate that the tested method can support circular processes in the e-waste chain at lower costs than market prices for high-purity raw material oxides used in the pharmaceutical sector, making the production of secondary raw materials preferable to the production of virgin raw materials derived from extraction processes with high environmental and social impact on the territories.

items.title: Environmental sensing-based assessment of trees outside forests and land use and land cover change patterns in the Bundelkhand agroforestry landscape
items.abstract: This study assesses land use and land cover (LULC) dynamics and Trees Outside Forests (TOF) in Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh, within the semi-arid Bundelkhand landscape. The study addresses the need to distinguish tree resources occurring outside officially defined forest areas from conventional LULC classes and to examine their spatial significance for land management. Landsat imagery was used to produce LULC maps for 2015, 2020 and 2025 using supervised Maximum Likelihood Classification (MLC), while high-resolution canopy-height data were used to derive total tree cover. A one-hectare circular neighbourhood and a 10% canopy-density threshold were then used to identify forest areas according to the operational framework applied from the Forest Survey of India (FSI), and TOF was estimated as tree cover outside that forest mask. The reported LULC results show an increase in agricultural area from 2,351.29 km² (47%) excluding the drought fallow land (1440 sq km) in 2015 to 3,776.26 km² (74%) in 2020, followed by 3,704.66 km² (72%) in 2025, while open forest declined from 1,383.43 km² (27%) to 417.97 km² (8%). The Forest & tree-cover assessment estimated 203,969 ha (40.34%) of tree cover, of which 63,697 ha (12.60%) met the applied forest-density criterion and 140,272 ha (27.74%) were classified as TOF. These findings indicate that a substantial share of mapped tree cover occurs outside the FSI-defined forest category. The combined LULC and TOF framework provides a spatial basis for agroforestry planning and sustainable land management, while the limitations of MLC, the canopy-height threshold, and the available validation information should be considered when interpreting the estimates.

items.title: Unlocking the Selective Extraction and Direct Reduction of Gold From E‐Waste Leachate Through Robust Bismuth‐Based Metal–Organic Frameworks
items.abstract: The rapid increase in electronic waste (e‐waste) and the growing demand for rare metals underline the urgent need for effective technologies to recover valuable elements such as gold from waste, a process known as urban mining. However, the development of sustainable and cost‐effective adsorbents with high capacity and selectivity remains challenging. Here, two novel bioinspired bismuth metal–organic frameworks using the edible polyphenolic ellagic and gallic acids as building blocks, namely, bismuth‐ellagate (Bi‐EA) and bismuth‐gallate (Bi‐GA), are synthesized to evaluate for gold extraction from various matrices, including river water, seawater, and leaching solutions from computer central processing units (CPUs). Both chemically stable bismuth‐based metal–organic frameworks (bioMOFs) exhibit an ultrahigh adsorption capacity (2989.9 mg/g for Bi‐EA and 2516.3 mg/g for Bi‐GA), with high Au 3+ removal efficiency (> 99%) within 10 min, high selectivity, and recyclability. The excellent gold recovery performance is attributed to the adsorption‐reduction mechanism resulting from the phenolic hydroxyl groups in these frameworks. This work provides a sustainable and cost‐effective method for gold recovery with superior efficiency and environmental compatibility compared to existing technologies, thus contributing to the sustainable management of gold resources.

items.title: Biotechnological Advances in Biorecovery of Precious Metals from Electronic Scraps
EVALUATING THE ROLE OF URBAN DESIGN TOOLS IN ENHANCING ENERGY EFFICIENCY IN HIGH-DENSITY URBAN DEVELOPMENTS: INSIGHTS FROM LAGOS METROPOLIS
items.venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Earth Science
items.abstract: Urbanisation in Lagos Metropolis has increased the rate of creating high-density urban centres, thus aggravating energy demands and environmental pressures. It is in this paper that we have evaluated how urban design tools can help to reduce energy use in high-density developments in Lagos. With the Compact City Theory, Sustainable Urban Development Theory, Urban Metabolism Theory and Climate-Responsive Urban Design Theory, we used a descriptive and analytic design and preferred quantitative approaches in a mixed-method approach. The data were collected in the form of structured questionnaires filled by 384 participants, with the supplement of the information by the direct observation and GIS-based spatial analysis of the three purposely chosen high-density districts, Victoria Island, Ikeja GRA, and Surulere. The results demonstrate that mixed-use development, compact-city ideologies, passive design approaches, the street orientation, and green infrastructure have a positive effect on energy efficiency. Victoria Island was a study that proved to be a model region that has been able to adopt design tools more than Surulere and Ikeja GRA, especially using green infrastructure and orientational planning. The results of statistical analyses showed strong, positive correlations between the urban design features and the lower energy consumption, which were supported by the results of spatial overlays, which display favourable morphological patterns. The paper concludes that energy efficiency in Lagos can be significantly enhanced by imposing energy-conscious urban design tools in planning policies and development guidelines. We would, therefore, suggest changes to the regulatory framework, the imposition of the design standards and the enhancement of the capacity-building programmes of urban planners and architects. The results are relevant to evidence-based urban planning and the sustainable development strategy of tropical megacities.

items.title: Rethinking sustainable urban planning in the Global South: six paradigm shifts for the next decade
items.abstract: Cities across the Global South are entering a decisive decade for sustainable development.Rapid urbanization and intensifying climate change are placing growing pressure on urban sustainability, increasing environmental risks while challenging cities' social, economic, and infrastructural systems (Almulhim & Cobbinah, 2026;UN-Habitat, 2024). These pressures are unfolding alongside widening socio-spatial inequalities, infrastructure and resource constraints, and profound technological and economic change, with climate impacts often falling disproportionately on vulnerable and marginalized urban populations (UN-Habitat, 2024).Climate-induced migration adds another layer of complexity, as environmental stress can accelerate rural-to-urban mobility, placing additional pressure on infrastructure, services, and informal and peri-urban development in receiving cities (Almulhim et al., 2024). These pressures do not occur independently. They interact within increasingly complex urban systems, where decisions about land use, housing, mobility, infrastructure, ecosystems, and public services can generate consequences far beyond the sectors in which they originate. The significance of these interactions also extends beyond city boundaries, as urban growth increasingly shapes land cover, hydrological systems, climate, biogeochemical processes, and habitats at broader scales (Espey et al., 2024).Although the term Global South encompasses highly diverse urban contexts and should not imply a single development trajectory, the nature and intensity of urban challenges vary considerably across regions, from rapid urban expansion and informality to housing pressures, climate vulnerability, displacement, and resource scarcity (United Nations, 2026). Nevertheless, many cities across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East face a common challenge: the pace and complexity of urban change increasingly exceed the capacity of conventional planning institutions and instruments to resp

items.title: Contextualizing a process information approach in material passports: a case on modelling circular façade product requirements
items.abstract: Information gaps are a key challenge in transitioning to a circular economy, particularly beyond the first use of building products. Material passports could bridge these information gaps by acting as shared information repositories across actors and product stages. However, current material passport research primarily defines product-centric information requirements addressing the here and now, while process-related information to enable future reuse remains less examined. This research developed a stepwise method to identify contextual process information requirements. The method combined a canvas linking process, organizational and information dimensions from the end of use to next use with process modelling. The canvas was tested in a workshop that produced a window maintenance contract case, which was translated into a BPMN process model to derive its information requirements. Their analysis confirmed that across literature and regulations, process information is largely overlooked, a gap that widens towards next use. Overlooked requirements concern capabilities, sequencing dependencies, actors’ roles and agreements. The results suggest material passports should shift from accumulating perishable product descriptions towards sustaining circular models. The maintenance contract case illustrates how service agreements could initiate this shift and keep material passports updated, while the method offers practitioners a way to design circular model adoption.

items.title: Machine-Readable Material Passports for Photopolymer Products: Composition Boundaries, Process History and End of Life
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Digital product and material passports are moving from conceptual circular-economy tools toward operational lifecycle information systems. For photopolymer products, a useful passport must represent more than product identity: it must preserve formulation boundaries, print and post-cure history, service-relevant state changes, repair or recoating events, and end-of-life constraints. This review proposes a machine-readable passport architecture that separates public, controlled and confidential information while retaining provenance. It emphasises state transitions and uncertainty, because a printed photopolymer component can no longer be described adequately by the identity of the original liquid resin alone. items.title: Automation readiness of material passports in construction: Passport-centred systematic review of lifecycle information infrastructures
Integrating BIM and material passports to foster circularity in offsite construction: a five-layer digital framework
items.venue: International Journal of Building Pathology and Adaptation
items.abstract: Purpose Circular economy (CE) integration in offsite construction (OSC) is increasingly recognised as a pathway to reduce waste, carbon emissions and inefficient material practices. However, the digital mechanisms required to operationalise circularity across design, construction and reuse phases in OSC remain fragmented and underdeveloped. Design/methodology/approach This study develops a five-layer digital integration framework that aligns building information modelling (BIM) with material passports (MPs) to support circular workflows. Drawing on a systematic literature review (SLR) of 40 peer-reviewed studies, the framework comprises: (1) Data Input Layer, (2) BIM Platform Layer, (3) Integration Layer, (4) Lifecycle Feedback Layer and (5) Circular Decision Support Layer. Findings The synthesis layer identifies key digital bottlenecks across the five layers, including missing CE metadata, poor interoperability and a lack of lifecycle feedback loops. By embedding circular material intelligence within BIM environments, the framework offers a scalable roadmap for traceability, reuse planning and CE-driven decision-making in OSC. Practical implications The framework provides industry stakeholders with a scalable roadmap to enable material traceability, reuse planning and circular decision-making across the OSC lifecycle. It supports practical alignment with emerging CE policies and market incentives. Originality/value This study contributes a theoretically grounded framework and practical recommendations for advancing digital circular construction. It lays the groundwork for future digital tool development and policy alignment to supports CE adoption in the built environment.
