items.title: Fear in the city: a systematic integrative review of gender, crime, and urban space with Colombo as a case lens
items.abstract: Fear of crime is a persistent urban concern with significant implications for women's mobility, perceived safety, and spatial autonomy. This study presents a systematic integrative review examining how gender norms, urban environments, sociocultural expectations, media narratives, and institutional conditions shape gendered experiences of fear across diverse urban contexts, with Colombo, Sri Lanka, used as an interpretive case lens. The review integrates a 25-source corpus comprising empirical, theoretical, methodological, and contextual literature, with PRISMA 2020 used to structure and report the systematic identification and screening process. Thematic synthesis identified interconnected patterns involving gendered social regulation, perceived vulnerability, spatial restriction, media-mediated fear, institutional responses, community resilience, and intersectional inequalities. The findings indicate that fear of crime cannot be understood solely as an individual psychological reaction to perceived victimization risk; rather, it is mediated through interactions among sociocultural expectations, environmental conditions, institutional arrangements, and social position. Building on these findings, the article develops the Gendered Spatial Autonomy Model (GSAM), an integrative framework linking gendered interpretations of vulnerability and risk to emotional fear, precautionary and avoidance behaviours, and negotiated or restricted spatial autonomy. Colombo is employed as a theoretically relevant case lens through which the transferability and contextual implications of the international evidence are considered. The review contributes to feminist criminology and urban safety scholarship by reframing fear of crime as both an affective experience and a mechanism through which access to urban space may become socially differentiated.

items.title: The material flow analysis model REMIND-MFA: Global demand scenarios and circular flows for plastics, steel, and cement
items.abstract: Plastics, steel, and cement production are responsible for roughly one-fifth of global greenhouse gas emissions, and demand for these materials is rising rapidly. Low-emission production technologies remain costly, resource-constrained, and slow to scale. Circular economy measures are needed to reduce virgin material production. Robust demand modeling is a prerequisite for assessing both supply-side mitigation and demand-side circular economy strategies. We present REMIND-MFA, a global, top-down, economy-wide, stock-driven, prospective material flow analysis model for plastics, steel, and cement. We publish it here as a fourfold contribution of methods, open-source code, results, and a comprehensive data set of prospective stocks and flows. To our knowledge, it is the first material flow analysis which combines all of these characteristics while covering all three materials at country-level resolution. The main methodological innovations and distinguishing contributions are: a three-step stock extrapolation algorithm that derives consistent regional demand scenarios directly from gross domestic product and population trajectories of the shared socioeconomic pathways with minimal regional assumptions; a trade extrapolation method accounting for shifting patterns; recent historical data through at least 2022, capturing the globally significant peaks in China’s steel and cement demand and the onset of their decline; and a modular, automated codebase built for coupling with models like the integrated assessment model REMIND. We show baseline and illustrative circular economy scenario results, displaying strong demand growth under current policies and the potential for circularity to reduce virgin production.

items.title: Impact of Government Demolition on Masses' Buildings in Jalingo Metropolis, Taraba State
items.venue: JOURNAL OF PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION AND SOCIAL WELFARE RESEARCH
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of government demolition exercises on non-human agents (houses and shops) in Jalingo, Taraba State, analysing their structural, economic, and urban planning implications. Anchored in Urban Displacement Theory and Structural Functionalism, the study investigates the consequences of demolitions on urban stability, local businesses, and alternative planning strategies. A descriptive qualitative research design was employed, utilizing purposive random sampling to select demolished structures. Data collection involved observation, satellite imagery, GIS mapping, and policy document analysis, while thematic and comparative analyses were used for data interpretation. Findings reveal that demolitions weaken adjacent buildings, disrupt businesses, and increase economic hardship, with affected traders facing financial instability due to forced relocations. The study concludes that phased redevelopment and compensation-based relocation strategies can mitigate these negative impacts. Recommendations include structural impact assessments, alternative business relocation schemes, and participatory urban planning. This study contributes to knowledge by highlighting the long-term consequences of urban demolitions and proposing sustainable planning solutions to balance development with economic stability.

items.title: FROM CIRCULAR ECONOMY INITIATIVES TO CONSERVATION OUTCOMES: A CRITICAL REVIEW AND MULTILEVEL GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK FOR RESOURCE, WASTE, AND BIODIVERSITY TRANSITIONS
items.venue: Bulletin of Engineering Science Technology and Industry
items.abstract: Circular-economy policy has expanded rapidly, yet its practical success is still commonly judged through recycling, investment, or project counts rather than verified reductions in resource pressure and ecological harm. This critical review updates the governance-oriented analysis of circular-economy initiatives in Andalusia with 32 recent Scopus-indexed records spanning regional policy, manufacturing, consumption, tourism, agri-food systems, infrastructure, finance, social enterprise, and waste management. A structured narrative synthesis was used to compare problem definitions, causal mechanisms, methods, outcomes, and transferability. The evidence shows that circular transition is strongest when five functions operate together: binding direction, coordinated delivery, demand-side participation, finance and infrastructure, and transparent outcome monitoring. Policy fragmentation, weak targets, limited data comparability, and the marginal treatment of biodiversity remain persistent constraints. Firm-level studies identify management commitment, reverse logistics, skills, technology, and customer demand as important enablers, but frequently stop at organizational performance. Regional studies reveal that normative pressure, absorptive capacity, and public-private investment shape adoption, although ecological additionality is rarely tested. We therefore propose a multilevel conservation-governance framework that connects circular inputs and practices to intermediate changes in material flows and then to climate, pollution, habitat, and distributional outcomes. The framework distinguishes process indicators from outcome and safeguard indicators, preventing recycling gains from being mistaken for absolute sustainability. It also embeds spatial differentiation, social inclusion, rebound-risk assessment, and adaptive monitoring. The review concludes that circular economy can support conservation only when it reduces primary extraction and residual waste in absolute term

items.title: Beyond compliance: the role of urban design guidelines in shaping development outcomes in Tokyo
items.abstract: This study examines how urban design guidelines relate to project-level development outcomes in Tokyo’s Otemachi–Marunouchi–Yurakucho district. It analyzes 33 redevelopment projects (51 buildings), comparing streetscape-oriented and open space network-oriented areas from the perspectives of urban functions and urban spaces. The findings show that development outcomes are shaped through interactions among statutory planning tools, urban design guidelines, market conditions, and project-level decisions, with differences between the two spatial typologies. The study also examines beyond-compliance development and contributes to urban design governance research by positioning urban design guidelines as official non-binding guidance mediating between statutory planning conditions and project-level design decisions.

items.title: Putting Place at the Heart of Growth:How Evidence Can Make Multi-Level Governance Work
items.venue: University of Birmingham Research Portal (University of Birmingham)
items.abstract: Output summary (short paragraph to describe the output): On 27 September 2026, the Labour Party Conference fringe event, Putting Place at the Heart of Growth: How Evidence Can Make Multilevel Governance Work, brought together policymakers, researchers, local government leaders, universities, colleges and organisations working across communities and regions. Provocation Before the event, attendees were sent a provocation. The provocation argued that successful devolution and economic growth require more than transferring powers and funding from central government to places. Drawing on evidence from the LPIP Hub and City-REDI, it highlighted the importance of building local capability, institutional capacity, and long-term governance arrangements alongside fiscal devolution. The document emphasised that strong relationships, effective funding systems, robust business case development, and sustained policy commitment are essential to reducing regional inequalities and unlocking growth across the UK. It concluded with recommendations to prioritise capability-building, invest in local governance capacity, reform Whitehall practices, and provide stable, long-term support for place-based development. (You can download the provocation below.) items.title: Demountable and Relocatable Steel Hotel Buildings for the Haramain Central Areas: Structural Performance of a Standardised 18-Storey Module and Design Guidelines for Reuse
items.abstract: This paper examines hotels and commercial buildings around the two Holy Mosques of Makkah and Madinah, which must be demolished in 10–20 years to make room for mosque precinct expansions, even though their reinforced-concrete (RC) frames are designed for 50 years or more. Instead of the current build–demolish–rebuild practice, the proposal is a set of identical, fully demountable steel buildings that can be unbolted, moved, and re-erected on a new site when a precinct is cleared. A reference module (18 storeys and 63.2 m above a permanent RC basement “dock”, on a 3 × 4 grid of 8 m bays) is derived from the stock of recent central-area hotels and analysed in COMSOL Multiphysics as a three-dimensional beam finite-element model with floor diaphragms, S355 sections and bolted connections, under gravity, SBC 301 wind and equivalent-lateral-force seismic actions and in free vibration. It is found that the bare moment-resisting frame satisfies the strength (utilisation 0.80) and seismic drift (0.0076) requirements but not the wind serviceability limit (inter-storey drift 1/209 > 1/400). Demountable CHS X-bracing in the two end bays of each long face reduces the roof sway under wind from 209 mm to 83 mm and the governing drift to 1/654. Over 60 years with three occupations, building once and relocating twice requires about one-third of the structural embodied carbon (195 against 570 kgCO₂e/m²) and about 55% of the structural cost of the RC practice. Design guidelines covering standardisation, the RC dock interface, connection detailing, tolerances, transport and inspection before reuse are formulated for the engineers and authorities involved in the development of the Haramain central areas.

items.title: Immigrant Political Integration in Times of Permanent Crisis: A Multi-Level Governance Perspective from Italy
items.abstract: This article investigates immigrant political integration in Italy through the lens of Multi-Level Governance (MLG), examining whether a framework so far applied mainly to socio-economic integration and refugee reception also illuminates the political dimension, and how its core dynamics unfold there. Building on three concepts associated with MLG in immigrant integration studies – the local turn, governance decoupling, and battleground – the article examines how these unfold when the focus shifts from service provision and social inclusion to political participation and representation, drawing on national policy analysis and a case study of immigrant consultative bodies in the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna, focusing on the city of Parma. The findings confirm the relevance of the local turn and governance decoupling, but in a more pronounced form than in socio-economic integration, whereas the battleground dimension proves the most distinctively reshaped in this policy field, mobilizing a partially different constellation of actors and introducing stronger internal fragmentation within immigrant constituencies. The analysis reveals a broader weakening of immigrant councils in Italy – marked by declining activity, a shift from elected to appointed membership, and persistent ambiguity over their representative mandate – as institutional retrenchment unfolds within a broader process of “permanent crisis” (crisification). The article contributes to MLG theory by exposing distinctive governance dynamics challenging representation, legitimacy, and voice under conditions of weak institutional consolidation.

items.title: COASTAL DISASTER EVACUATION ASSESSMENT IN THE COASTAL MPA SETTING OF PARIAMAN CITY, INDONESIA: INTEGRATING PTVA-3, GIS NETWORK ANALYSIS, AND MARINE–COASTAL ACTIVITY NODES
items.abstract: Pariaman City is the second coastal municipality in West Sumatra Province, Indonesia, after Padang City.Geographically, Pariaman City is fronted by a chain of small offshore islands facing the Indian Ocean, namely Angso Duo, Kasiak, Tangah, Ujung, and Gosong Sibarat, which are part of the marine protected area (MPA) and support conservation, navigation, and coastal tourism.This study assesses evacuation accessibility, Vertical Evacuation Shelter (VES) suitability, Tsunami Evacuation Route (TER) connectivity, and Final Evacuation Site (FES) availability in Pariaman City using the Papathoma Tsunami Vulnerability Assessment Version 3 (PTVA-3) and Geographic Information System (GIS)-based network analysis.40 existing buildings were assessed as candidate VES, and 28 horizontal evacuation routes were inventoried.Most candidate buildings were classified as having low to medium vulnerability, indicating that several public facilities may support vertical or temporary evacuation.North Pariaman has 7 existing FES, 8 feasible VES, and 15 TER.Central Pariaman has 36 FES and 14 feasible VES, but no TER was identified.South Pariaman has 7 FES, 3 feasible VES, and 1 TER.Evacuation distances range from 233 m to 2,155 m, with estimated travel times between 3 and 35 minutes, while only 6 of 22 route cases fall within the 541 m walking-distance threshold.Overall, effective evacuation planning in Pariaman City must integrate route connectivity, travel time, and shelter suitability with MPA management, particularly through the arrangement of conservation zones, evacuation infrastructure, and coastal tourism spaces.The assessment further indicates that evacuation planning must be connected to the real-life conditions of coastal communities and to activities occurring around the city's uninhabited small offshore islands, because warning response, shelter access, route choice, and evacuation timing are shaped by daily mobility.

items.title: Challenges in Daytime Outdoor Glare Evaluation Within the Built Environment: A Review
items.abstract: Direct sunlight and reflections from buildings and ground surfaces create multi-source highlights in high-density built environments, potentially affecting outdoor visual safety and spatial use. This integrative review synthesizes daytime outdoor glare research in terms of physical characteristics, observer effects, and assessment methods. Solar movement, surface reflection, spatial obstruction, and observer movement jointly alter the intensity, direction, scale, and number of bright regions. Outdoor glare is therefore high-luminance, multi-source, non-uniform, and time-varying, occurring as concentrated, continuous-area, and discrete-patch highlights. Evidence indicates that outdoor glare causes visual discomfort, impairs target recognition, and may induce immediate behavioral adjustments. However, studies focus mainly on static viewpoints, short-term perception, and driving tasks, with limited direct observation of spatial-use outcomes such as dwell time, detouring, and location choice. Current assessments identify potential exposure through geometric-path analysis or quantify glare stimuli using established indices and extended models. Some metrics support relative comparisons within specific settings but cannot simultaneously characterize spatial reachability, stimulus intensity, dynamic exposure, and observer responses. Future research should develop hierarchical, type-specific dynamic assessment methods based on glare source, spatial scale, and visual task to inform building-envelope design, material selection, and outdoor glare-risk control.

Modelling Social and Environmental Determinants of Urban Housing in Developing Countries: A Delphi Approach
items.abstract: Urban housing development is an outcome of several predictors ranging from finance, governance, land tenure security, and social and environmental factors, among others. However, despite scholars acknowledging their importance, social and environmental dimensions remain inadequately conceptualised within the housing development agenda from a developing country's perspective, as evidenced by socially and environmentally constrained human settlements. Using Zambia as a case study, this research models social and environmental determinants of urban housing development. Methodologically, a Delphi approach was employed, with data collected over two iterative rounds from a panel of ten experts drawn from the Ministry of Local Government, non-governmental organisations, financial institutions, property developers, housing institutions, and academia. Twelve environmental and thirteen social attributes were evaluated, achieving strong second-round consensus (interquartile deviation ≤ 1) on most items. Findings reveal that promoting culturally reflective designs, linking housing to broader urban fabrics, sustainable policies, and local building materials will yield viable housing solutions for communities. The study recommends mandatory, enforceable eco-friendly and socially adaptive housing regulations, guiding policymakers on prioritising environmental and social attributes to advance climate-responsive, socially cohesive, well-linked human settlements that promote economic inclusion.

items.title: Road material stock and circularity potential in growing cities: the case of Singapore
items.abstract: In dense and land-constrained cities, road infrastructure systems may transition from expansion-led growth towards a greater reliance on maintenance, with implications for material demand and circularity. Using Singapore as an illustrative case, this study applies a bottom-up material flow analysis to quantify material stocks and flows in the urban road network from 1990 to 2022. Total road material stock increased from approximately 37.2 Mt in 1990 to 50.6 Mt in 2022. Granite aggregate accounted for the largest share of this stock, with smaller contributions from bitumen and steel slag aggregate. Although net stock growth was primarily associated with recorded road-network expansion, maintenance generated a persistent annual material demand through wearing course renewal. The cohort-based maintenance model estimates that 615 lane-km required resurfacing in 2022, generating 0.214 Mt of removed asphalt. Under the baseline assumption, 98% of this material was recovered as reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP). However, the use of RAP was constrained by the maximum incorporation limits applied to wearing- and base-course asphalt demand, indicating that high recovery does not necessarily result in high internal reuse. Road material stock per capita is approximately 9 t/cap in 2022, reflecting Singapore’s compact urban form and intensive use of shared infrastructure. Material efficiency declined from approximately 460 to 423 vehicle-kilometres per tonne between 2012 and 2022. The findings offer transferable insights for other high-density cities facing limited scope for network expansion, underscoring the need to shift policy attention from supporting infrastructure growth towards extending asset lifetimes, optimising renewal cycles, and improving material circularity in existing road networks.

items.title: Urban heat as a structural development challenge in rapidly growing cities
items.abstract: Urban heat is increasingly emerging as a major constraint on sustainable development, particularly in rapidly growing cities of the Global South. Although urban heat is commonly addressed through local adaptation and urban heat reduction measures such as urban greening, cool and super cool roofs, and building retrofits or passive design, these interventions are increasingly implemented against a backdrop of accelerating planetary warming, fiscal constraints, and persistent socio-economic inequalities. This Essay argues that urban heat should be understood not merely as an environmental, technological, or urban planning challenge, but as a structural development problem arising from the interaction of climate change, rapid urbanization, uneven governance capacity, and political-economic processes that shape vulnerability and adaptive capacity. Drawing on evidence from urban climate, adaptation, development, and climate justice literatures, we examine how escalating heat risks intersect with infrastructure deficits, debt burdens, limited access to climate finance, and unequal access to cooling resources across rapidly growing cities. We show that climate change mitigation and local action, including urban heat reduction and broader adaptation measures, perform distinct but complementary functions, and that local interventions alone cannot overcome the broader climatic and structural conditions that increasingly constrain their effectiveness and scalability. Urban heat risks are further amplified by profound inequalities in exposure, vulnerability, and access to adaptation resources, creating a widening mismatch between those facing the greatest heat burdens and those possessing the greatest capacity to respond. We, therefore, argue that effective urban heat governance requires moving beyond predominantly local and technocratic approaches toward integrated strategies that combine climate change mitigation, equitable climate finance, enhanced fiscal capacity, and multi-

items.title: Delphi method-derived homogeneous nursing protocol for children with vasovagal syncope in national regional medical centers
items.abstract: Background To construct a scientific and feasible homogeneous nursing protocol for children with vasovagal syncope (VVS) - a standardized, evidence-based nursing protocol adaptable across different healthcare settings-providing an evidence-based tool for the standardization and homogenization of pediatric syncope nursing globally. Methods A three-step approach of “literature analysis-Delphi expert consultation - pre-test” was adopted to develop the protocol: systematic retrieval of evidence from 7 core domestic and international databases (from inception to October 2024); two rounds of Delphi consultation with 15 multidisciplinary experts from pediatrics, nursing, cardiology and emergency medicine to optimize items; and a pre-test involving 10 children to verify feasibility. Results The final homogeneous nursing protocol consisted of 7 level1 items, 32 level2 items, and 7 level3 items. The effective recovery rate of both rounds of expert consultation was 100%, the expert authority coefficient was 0.85 for each round, the coefficient of variation (CV) for item importance scores ranged from 0 to 0.15, and the Kendall’s harmony coefficients were 0.349 and 0.213 respectively ( P < 0.001), indicating good coordination and reliability of expert opinions. After the pre-test, unified criteria for indicator assessment were established through specialized training, and nursing documentation consistency (measured by inter-rater agreement) reached 95%, significantly improving the protocol’s operability. Conclusions Based on evidence-based nursing and expert consensus, the protocol is scientific, rigorous, and hierarchically clear. It provides a scientifically-grounded, hierarchical framework adaptable to varying resource levels, supporting standardized nursing care for children with VVS across national regional medical centers. It can provide a standardized nursing paradigm for medical institutions at different levels of medical resource availability, facilitating the construct

items.title: An integrative review on the development of health literate organizations
items.abstract: To analyze and synthesize scientific evidence on structured actions and institutional practices aimed at promoting organizational health literacy within healthcare organizations. This is an integrative literature review conducted across eight international and regional databases. Studies describing planned or implemented actions to promote organizational health literacy were included. The selection process followed predefined eligibility criteria, with screening by title, abstract, and full-text review. Data analysis focused on identifying implemented strategies, attributes of health literate organizations, and barriers and facilitators to implementation, based on established theoretical frameworks. Twenty-two studies published between 2014 and 2022 were included, predominantly conducted in Europe and the United States. Identified actions were grouped into four main thematic axes: institutional diagnostic assessment; adaptation and simplification of communication materials and processes; workforce training and capacity building; and user and community involvement, often through co-design approaches. The studies addressed the ten attributes of health-literate organizations to varying degrees, with greater emphasis on clear communication, facilitated access to services, and leadership engagement. The most frequently reported barriers were limited leadership buy-in and insufficient resources, each identified in 11 studies (50%), followed by time constraints, reported in 9 studies (40.9%). The findings indicate that organizational health literacy should be understood as a systemic and integrated approach rather than isolated interventions. The identified actions show potential to foster health literate organizations, provided they are supported by committed leadership, internal policies, and continuous evaluation and training processes.

items.title: Accelerating transport decarbonization through second-generation biofuels in Australia: A DSIT-informed statistical forecasting and scenario modelling framework
Exploring the Validity of the RISE ‐ UP Framework for Sustainability Education in Super‐Diverse Urban Schools: A Delphi Approach
items.abstract: Despite many frameworks for sustainability education (SE) developed over the past two decades, and the specific call for contextual anchoring, none address its implementation in the distinctive context of super‐diverse urban environments. Yet the complexity and diversity of urban contexts demand tailored approaches. Urban schools offer unique opportunities for SE, where diverse perspectives on sustainability meet context‐specific challenges. This study offers a conceptual validation of a recent framework, developed for secondary education, combining key elements of SE and urban education (UE). It was validated by 23 international experts across research, policy, and practice. Using a three‐round Delphi study, experts assessed the framework's relevance, clarity, completeness, and specificity. The majority agreed on its relevance, addressing a recognised need, and the potential to support SE in urban settings. While the four building blocks of the framework namely—competences; effective teaching strategies; community engagement; and school culture—were retained, experts proposed several refinements to enhance its clarity, completeness, specificity, and usability. These included clarifying the urban context, incorporating pupils' intercultural competences, and merging parental and local community engagement. The refined framework represents one of the first frameworks of sustainability education contextualised for super‐diverse urban secondary schools, offering a validated conceptual foundation for implementation.

items.title: A Systems-Based Framework For Evaluating Circular Resource Flows In Sustainable Urban Infrastructure Development
items.venue: Journal of Smart Infrastructure and Environmental Sustainability
items.abstract: The pace of urbanisation has brought with it an increased demand for resources, waste production and environmental degradation, and its issues call for circular resource management of urban infrastructure. This study introduces a systems-based conceptual framework for assessing circular resource flows using Material Flow Analysis (MFA), systems thinking, sustainability assessment and resource efficiency evaluation. It integrates a comprehensive material, water, energy and waste stream analysis to measure the circularity of a product and to pinpoint opportunities for recovery and reuse. A composite sustainability assessment is used to determine resource efficiency, the circularity rate, environmental performance and infrastructure resilience. This proposed framework had a resource efficiency of 84.6%, circularity rate of 71.8%, water reuse efficiency of 66.4%, carbon emission reduction of 29.7%, and an overall Composite Sustainability Index of 0.87, which were significantly better than that of conventional linear infrastructure systems. The results of the study suggest that Circular Resource Management (CRRM) based on a systems approach can increase the environmental performance and long-term infrastructure function. The proposed framework offers a work-in-progress decision support tool for planners and policy makers to encourage resilient, resource efficient and sustainable urban infrastructure development.

items.title: Building a work–life balance framework for allied health professionals: Key stakeholder perspectives via e-Delphi
items.venue: Focus on Health Professional Education A Multi-Professional Journal
items.abstract: Background: Allied health professionals face increasing workforce pressures, with work–life balance recognised as a key determinant of wellbeing, job satisfaction and workforce retention. While professional development is central to sustaining the allied health workforce, there is limited evidence to guide the design of work–life balance training. This study aimed to develop a consensus-driven set of learning objectives to inform work–life balance training for Australian allied health professionals. Methods and procedures: A three-round e-Delphi study was conducted with members of an Australian allied health professional training needs analysis network. Round 1 explored perceived challenges to work–life balance and priority areas for training. In Round 2, participants grouped items into domains and proposed draft learning objectives. Round 3 sought consensus on the final work–life balance training framework. Outcomes and results: Sixty-four participants contributed across the three rounds (Round 1: n = 19; Round 2: n = 27; Round 3: n = 18). In Round 1, consensus was achieved for 40% of identified work–life balance challenges, 43% of important work–life balance components and 60% of proposed training components. These findings informed a draft framework presented in Round 2, where agreement was reached on four domains and 22 learning objectives, with 13 (59%) achieving consensus with domain alignment. Final endorsement in Round 3 resulted in a framework comprising four domains: collaborative communication and relationships, workload and workforce management, personal wellbeing and resilience, and supportive leadership and culture, with 22 learning objectives, including 19 core objectives and three flexible objectives spanning multiple domains. Conclusion and implications: This study developed a consensus-based framework to support work–life balance training for allied health professionals. Strong agreement across four domains highlights shared priorities related to e

items.title: Adapting Global Sustainability Indicators to Local Contexts: A Framework Expansion for Urban Residential Buildings in Pakistan
items.venue: Journal of Urban Planning and Development
items.abstract: Sustainable residential construction plays a vital role in reducing environmental impact. However, achieving sustainability in housing remains a challenge, because many structures in developing countries like Pakistan lack certification and adherence to established standards. While various frameworks exist, they often lack comprehensiveness, and the adoption of Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) in Pakistan is limited due to resource constraints and strict compliance requirements. This study assesses the sustainability performance of 104 residential buildings in Peshawar, a major city in Pakistan, using both LEED v4.1 and a local framework. A questionnaire-based survey revealed that the local framework achieved a higher efficiency score (74%) compared with LEED (52.65%), highlighting gaps in environmental, economic, and governance indicators. Sixteen underutilized LEED indicators, absent in over 40% of residential buildings, were identified, along with five additional indicators commonly present but missing from the local framework. These indicators were evaluated using the Delphi technique and the Likert scale to assess their feasibility and local impact. As a result, the local framework was expanded from 54 to 75 indicators, significantly improving its comprehensiveness. This enhanced framework can facilitate the transition to sustainable cities by aligning global best practices with local requirements.

items.title: Construction Logistics Optimization for Complex Urban Development and Infrastructure Projects Under Saudi Vision 2030
items.abstract: The importance of construction logistics in the delivery of dense urban developments, linear infrastructure, and the range of giga-projects outlined in Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 has been growing, since in these cases compressed timeframes, limited site areas, the need to import materials, the extreme climate conditions, and the fact that several projects are going on at the same time result in a number of closely linked logistics risks. This review gathers together evidence from peer-reviewed sources on urban construction logistics, construction supply-chain management, consolidation centres, Building Information Modelling (BIM), digital twins, off-site construction, resilience, transport decarbonisation and circular flows. The present paper employs an integrative review approach in order to compare different mechanisms, rather than combining incompatible effect sizes. The evidence shows that logistics performance improves as we move upstream from site expediting to coordinated demand planning, time-slot control, consolidation, visualised 4D logistics and data-led exception management. However, no single technology overcomes the problem of fragmented incentives: consolidation may shift costs between the various parties involved, internet platforms require a high degree of data discipline and interoperability, and just-in-time strategies may reduce storage but at the same time raise vulnerability to unreliable transport. The most credible optimisation model for achieving the objectives of Saudi Vision 2030 is therefore a multi-level system which includes common performance indicators covering strategic network design, tactical procurement and consolidation, and operational dispatch. The paper suggests a framework that is sensitive to the particular context and which focuses on logistics governance, digital visibility, resilient sourcing, low-emission transport, and reverse logistics. The areas that demand further research include freight data specific to Saudi Arabi

items.title: MOVING TOWARD ROBOT FRIENDLY CITIES: A FIVE-DIMENSIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR URBAN PLANNING AND DESIGN
items.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence, autonomous navigation, sensing, and robotics are accelerating the deployment of autonomous robots in streets, buildings, and public spaces. Yet existing research remains fragmented across robotics, human–robot interaction, architecture, engineering, and policy, leaving an integrated urban planning framework for human–robot coexistence underdeveloped. This study conceptualizes the Robot-Friendly City as an urban environment capable of accommodating autonomous robots while supporting safe, inclusive, and responsible coexistence with humans. Through a systematic literature review and thematic analysis, the study identifies and synthesizes key considerations for integrating autonomous robots into urban environments. The analysis identifies five interdependent dimensions: (1) physical and spatial environment, (2) environmental sustainability, (3) digital and technological environment, (4) social and human–robot interaction, and (5) governance and institutional arrangements. Together, these dimensions provide an integrated framework for understanding the urban conditions and design considerations associated with human–robot coexistence. By shifting the focus from adapting individual robots to existing environments toward considering how urban environments should accommodate robots, this study positions robotic integration as a multidimensional urban planning challenge and provides a conceptual foundation for future planning strategies and urban design guidelines for Robot-Friendly Cities.

items.title: Linking Smart City Strategies, Urban Brand Identity, and Territorial Attractiveness: An Integrative Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Smart city strategies are increasingly used not only to improve urban services but also to shape intercity positioning, place reputation, and territorial attractiveness. However, the mechanisms through which digital and governance capabilities become credible and socially recognized urban brand assets remain insufficiently specified. This review develops an integrative conceptual framework linking smart city capability portfolios, stakeholder-experienced urban value, institutional urban brand identity, symbolic capital, territorial attractiveness, and durable urban competitiveness. A structured narrative review and concept-centric framework-building design synthesizes 77 substantive scientific and institutional sources; three additional methodological references support the review design. The revised framework specifies a serial but non-deterministic pathway from capability to experienced value, institutional identity and identity congruence, symbolic recognition, attraction, and resource embedding, while also allowing direct experienced-value effects. The synthesis groups the evidence into five capability domains, four forms of stakeholder-experienced value, and three symbolic-capital formation processes and assigns inclusion, co-creation, communication credibility, contextual fit, and multi-level governance to specific conversion paths. The reviewed literature suggests that technology does not create brand value automatically: smart-city capabilities are more likely to support identity and attractiveness when they generate useful, inclusive, visible, and contextually relevant experiences and when identity claims remain consistent with independently observable performance. The contribution therefore lies not in asserting a previously unknown link between smart cities and place branding but in specifying construct boundaries, conversion mechanisms, and empirically testable path-specific propositions.

items.title: Climate-responsive prioritization of occupational heat-stress mitigation strategies for outdoor construction workers: An integrated fuzzy Delphi–FAHP approach
items.abstract: Occupational heat stress poses a critical risk to the health, safety, and productivity of outdoor construction workers, as the operational suitability of mitigation strategies is highly dependent on climatic conditions. This study developed a climate-responsive multi-criteria decision-making framework tailored to three distinct climatic archetypes: hot-humid (Abadan), hot-dry (Isfahan), and temperate-humid (Gorgan). Between June and September 2025, 30 experts participated in this study. The methodology integrated the Fuzzy Delphi Method (FDM) for criterion screening and the Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (FAHP) for strategy prioritization. Seven evaluation criteria and 14 control strategies were retained, with “Thermal mitigation effectiveness” identified as the most critical criterion (normalized weight: 0.258). Results revealed that the prioritized strategy sets varied notably across climatic contexts; while “hydration and electrolyte replenishment” and “breathable clothing” remained consistent baselines, the ranking of other measures, such as “evaporative cooling,” fluctuated significantly based on regional humidity. Sensitivity analysis confirmed the stability of the model, with ±10% weight perturbations resulting in minor score variations (1.9–3.8%) and no rank reversals. This FDM–FAHP framework provides an evidence-based, decision-support approach to assist safety managers in establishing a two-tiered heat-stress control program: a universal baseline supplemented by climate-tailored adjustments.

items.title: Public Infrastructure and Housing Policy Management: An Integrative Review of Affordability, Governance and Delivery
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Housing policy is often discussed as if the main problem were simply the number of houses produced. In practice, however, a dwelling becomes useful and affordable only when it is connected to serviced land, roads, transport, water, sanitation, electricity, drainage, schools, health facilities and a workable system of finance and maintenance. This article examines public infrastructure and housing policy management as one connected policy problem. It uses a structured integrative review with particular attention to Nigeria and comparable developingcountry settings. The reviewed studies were grouped into six main areas: government and institutional coordination, land and planning, housing finance and affordability, infrastructure and basic services, publicprivate housing delivery, and community participation and maintenance. The findings show that housing programmes underperform when governments focus on construction targets while land servicing, infrastructure finance, transport costs, maintenance responsibilities and local implementation capacity remain weak. The literature also shows that public-private partnerships can expand delivery, but they do not automatically protect affordability or the public interest. Strong regulation, clear risk allocation, transparent beneficiary selection and long-term affordability rules are necessary. Findings from Nigeria further indicates that private-led housing and ownership-oriented programmes commonly exclude lower-income households where mortgage access is shallow and serviced land is expensive. The study proposes an Integrated Infrastructure–Housing Policy Management Cycle that links diagnosis, planning, financing, delivery, maintenance and monitoring. It argues that housing affordability should be assessed through the total cost of living in a location rather than the purchase price or rent alone. Policy should therefore prioritise serviced land, mixed tenure, transport-linked development, lifecycle maintenance budgets, tra

items.title: Inflow turbulence data obtained from computation on appropriate region of urban area under typhoon conditions
Enhancing Occupant Comfort: A Sustainable Building Internal Design (SBID) Approach to Alleviating Summer Indoor Discomfort in Urban Villages of Wenzhou, China
items.abstract: Urban villages are a distinctive spatial phenomenon in rapidly urbanising Chinese cities. In Wenzhou, a humid-subtropical coastal city, densely built urban-village dwellings suffer severe summer indoor overheating, yet most renovation strategies in the literature remain at policy, management, or large-scale demolition levels rather than addressing the dwellings themselves. This study proposes a Sustainable Building Internal Design (SBID) framework that prioritises interventions within the building envelope and interior layout, drawing on the passive climatic logic of Wenzhou’s vernacular architecture. Three parallel objectives guide the work: (O1) identify the envelope and interior-layout aspects that drive summer indoor overheating in Wuma Street urban-village dwellings; (O2) document the climate-adaptive strategies embedded in Wenzhou vernacular architecture from an SBID perspective; and (O3) assess the effectiveness of SBID interventions in mitigating summer indoor overheating through calibrated building performance simulation. The study adopts a sequential mixed-methods design comprising (i) field survey and observational assessment of ten households in the Wuma Street urban-village cluster in Lucheng District, Wenzhou; (ii) on-site indoor environmental monitoring of representative dwellings during summer 2024; and (iii) calibrated EnergyPlus / DesignBuilder simulations of five SBID retrofit scenarios (V1–V5) against an as-found baseline (V0). The reported results indicate that combining vernacular-inspired envelope treatments (deep eaves, high-albedo lime render, ventilated double-skin construction) with interior layout reconfiguration significantly reduces summer indoor overheating hours and improves indoor thermal conditions with the aim of limiting cost and disruption to residents. The study presents an operational SBID framework, a set of evidence-informed design guidelines for subtropical urban-village retrofit, and a replicable empirical dataset for futur

items.title: Urban morphology and building energy patterns: A three-level meta-analysis of multi-scale global evidence
Building-Stock Turnover Reshapes Mitigation Priorities in China’s Building Sector
items.abstract: China's building sector is pivotal to the 2060 carbon-neutrality ambition, yet prospective assessments often insufficiently capture regional heterogeneity and life-cycle emission dynamics. Here, we develop a provincial-level dynamic framework integrating material flow analysis, life-cycle assessment, and machine-learning-informed parameter trajectories to project emissions through 2060. Under a business-as-usual (BAU) scenario, China's building life-cycle emissions are projected to peak in 2031-2033, while carbon neutrality remains challenged by persistent pressures from both material use and building operations. These pressures arise from the existing stock, whose continued use sustains energy demand while increasing building retirements shift construction from stock growth to the replacement of retired buildings. Implementing a high-efficiency scenario with regionally differentiated deployment of material- and energy-efficiency strategies could reduce China's building-sector life-cycle emissions by 90% in 2060 relative to the BAU scenario. Provincial analysis further reveals that similar overall mitigation potential masks substantial differences in the composition of effective mitigation portfolios, reflecting local building-stock and energy-use characteristics. To close the remaining gap, deeper operational decarbonization should be coupled with stock-management strategies that extend building lifetimes, avoid premature demolition, and prioritize renovation and reuse.

items.title: A BIM-Driven Collaborative Management Model for Design–Construction Integration in Building Projects in Xi’an: A Conceptual Framework and Research Design
items.abstract: Building Information Modelling (BIM) is now widely adopted in Chinese construction, yet its collaborative benefits are not automatic. Empirical evidence from the Chinese market shows that BIM application is shaped by contractual, organisational and relational conditions rather than by software use alone. The design–construction interface therefore remains vulnerable to information discontinuity, responsibility ambiguity, late coordination and fragmented workflows. This paper addresses the gap between barrier diagnosis and management design. Drawing on a structured review of recent BIM and construction-management literature, together with international and Chinese information-management standards and national and local policy, it makes three contributions. First, it synthesises eight literature-informed candidate barrier domains—organisational, responsibility and governance, collaboration and relational, process, information management, technological, human and competency, and institutional and contractual—and positions BIM as a socio-technical enabling environment rather than a stand-alone solution. Second, it proposes a Structured Barrier–Evidence–Requirement Mapping procedure that converts empirically identified critical barriers into traceable collaborative management requirements, supported by a Barrier–Evidence–Requirement Traceability Matrix. Third, it outlines a requirements-driven model development and modified Delphi validation design for a context-adapted collaborative management model for building projects in Xi’an, a national intelligent-construction pilot city. The proposed approach connects the identification of barriers, the determination of requirements, model development, and validation, providing a transparent and auditable process for developing an expert-validated management model.

items.title: Drivers, Barriers and Sustainability Outcomes of Green Innovation Adoption in Municipal Solid Waste Management in Southeast Asia: A Structured Integrative Review
items.venue: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences
items.abstract: Southeast Asian cities are generating rapidly increasing volumes of municipal solid waste (MSW). Yet the green innovations that could divert waste from landfills have diffused slowly, and evidence on why they are adopted remains fragmented. This study conducts a structured integrative review of empirical research on the adoption of green innovation in MSW management in Southeast Asia. Twenty-six structured queries across a web search engine, scholarly platforms, and institutional repositories returned 242 records; 30 were assessed in detail, and 16 empirical journal articles published between 2015 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The studies were appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and synthesized using the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework, informed by diffusion of innovations and circular economy theory. Seven groups of green innovation were identified: source separation and household recycling; community waste banks; composting and biodigesters; smart and digital systems; municipal systems and materials recovery facilities; waste-to-energy; and producer responsibility. Environmental context factors were the most frequently reported, appearing in 14 of the 16 studies: regulation, enforcement, incentives, information, and social norms acted as drivers when strong and as barriers when weak. Organizational factors, notably financial support, partnerships, and local leadership, determined whether schemes could be sustained, while technological factors, chiefly infrastructure and cost, shaped implementation. Social and economic benefits were reported, but no study measured landfill diversion or emission reductions over time, and most studies lacked an explicit theory. The review proposes a sequential TOE-based framework, expressed as four propositions, that links institutional conditions, organizational capacity, and infrastructure to sustained adoption. It sets out a research agenda for green innovation adoption in emerging economi
