items.title: Roof Systems as Socio-Technical Environmental Mediators in Climate Responsive Housing: An Integrative Review and Conceptual Framework for Warm-Humid Tropical Environments
items.venue: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHY AND ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT
items.oa_url: https://iiardjournals.org/get/IJGEM/VOL. 12 NO. 8 2026/Roof Systems as Socio-Technical Environmental 56-78.pdf
items.abstract: Rapid urbanisation, a warming climate and growing reliance on mechanical cooling have sharpened concern about the thermal performance of residential buildings in warm-humid tropical environments. Because roofs bear the longest and most direct exposure to solar radiation of any envelope component, they are the principal mediators of heat exchange between the outdoor climate and the occupied interior. A large literature already exists on cool roofs, insulation, attic ventilation, radiant barriers and roofing materials, yet this knowledge sits awkwardly across building physics, architectural design, thermal-comfort research, energy studies and housing governance, rarely speaking across those boundaries. This paper responds through a theory-informed integrative review of residential roof systems in warm-humid tropical environments, synthesising literature from major academic databases thematically and reading it through Systems Theory and Ecological Modernisation Theory. The synthesis shows that roof performance is not a fixed material property but an emergent, socio-technical outcome produced by the interaction of climatic forcing, roof-system configuration, attic behaviour, ventilation, insulation and ceiling characteristics with occupant adaptation, construction practice, market conditions and institutional governance. No single roofing material or technology can explain thermal outcomes in isolation. The review further shows that roof-induced overheating shapes thermal comfort, cooling demand, household energy expenditure and wider environmental outcomes, while the diffusion of climate-responsive roofing technologies is itself governed by affordability, material availability, professional knowledge, construction competence and regulatory capacity. To hold these relationships together, the paper proposes a Socio-Technical Roof-System Framework built from three nested, interacting subsystems: a building-thermal subsystem, a household and construction market subsystem,

items.title: Revitalization of The Ex-Bank UOB Building with an Adaptive Reuse Approach to Become a Center of Creative and Retail Activities in the Old Town Area
items.abstract: Jakarta's Old Town area holds significant historical value as a colonial-era commercial center; however, many of its heritage buildings have been abandoned or have lost their original functions. This study aimed to examine strategies for revitalizing the former United Overseas Bank (UOB) building in Jakarta's Old Town through an adaptive reuse approach, transforming it into a center for creative and retail activities. The adaptive reuse of cultural heritage buildings presents challenges in balancing the preservation of historical significance with contemporary functional requirements and long-term sustainability. Employing a qualitative approach with an in-depth single-case study design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders, including conservation architects, area managers, and creative industry practitioners, supplemented by field observations and archival document analysis. Thematic analysis identified three principal themes: the integration of historic spatial elements with contemporary functional requirements, the development of retail spaces responsive to the architectural characteristics of heritage buildings, and the establishment of a creative ecosystem that encouraged public interaction. The findings suggested that adaptive reuse could extend beyond physical and functional transformation by contributing to the revitalization of an area's socioeconomic value while maintaining its historical and architectural integrity. The study provided practical insights for architects, conservation professionals, and policymakers in developing adaptive conservation design guidelines for historic urban areas. Further research was recommended to evaluate post-occupancy performance, long-term economic sustainability, and socioeconomic impacts on local communities.

items.title: Sectoral Coordination to Maximize China’s National and Provincial Building Carbon Emissions Mitigation
items.abstract: The building sector is central to achieving China’s carbon peak and neutrality targets, yet existing assessments seldom integrate full life cycle emissions into subnational policy design. Here we develop a building material–energy–emission (BMEE) model to quantify direct, indirect, and embodied CO 2 emissions from all building types across 31 Chinese mainland provinces from 2000 to 2060 and to evaluate 50 policy scenarios that combine five strategies: urban renewal, green buildings, low-carbon construction, circular economy, and energy transition. The model links dynamic material flow analysis with energy balance sheet splitting, supported by newly compiled national databases on building material and operational energy intensities, and incorporates a renovation module that prioritizes renovation over demolition. We find that China’s building emissions have peaked around 2017 and can decline to between 0.69 and 2.48 Gt (10 9 tonnes) CO 2 by 2060. Under the lowest-emission pathway, cumulative emissions are reduced by 39.5% relative to business-as-usual, with urban renewal providing the largest contribution to total mitigation, followed by green buildings and energy transition. Public buildings, the material sector, and northern provinces exhibit the largest mitigation potentials, while provincial results highlight distinct strategy priorities. Monte Carlo analysis confirms that these conclusions are robust despite widening parametric uncertainty. Our findings underscore the importance of sectoral coordination and regionally tailored policy packages to maximize building decarbonization in China and provide a scalable framework for other large countries facing concurrent new construction and stock-renewal challenges.

items.title: Urban fabric and climate crisis in the European framework
items.abstract: This chapter examines the evolving role of European cities in the climate crisis through the lens of multi‑scalar urbanisation and European climate governance. It first interrogates dominant “urban age” narratives and institutional claims that cities are both principal emitters and privileged sites of climate action, drawing on recent debates on methodological cityism and planetary urbanisation. It then maps the European Union’s urban climate architecture, focusing on the Urban Agenda for the EU; the Mission “Climate‑Neutral and Smart Cities”; the Covenant of Mayors; the Green City Accord; and related initiatives such as the New Leipzig Charter, Driving Urban Transitions, and the New European Bauhaus. Building on an original analysis of Framework Programme data and EuroSciVoc concepts, the chapter shows how climate‑related research and innovation funding have remained a modest share of total EU investment, are increasingly framed through economic logics, and only partially centre the urban dimension. Three emblematic projects are discussed as key vehicles for operationalising the Cities Mission. The chapter concludes by arguing that meaningful urban climate action must be grounded in multi‑level governance, territorial interdependencies, and climate justice.

items.title: A Delphi Study on the Integration of Digital Public Health and AI in Public Health Education
items.abstract: Background Digital transformation (DT) reshapes public health practice, governance, and education. Realising the potential of digital tools for surveillance, communication, and population health interventions depends on a workforce equipped with appropriate digital competencies. Existing public health education frameworks only partially address the skills needed to design, implement, and critically assess digital public health (DiPH) approaches, risking slower adoption and persistent structural weaknesses. The study developed a DiPH competency framework to inform public health education and continuing professional development in Europe. Methods We conducted a three-round online Delphi study followed by a validation workshop. Experts were recruited based on DiPH expertise and involvement in European public health education. Participants rated the relevance of proposed competencies on a 9-point Likert scale and suggested additional ones; consensus was defined as mean ratings of 1–3 (exclusion) or 7–9 (inclusion). Results 33 experts participated in the study. Building on ASPHER’s Public Health Core Competence Framework, we developed an initial set of 19 DiPH competencies across multiple public health domains, which were iteratively refined across rounds. The agreed 44 competencies covered content related to digital (health) literacy; health data collection, analysis, management, and governance; ethics and regulation of the digital transformation of health systems; and the spread of information in digital networks. All 12 essential public health functions were addressed, underscoring that the DT is reflected across every public health area. 15 experts joined the validation workshop, shaping the final structure and prioritisation of the consented competencies. Conclusions The framework highlights the cross-cutting relevance of digital competencies across public health domains and offers a structured basis for integrating DiPH into education and workforce development.

items.title: Delphi War Room - Lectio magistralis di Donatello D'Andrea su Crisis Communication
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Crisis communication: prevedere è potere (Crisis communication: foresight is power) Slides of the lectio magistralis delivered online on 2 November 2026 by Donatello D’Andrea, Vice President of the Delphi Institute, as part of the public lecture series preceding the Delphi War Room, the Institute’s simulation-based programme on international crises. The lecture argues that crisis communication is decided before the crisis begins. It distinguishes the communicative crisis from the operational one, showing that the former often precedes the latter and outlasts it. It then treats the frame, the interpretive context within which an event is read, as the real stake of crisis communication, and observes that in the current media environment the window for a first response has shrunk from hours to minutes. The presentation reviews the main strands of the crisis communication literature, including Situational Crisis Communication Theory and image repair theory, and discusses their limit: they mostly address how to respond once a crisis is underway, when the context of reception has already been set. Against this background, it introduces the notion of communicative awareness: anticipating how the opponent will act, what it will say, and responding before it says it. The argument is illustrated through a case drawn from the author’s experience as spokesperson in regional politics, in which a prepared communication plan had to withstand a news leak. The lecture closes with five questions for building a crisis communication plan in advance, and with a reflection on foresight as a source of strategic advantage. Language of the slides: Italian.

items.title: Regional end-of-life embodied carbon emissions of wood-frame housing: A hybrid-parametric assessment of single-family houses in Canada
items.abstract: The aging wood-frame single-family housing stock in North America represents a major future source of demolition waste and a substantial supply of recoverable wood materials. However, the embodied carbon implications of alternative end-of-life (EoL) strategies remain poorly understood at the regional scale due to limitations in temporal resolution, empirical validation, and carbon pathway characterization. This study develops a hybrid-parametric modelling framework that integrates historical construction eras, material flow analysis, the 9R circular economy hierarchy, and life cycle module-based carbon accounting (C1 D) to assess 81,598 single-family houses in Vancouver, Canada. The framework incorporates uncertainty through Monte Carlo simulations and is validated against four real-world deconstruction projects, demonstrating its capability to represent both material flows and carbon outcomes. The modelled wood generation (155.9 kg/m 2 ) and diversion rate (90%) fall within the observed ranges (120.8–179.0 kg/m 2 and 84–99%). Results show that EoL scenario selection has a substantially greater influence on embodied carbon performance than building age. Conventional demolition generates average net emissions of 9.39 kgCO₂e/m 2 . Moderate deconstruction (75% diversion) reduces this to 3.12 kgCO₂e/m 2 (−67%), whereas high-diversion pathways achieve net savings of 1.23 and 6.92 kgCO₂e/m 2 at 90% and 95% diversion. Structural lumber represents the largest recoverable material fraction and the primary source of mitigation potential. Sensitivity analysis identifies labour intensity, recovery efficiency, and allocation among reuse, repurposing, and recycling pathways as the dominant determinants of carbon outcomes. Biogenic carbon assessment further demonstrates that circular strategies primarily alter the timing and distribution of carbon flows through material substitution and emission deferral rather than permanent carbon sequestration. A critical circular economy gap i

items.title: Development of the Systems Tool for Readiness, Implementation anD malaria Elimination (STRIDE): an online Delphi study
items.abstract: Background Countries in the Greater Mekong Subregion are committed to eliminating malaria by 2030. Despite the critical role of health system readiness in malaria elimination, there is no assessment tool available to comprehensively evaluate an area’s readiness towards malaria elimination across six WHO health system building blocks which are service delivery, surveillance, elimination workforce, products and commodities, programme financing, and leadership and governance. The aim of this study is to develop a comprehensive health system readiness assessment tool for malaria elimination in the Greater Mekong Subregion. Methods Based on the findings from recent studies, a health system readiness assessment tool called STRIDE (Systems Tool for Readiness, Implementation anD malaria Elimination) was drafted. Two rounds of modified Delphi consultation were conducted during May and September 2025 to finalise and endorse the STRIDE with a priori percent agreement of 70%. A panel of experts consisting of representatives from national programmes, donor organisations, technical agencies, and implementing partners and independent experts evaluated the proposed items for assessing the health system readiness for malaria elimination. Content validity of the final STRIDE was assessed by item-level and scale-level content validity indexes. Results The draft STRIDE was developed with two modules: the National Module and the Sub-National Module comprising 58 and 49 questions respectively. The draft STRIDE underwent two rounds of online Delphi consultation with 24 and 18 experts. Incorporating expert feedback, the STRIDE was finalised with 66 questions in the National Module and 55 in the Sub-National Module, each assessing readiness across service delivery, surveillance, elimination workforce, products and commodities, programme financing, and leadership and governance for malaria elimination. Item-level content validity indexes of the questions ranged from 0.83 to 1.00, while scale

items.title: From financial regionalism to capital market regionalization: Asian bond market development and China-ASEAN financial connectivity
items.abstract: Since the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, East Asian economies have engaged in multiple official cooperative initiatives to strengthen the region’s financial resilience. While numerous studies have sought to examine how such inter-state efforts constitute the rise of East Asian “financial regionalism”, few have explored whether this top-down cooperation has translated into “capital market regionalization”—the bottom-up integration of regional capital markets. This paper fills this gap by investigating the extent to which and how regional institution building facilitated capital market integration. Utilizing the IMF Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey data (1997–2024), we identify a significant rise in intraregional portfolio investment in the debt securities market, driven largely by China’s emergence as a major regional creditor post-2008. Through a process tracing analysis of the Asian Bond Markets Initiative (ABMI), we argue that financial regionalism has indeed actively facilitated capital market regionalization. Specifically, we demonstrate that regional institution building efforts at the official level and China’s strategic financial opening up in portfolio investment have substantially strengthened China-ASEAN bond market connectivity, showing that East Asian capital market integration is deeply rooted in state-led cooperative frameworks.

items.title: Quantifying land transfer in China: Integrating its impacts on urban economy
items.abstract: In China's hierarchical land-governance system, the central government establishes the regulatory framework, while provincial and municipal authorities adapt the implementation according to local fiscal capacity, development priorities, and spatial constraints. Despite the importance of land transfer in shaping urban economic development processes, empirical research has long relied on fragmented samples or single-scale observations, and a unified long-term dataset spanning multiple administrative levels remains unavailable. To address this gap, this study constructs a multi-level spatiotemporal dataset of land transfer in China covering the period 2000-2024 at the national, provincial, and city levels. The dataset integrates seven standardized indicators, including land supply area, transaction price, gross floor area (GFA), payment amount, floor area ratio (FAR), building density, and greenery rate. Data are compiled from official land-market disclosure platforms and verified administrative transaction records and undergo systematic quality-control procedures, including cross-source reconciliation, unit harmonization, coverage diagnostics, and outlier screening to ensure temporal consistency and spatial comparability. The resulting database supports analyses of long-term land transfer dynamics, regional heterogeneity, and multi-level governance patterns. In addition, an illustrative empirical application demonstrates the analytical utility of the dataset for examining associations between land allocation and urban economic development indicators. This dataset provides a comprehensive empirical foundation for future research on land governance, land finance, urban spatial development, and regional transformation in China.

items.title: Rooftop Alternatives: Exploring Practical Greenhouse by Design Simulation for Sustainable City
items.abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified the demand for sustainable strategies that balance food production, energy efficiency, and environmental quality within cities. Rooftop greenhouses (RTGs) have emerged as a promising architectural typology that integrates urban agriculture with building energy systems. This study explores practical alternatives for integrating rooftop greenhouses in urban contexts through design simulation. Using a parametric modeling and energy simulation framework, multiple RTG configurations were analyzed across different building types and uses. A key performance indicator—the energy balance—was assessed to identify optimal design strategies. The results demonstrate that design-integrated RTGs can significantly improve building energy performance and contribute to urban sustainability, particularly when adapted to regional climatic conditions. The findings provide quantitative evidence and design guidelines for architects and policymakers to support the adoption of rooftop greenhouse systems as a component of the sustainable city model.

items.title: Risk identification and assessment of passive roofs for rural housing in hot and dry regions using Delphi method
items.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Passive roofs are increasingly recognized as effective solutions for improving thermal performance and reducing energy consumption in buildings. Nevertheless, the execution of these measures in rural housing sectors is frequently compromised by a complex array of uncertainties, including those related to policy management, financial constraints, environmental factors, health and safety, and quality control. Existing studies mainly focus on roof performance and energy benefits, while systematic risk assessment remains limited, particularly in rural areas with constrained resources and technical capacity. The study objectives were to develop a structured framework to identify and assess the risks associated with passive roofs in the hot–dry regions of Southwest China.METHODS: A two-round Delphi survey was conducted to evaluate impact and frequency, and consensus was tested using Kendall’s W and interquartile range. Risk levels were subsequently evaluated through the application of a modified risk matrix featuring 0.8-interval classification..FINDINGS: A total of 49 preliminary risk factors were identified through literature review and expert judgment. After screening using the content validity ratio, 47, 35, 48, and 42 risk factors were retained for blue roofs, cool roofs, green roofs, and ventilated roofs, respectively. The findings demonstrate that the highest cumulative risk levels are associated with green and blue roofing systems. Blue roofs contain 15 high-risk and 5 very high-risk factors, while green roofs contain 16 high-risk and 5 very high-risk factors. Cool roofing alternatives presents fewer extreme vulnerabilities but conversely generate the highest percentage of high-risk outcomes. Ventilated roofs show relatively lower overall risk levels, although several critical risks remain. Across all roof types, high-risk factors were primarily associated with construction quality, management capacity, maintenance requirements, and econ

items.title: Development and validation of a tool to aid writing and reviewing of healthcare safety investigation reports: A modified Delphi study
items.venue: Journal of Patient Safety and Risk Management
items.abstract: Introduction Healthcare organisations worldwide are expected to investigate or review incidents that unintentionally harm or could cause harm. Investigation findings are presented in a written report, which is arguably a proxy measure for the quality of investigations. The report is an important document to be read and acted upon. The aims of this study were: (1) to design a tool to support the writing and review of healthcare safety investigation reports, and (2) to validate the content of the tool. Methods The study was conducted in two phases. Phase 1: The initial content of the tool was developed using relevant published literature and building consensus with 25 specialist participants from the UK and Australia. Phase 2: Content validity of the tool was assessed for relevance and clarity in two e-Delphi survey rounds with users of the tool. Using a 4-point scale, a median of 3 or 4 and an interquartile range of less than or equal to 1.5 were used to determine consensus. Results Phase 1: A tool containing eight areas of review with accompanying descriptors was developed. For each area of review, a three-point ordinal rating scale along with a comments box for formative self-assessment was included. Phase 2: At the end of the round 1 survey, there was consensus on all but one area of review in the tool. By the end of the round 2 survey, consensus was reached on all areas of review. No additional areas of review were added and none were removed. Some descriptors were amended to improve clarity. Conclusion We co-designed and validated the content of a tool that can be used to inform the quality of safety investigation reports and learning in terms of a systems-based approach. The tool has multiple uses ranging from self-assessment for report writers to facilitating oversight of the quality of healthcare safety investigation reports. Future work could focus on building further evidence of the tool's overall utility.

items.title: Urban Governance and the Choreography of Intermediary Roles in a Waste Cooking Oil-to-Biodiesel Loop in Shiga Prefecture, Japan
items.venue: The International Journal of Sustainability Policy and Practice
items.abstract: Local circular-economy initiatives often stall not because conversion technologies are unavailable but because material flows, operational routines, and responsibilities must be aligned across heterogeneous actors. This article traces a four-decade waste cooking oil (WCO) to biodiesel fuel (BDF) loop in Shiga Prefecture, Japan, and explains how intermediary roles overlapped and migrated among civic groups, municipalities, and a local fuel distributor as the loop moved from experimentation to routine service provision. Based on interviews (n = 10), municipal and organizational documents, and process tracing, the analysis applies a four-mode intermediation lens—facilitating, brokering, configuring, and structuring—to map how actors addressed three recurring coordination challenges: mobilizing dispersed household feedstock, stabilizing quality and compliance in conversion and logistics, and securing reliable offtake through procurement and fleet routines. The findings show that durable circular loops rely on redundant intermediation: rather than a clean handover between actors, multiple intermediaries simultaneously perform different modes, creating fallback capacity when political priorities, markets for used oils, or operational constraints shift. The article distills transferable design principles—early offtake commitments, visible and convenient collection infrastructure, shared quality gates, and hybrid municipal–private operating models—for cities building local circular ecosystems.

items.title: Material Stocks and Flows of the Road Network in the Philippines: Implications for Resource Productivity and Circular Infrastructure Planning
items.abstract: Road infrastructure is a major driver of construction mineral demand, yet its long-term material implications remain underexamined in the Philippines. This study applies a bottom-up dynamic material flow analysis to estimate material inflows, outflows, and in-use road material stocks (MS) from 1982 to 2024. Results show that the road network expanded by 45,285 km (29%) over the study period, along with a shift from unpaved to more material intensive paved surfaces. During the last decade, road construction, upgrading, and maintenance required an average annual material inflow of 32 Mt, of which 56% was associated with road maintenance works. In-use road MS increased from 380 Mt in 1982 to 792 Mt in 2024. The 2024 regional stock productivity, defined as gross regional domestic product (GRDP) per unit of road MS, was evaluated to compare regional economic output relative to the embedded road materials, together with other complementary indicators, namely GRDP per capita, road MS per capita, and road stock density. Results further showed considerable variation in regional stock productivity, indicating that larger road MS does not necessarily correspond to higher economic output per unit of road MS. Overall, the findings show that road infrastructure should be viewed not only as a transport asset, but also as a long-term material system requiring continued maintenance and eventual material management. The study highlights the need for more stock-aware infrastructure planning, stronger recovery and reuse of road materials, and better regionally differentiated strategies to improve resource circularity and productivity in the Philippines’ road infrastructure.

items.title: "NOT AI BUT SUPERINTELLIGENCE": The Next Turn of Events An Integrative Review of Pathways, Prospects, Risks and Governance of Artificial Superintelligence, with Implications for Developing Economies
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Abstract: For more than seven decades, the dominant ambition of computing research has been artificial intelligence (AI): machines that perform tasks which ordinarily require human intelligence. The rapid progress of deep learning, transformer-based foundation models and large-scale reinforcement learning since 2012 has moved that ambition from laboratory curiosity to everyday infrastructure. This paper argues that the next technological turn of events is not "more AI" in the incremental sense, but the possible emergence of superintelligence (ASI): systems whose cognitive performance greatly exceeds that of the best human minds across virtually all domains of interest. Using an integrative literature review of peer-reviewed scholarship, expert surveys, technical reports and policy instruments published between 1950 and 2025, the paper (i) clarifies the conceptual distinction between narrow AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI) and superintelligence; (ii) traces the intellectual history of the idea from Turing and Good to contemporary scaling research; (iii) analyses six plausible pathways to superintelligence, namely compute and data scaling, algorithmic and architectural innovation, recursive self-improvement, whole brain emulation, biological and neural-interface enhancement, and networked collective intelligence; (iv) evaluates the evidence and counter-evidence on timelines and "takeoff" speeds; (v) maps the transformative opportunities and the systemic and existential risks; and (vi) reviews emerging governance responses at global, continental and national levels, with particular attention to Africa and Nigeria. The review finds that superintelligence differs from present-day AI not merely in degree but in kind: it shifts the central problem from building capable tools to aligning and governing autonomous agents more capable than their designers. The paper proposes a Superintelligence Readiness and Governance Framework (SRGF) built on five interlocking layer

items.title: Investigating Ethical, Security and Pedagogical Challenges of Generative AI Adoption in Higher Education: A Fuzzy Delphi-DEMATEL Approach
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education by enhancing teaching, learning and academic administration. However, its widespread adoption has introduced critical ethical, security, pedagogical and governance concerns that remain fragmented across existing literature. Grounded in Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Responsible AI Framework, this study aims to identify, validate and examine the interrelationships among the key challenges associated with GenAI adoption in higher education. To achieve this objective, a hybrid Fuzzy Delphi–Fuzzy DEMATEL approach was employed to establish expert consensus on the identified challenges and to analyse their causal relationships. The findings reveal five major challenge dimensions: ethical education, security concerns, training and resource availability, student engagement and monitoring and regulation and governance. The results indicate that ethical education and regulatory governance act as the primary driving factors influencing the responsible and effective implementation of GenAI, whereas security, faculty preparedness and student engagement emerge as dependent challenge areas. The study highlights the need for comprehensive AI governance mechanisms, ongoing faculty and student capacity building, strengthened ethical awareness and robust cybersecurity practices to enable sustainable GenAI integration in higher education. This research contributes to the existing body of knowledge in three ways. First, it extends the application of Socio-Technical Systems Theory and Responsible AI principles to the context of GenAI adoption in higher education. Second, it integrates Fuzzy Delphi and Fuzzy DEMATEL methods to provide a structured and systematic framework for prioritizing and analysing adoption challenges. Third, it offers actionable insights and practical recommendations for policymakers, university leaders and educators to support responsible, secure and sustainable implementatio

items.title: Assessment of Electronic Waste Management Environmental Pollution and Associated Health Risks in Gazipur City Bangladesh
items.abstract: Electronic waste (E-waste) is a rapidly growing environmental challenge in developing countries. This study assessed E-waste generation, management practices, environmental and occupational health risks, and institutional challenges in Gazipur City Corporation, Bangladesh. Using an integrated mixed-methods approach, including Material Flow Analysis (MFA), surveys, stakeholder interviews, and institutional assessment, data were collected from 375 respondents. The city generated 6,245.21 tons of E-waste in 2024 (2.43 kg person⁻¹ year⁻¹), with refrigerators, televisions, and microwave ovens as the major sources. Informal recycling dominated E-waste management, while unsafe handling practices increased environmental and occupational risks. Key barriers included inadequate recycling infrastructure, weak policy implementation, and limited institutional capacity. This study provides an integrated framework to support sustainable E-waste management, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), and circular economy implementation in Bangladesh and other developing countries.

items.title: Environmental impacts and mitigation potential of post-conflict building reconstruction
Protocol for an international e-Delphi study to develop an updated consensus-based European competence framework for inclusive education professionals
items.abstract: Inclusive education remains a key European policy and research priority, yet competence frameworks guiding professional learning may require updating. The Profile of Inclusive Teachers (2012) and its extension, the Profile for Inclusive Teacher Professional Learning (2022), established core values and competences underpinning inclusive practice across Europe. However, major societal, technological, and policy developments, such as the systemic broadening of inclusion, the integration of digitalisation and artificial intelligence, and the rising importance of wellbeing necessitate an updated and comprehensive competence framework. This study outlines the protocol for an international e-Delphi process designed to develop an updated, consensus-based European competence framework for inclusive education professionals by 2026, with attention to policy relevance and applicability across primary, secondary, and higher education. An international electronic Delphi (e-Delphi) study will be conducted to achieve expert consensus on the competences required for inclusive education professionals. A purposive sample of at least 25 experts, spanning researchers, policymakers, teacher educators, and practitioners from across Europe and beyond Europe, will be recruited to ensure both depth of expertise and breadth across educational levels. The study will follow the CREDES guidelines for Delphi research. Up to three iterative survey rounds will be administered via Qualtrics. In Round 1, experts will propose competence areas and assess the continued relevance of existing profile components; Round 2 will involve prioritisation and rating on a 9-point Likert scale; Round 3 will re-rate selected unresolved or revised items based on anonymised feedback to inform final consensus decisions. Consensus inclusion will require a median ≥ 7, interquartile range ≤ 2 and at least 70% of valid ratings in the 7–9 range, with valid ratings from at least 70% of the original Round 1 panel, rounded upw

items.title: INTEGRATED PROGRAMME GOVERNANCE FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE AND REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT IN SAUDI ARABIA UNDER VISION 2030
items.abstract: The expansion of tourism in Saudi Arabia, under the Vision 2030 initiative, covers a wide variety of areas such as destination development, transport, utilities, heritage conservation, digital systems, the public realm, hospitality capacity and regional economic policy as part of a wider programme of transformation. Given the scale of this project, a governance problem emerges that cannot be resolved by simply controlling each individual project. This review analyses how integrated programme governance can link the delivery of tourism infrastructure with regional development outcomes. In order to achieve this a structured critical integrative review of 30 peer-reviewed studies verified by the DOI was conducted between 2020 and 2025, the studies covering the fields of tourism development, urban and regional planning, megaproject governance, stakeholder management, construction delivery, sustainability and digital coordination. The synthesis identifies six interdependent governance requirements: strategic portfolio alignment, integration of regional infrastructure and utilities, explicit decision rights, interface and change control, assurance of sustainability and heritage, and benefits-led performance management. It is possible for optimisation at the project level to take place even if the overall programme is performing poorly provided that the shared dependencies and cumulative pressures are only dealt with at a late stage.

items.title: Analysis and Improvement of Building Energy Data Collection Systems for Green Remodeling of Aging Small Scale Residential Buildings in South Korea - Comparative Review of International and Domestic Practices
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze domestic and international building energy data collection systems and propose strategies to promote renewable-energy-based green remodeling in aging small-scale residential buildings in South Korea. A five-step review of the literature and relevant documents was conducted to examine European policies and financial support mechanisms, hybrid geothermal–photovoltaic demonstration projects, and building energy data infrastructure. Domestic conditions were assessed by examining the green remodeling system established under the Green Building Construction Support Act, the policies and regulations of five metropolitan cities, and public data systems, including Seumteo, V-World, Architecture HUB, and the National Building Energy Database. Spatial information was also examined using geographic information systems (GIS). The comparison identified six structural problems: the absence of systematic data collection, a policy focus on public buildings, insufficient renewable energy data, inadequate integration of passive and active systems, limited economic feasibility, and a lack of post-retrofit performance verification. Six corresponding improvement strategies are proposed: mandatory monitoring, national demonstration programs, diversified financing mechanisms, one-stop service centers, integrated design guidelines, and phased regulatory mandates. Finally, the study highlights the need to establish an integrated, multilayered data structure at the building level.

items.title: From practice to policy: scaling regional mental health action across Europe
items.abstract: Mental health is a growing priority in European public health policy, yet implementation remains uneven across territories. Regional and local health authorities are not merely implementing actors — they are innovators, conveners and leaders of mental health action, bridging European frameworks and the communities they serve. Yet their experience is rarely systematically captured or translated into European policy and practice. EUREGHA’s 2025 Annual Conference Together for Mental Health: Regions Building Europe’s Healthier Future confirmed this central role, showcasing how regions drive action through whole-of-government strategies, community-based programmes, and leadership in European Joint Actions including PRISM and MENTOR. Discussions highlighted shared challenges: fragmented multi-level governance, gaps between EU initiatives and territorial implementation, and the need for stronger cross-sector and cross-border collaboration. Building on these insights, in 2026 EUREGHA (European Regional and Local Health Authorities association) launched a structured collection of mental health practices across its 28-member network. The initiative maps diverse regional approaches to prevention, community-based care and integrated service delivery — ranging, for example, from Wales’ Mental Health and Wellbeing Strategy and Hapus community wellbeing campaign, the Basque Country’s Bizi suicide prevention programme developed within Joint Action PRISM, to cross-border mental health initiatives from the Gorizia area. The presentation will share findings from this collection, analysing common enablers and barriers - governance models, workforce capacity, cross-sector collaboration and community engagement - and exploring conditions for transferability across regions. Participants will gain actionable insights into strengthening equitable regional mental health systems and into how European initiatives can better support scaling and sustainability. Key messages • Regional authoritie

items.title: Coordination without Hegemony: RCEP and the Political Economy of Multipolar Regionalism in Asia
items.venue: European Journal of East Asian Studies
items.abstract: Author's accepted manuscript (peer-reviewed and copy-edited, before typesetting by the publisher) of: Chatzinikolaou, Dimos. 2026. "Coordination without Hegemony: RCEP and the Political Economy of Multipolar Regionalism in Asia." European Journal of East Asian Studies 25 (3): 325–351. https://doi.org/10.1163/15700615-bja10009. Please cite the published version. Abstract: Multipolarity is usually treated as a shift in the distribution of capabilities, yet its practical consequence is institutional: who writes the rules, and with what domestic consent. This article asks how cooperation is organised when no power can impose order, taking the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) as its case. An integrative review with theory-building purpose maps the Scopus literatures on multipolarity and the RCEP, synthesises a purposive pool of 36 studies, and anchors it against the treaty text and accounts of the negotiation. The synthesis supports reading the agreement as coordination without a hegemonic orchestrator: procedural leadership by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations steered the negotiation, while broad coverage with calibrated obligation preserves autonomy. Domestic authorisation is hypothesised, not shown, to be the binding constraint on deepening, with stated refutation conditions. The Multipolarity Governance Triangle organises these trade-offs as a heuristic and specifies indicators for testing it. Online supplement (search, screening, synthesis pool and coding materials): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21996163

items.title: Cultural Urbanism: A Relational, Humanist Paradigm for Place, Pluralism, Heritage and Spatial Justice
items.abstract: Objective: This article develops Cultural Urbanism as a relational, humanist, and place-based paradigm of urban planning and design. Although culture has long figured in urban theory, cultural planning, heritage, regeneration, and placemaking, these traditions remain conceptually fragmented, and culture is frequently treated as a sector, amenity, or economic resource rather than as a constitutive process of urban life. Methods: The article undertakes a critical integrative review and conceptual synthesis across urban theory, cultural studies, planning, urban design, public-space research, feminist and intercultural planning, Latino urbanism, heritage studies, placemaking, and just-sustainability scholarship. Following the paradigm-building method that Douglas Kelbaugh used to distinguish New Urbanism, Everyday Urbanism, and Post-Urbanism, this study positions Cultural Urbanism as a fourth analytical orientation and derives its propositions, methods, and risks. Results: Cultural Urbanism is defined as an urbanism of recognition, relationship, and continuity, in which culture is constitutive of urban space rather than an additional layer placed upon it. Seven propositions establish its conceptual core: the cultural production of urban space; the relational production of place; humanistic placemaking; the public realm as cultural commons; plural and intersectional urbanism; living heritage and memory; and culturally grounded justice and sustainability. International examples, spanning Latino spatial practice, feminist planning, multicultural public space, community stewardship, culture-led regeneration, and heritage tourism, illustrate how these principles operate and where they come under strain. Conclusion: Cultural Urbanism offers a framework for understanding culture not as an addition to the city but as one of the processes through which cities become meaningful, plural, and just places.

items.title: From foresight to implementation: building collaborative ecosystems for distribution grid planning
items.abstract: Extended abstract 5-210-26 The energy transition is increasingly shaped at the local and regional level, where electrification, DERs, and climate mitigation and adaptation intersect with territorial development. This work presents findings from a global co-creation project within ISGAN, an IEA Technology Collaboration Program, involving participants from 15 countries. The work forms part of the ISGAN Lighthouse Project and builds on a sense-making framework for long-term planning of smart distribution grids under uncertainty developed in an earlier project phase. The framework conceptualises grid planning as a multi-actor process spanning five phases, from foresight to implementation, underpinned by three essential framework conditions. One of these, effective actor collaboration and coordination, is the focus of this work. Taking a system innovation perspective, we explore the characteristics of a well-functioning actor ecosystem and how these can be developed and maintained to improve the quality and speed of distribution grid planning, drawing on complementary governance, relational, and operational perspectives, including multi-level coordination between top-down steering and bottom-up initiatives, and interfaces with spatial and cross-sector planning processes. Particular attention is given to the foresight phase, where actors need to develop a shared understanding of and agree on the long-term direction of the energy system and the role of the distribution grid within it. The analysis focuses on three actor groups influencing distribution-grid planning across governance levels: DSOs; local and regional government actors with territorial planning responsibilities; and energy policy makers and regulators, typically operating at the national level. We examine interdependencies across the planning process, including flows of data, information and decisions, and related coordination and sense-making challenges. Informed by insights from different national contexts,

items.title: Who pays for urban cleanliness? Governance cost, behavioral nudge design, and informal recycling in Bangkok's waste regime
items.abstract: Cities in the Global South increasingly consider market-based instruments such as Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) to encourage source separation, improve municipal cost recovery, and support circular-economy transitions. However, the fiscal promise of PAYT depends not only on fee design but also on operational awareness, institutional trust, behavioral readiness, and the inclusion of actors already embedded in recycling systems. This study assesses municipal fiscal exposure under constrained implementation conditions rather than conducting an ex-post causal evaluation or predicting long-term household compliance. Using Bangkok's 2025 waste-fee reform as a case study, the paper develops an exploratory, scenario-based diagnostic framework that combines Material Flow Analysis (MFA), municipal cost data, and publicly released NIDA Poll evidence from 1310 Bangkok residents. The evidence reveals a substantial acceptance–readiness gap: while 73.97% of respondents supported behavior-differentiated waste fees in principle, 80.76% reported no awareness of the registration requirement for the reduced 20 THB/month fee, and 60.46% anticipated low or no local cooperation with the program. Under the model assumptions, a higher-separation pathway (S = 30%; BMA, 2026) is associated with approximately 2.13 billion THB in annual municipal cost savings. Under lower-compliance conditions, represented by a conservative 5–10% effective separation range, scenario-calculated savings are substantially lower, with potential burdens shifting toward municipal budgets, households, informal recyclers, and peri-urban environments. The study operationalizes this divergence as the scenario-calculated fiscal component of governance cost: the opportunity cost of unrealized efficiency potential under weak implementation readiness. The Bangkok case suggests that urban governance capacity functions as an economic input shaping the financial and environmental viability of price-based urban reforms.

items.title: Safety Risk Assessment for Building Excavations Using Monte Carlo Simulation-Based Sensitivity Analysis
items.abstract: Building excavations in urban environments involve significant safety challenges arising from complex geotechnical conditions, adjacent structures, and construction uncertainties. This study proposes an integrated framework for identifying and prioritizing excavation safety risks and for quantitatively assessing their schedule consequences under uncertainty. An initial literature review identified 25 excavation-related safety risks, which were subsequently evaluated using the Fuzzy Delphi Method with input from 25 experts. The evaluated process resulted in the validation of 18 safety risks. The Shannon Entropy method was then employed to determine the relative importance of five project-performance criteria, while the VIKOR method was used to rank the identified risks based on expert assessments from 156 construction professionals. The five highest-ranked risks were transferred to a schedule-focused Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) of a steel truss-supported excavation project in Karaj, Iran. The Delphi survey screening scores are interpreted as expert-derived plausibility scores and are converted to associated subjective scenario probabilities through proportional possibility-to-probability normalization. The simulation results demonstrated that the inclusion of risk-related uncertainties increased the project duration from 62 days to approximately 132.5 days. A robustness check against equal scenario weights produced only small changes in the representative Phase 1 and Phase 2 expected durations (1.42% and 1.81%, respectively), indicating limited local sensitivity to the selected probability transformation. The principal contribution of the study is the explicit, excavation-specific linkage between expert consensus, multi-criteria risk prioritization, and probabilistic schedule-consequence analysis, and an uncertainty-transformation robustness check.

items.title: Beyond the Clinical Horizon: A Critical Futures Policy Delphi Framework for Dementia Prevention Literacy, Adult Vaccination and Digital Health Equity, 2030–2045
items.abstract: Public health messaging often assumes that publishing evidence on modifiable dementia risk factors will produce population-level behaviour change. A persistent translation gap suggests otherwise. This conceptual paper proposes a framework that shifts attention from individual accountability to structural health equity, focusing on two areas: adult vaccination, where observational studies report associations with lower dementia incidence, and digital health technologies. We describe a three-round mixed-methods Policy Delphi study for the 2030–2045 horizon that draws on Causal Layered Analysis, critical discourse analysis and realist evaluation. Building on Turoff's original Policy Delphi, which was designed to surface disagreement, the framework adds a structured Dissent Registry Matrix that records the rationale, context and policy implications of divergent expert views alongside conventional consensus statistics. Four seed scenarios, built on technology integration and structural equity, are proposed for panel critique. The framework offers policymakers, clinicians and educators a transparent method for examining how dementia prevention may be shaped by social and structural conditions, and it specifies the design decisions needed for empirical testing.

items.title: Advancing nutrient circularity in agriculture: Critical perspectives on recycling-derived bio-based fertilisers, production, and adoption challenges
Expert consensus on the clinical and organizational use of VNS therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy in the United Arab Emirates: a single-round modified Delphi study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Epilepsy affects over 50 million people worldwide, and approximately one third of patients develop drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), a major driver of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is an established neuromodulatory treatment option for DRE, but local guidance on its use in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) remains limited. This study aimed to establish an expert consensus to define best practices for the effective and efficient use of the VNS in the UAE setting. METHODS: A multidisciplinary Task Force conducted a literature review and developed 25 evidence- and experience-informed statements, which were refined during an in-person expert meeting to ensure clinical relevance for the UAE context. Statements were rated through a single-round modified Delphi process involving UAE neurologists and neurosurgeons. Participants rated their agreement with each statement using a 7-point Likert scale. Consensus was predefined as ≥ 70% agreement, corresponding to ratings of 6-7. Statements with 60-69% agreement were classified as moderate agreement but were not considered to have reached consensus. RESULTS: Fifty-six experts completed the Delphi round, corresponding to a 75.7% response rate. Item-level denominators varied across statements. Eighteen of 25 statements reached consensus, six demonstrated moderate agreement, and one did not reach consensus. Strong agreement was observed for patient selection, safety, structured parameter optimization, and multidisciplinary care pathways. Moderate agreement emerged for presurgical evaluation, timing of implantation, and selected clinical scenarios. CONCLUSION: Building on existing international guidance and previous Delphi work in other settings, this study provides a UAE-specific description of expert agreement and variability on the clinical and organizational use of VNS for DRE. The findings may inform future local pathway development and identify areas requiring clearer definitio

items.title: SUSTAINABLE INFRASTRUCTURE PLANNING FOR REGIONAL TOURISM DEVELOPMENT IN SAUDI ARABIA: A FRAMEWORK FOR RESILIENT AND SAFE GIGA-PROJECT DELIVERY
items.abstract: The growth of tourism in Saudi Arabia is taking place via a number of destinations spread across the region, and the success of these destinations relies on infrastructure systems that are reliable, ecologically compatible, safe when in operation, and capable of adapting afterwards. However, research in the field of tourism, studies in regional planning, and the literature on risk in large-scale projects are frequently regarded as separate areas of discussion. This review brings those different areas together and presents a lifecycle framework for the safe and resilient delivery of giga-projects. A structured integrative review was carried out using 30 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, all of which had resolvable digital object identifiers. The evidence was analysed according to six areas: regional accessibility, energy and water security, blue-green and heritage systems, construction safety and risk, governance and community value, and adaptive destination operations. The synthesis demonstrates that infrastructure should be planned as part of a interconnected regional service ecosystem rather than as a collection of separate project assets. In dry and coastal areas, ecological thresholds, heat exposure, the availability of water, the reliability of renewable energy, evacuation capacity, and the continuity of the supply chain must all be considered as design constraints before any capital is committed.

items.title: From agricultural residues to tradeable bio-assets in Africa: a policy and practice framework for circular agro-industrial value chains
items.abstract: Agricultural residues in Sub-Saharan Africa are often described as an underused resource, but their conversion into marketable products is constrained by feedstock variability, competing uses, logistics, product standards, environmental risks, and uncertain demand. Utilizing a critical narrative policy synthesis, this paper develops a policy and practice framework for assessing when selected agricultural residues can become credible circular bio-assets for local use and, where conditions permit, regional trade. The framework connects four decision layers: (1) technically and economically recoverable feedstock, ownership, and explicit smallholder and land-use safeguards; (2) technology and product selection; (3) environmental, technical, and economic evidence; and (4) quality assurance, finance, MSME AfCFTA compliance costs, and trade infrastructure. It examines cassava processing effluents, cocoa pod husks, palm oil mill effluents and other palm residues, sugarcane bagasse, and livestock manure across biochemical, thermochemical, bioconversion, and physicochemical pathways. Material Flow Analysis, Life Cycle Assessment, and Techno-Economic Analysis are treated as complementary evidence rather than as stand-alone proof of viability. The paper also examines the conditions under which AfCFTA trade facilitation, quality-assurance infrastructure, payment systems, and development finance can support commercialization. A critical comparison with existing African circular-bioeconomy reviews shows that prior work has largely focused on the potential and challenges of circular bioeconomy, the status of circular practices in selected food systems, or specific technology portfolios. This paper extends that literature by linking resource security, technology choice, evidence thresholds, product quality, market validation, and cross-border transaction requirements within one staged decision architecture governed by conditional decision gates. The framework is intentionally condit

items.title: Migrant Labour and the Unorganised Sector in a Remittance Economy: Labour Supply, Informality and Regional Development in Kerala
items.venue: International Journal of Commerce and Management Research Studies (IJCMRS)
items.abstract: This study examines the role of inter-state migrant labour in the unorganised sector of Kerala, a state whose economy is shaped simultaneously by large-scale emigration to the Gulf and large-scale in-migration from other Indian states. It combines an integrative review of 28 scholarly and institutional sources with a descriptive analysis of secondary data drawn from the Kerala Migration Surveys, the Gulati Institute survey of domestic migrant labour, the Reserve Bank of India's state-level wage statistics, the Periodic Labour Force Survey and the Kerala Economic Review. The data show that emigration has stabilised at about 2.2 million persons while remittances have risen to Rs 2.17 lakh crore, or 23.2% of net state domestic product, in 2023; that rural daily wages in Kerala exceed the all-India average by 109 to 125% across agricultural, non-agricultural and construction work; that agriculture has fallen to about 8% of gross state value added while services approach two-thirds; and that a domestic migrant workforce estimated at 2.5 million in 2013, drawn chiefly from West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha and concentrated in construction, fills the manual-labour gap that these conditions create. Four themes are developed: the Kerala labour market paradox, the structural shift of employment out of agriculture, the position of migrant workers as the flexible labour force of the unorganised sector, and the welfare balance between income gains at origin and precarity at destination. The findings are organised into a Supply–Absorption–Welfare framework and five research propositions. The paper argues that migrant labour has become a structural rather than a transitional feature of Kerala's economy, that the unorganised sector is the channel through which it is absorbed, and that the state's development model now depends on the inclusion of workers it does not formally count. Implications are offered for employers, industry bodies and policymakers.

items.title: Advancing the service-oriented transition of smart cities: Evaluating the intelligent approval quality
items.abstract: In the context of smart cities development and digital governance, administrative intelligent approval plays an effective and valuable role in government service transformation. However, the explosive application of technology has led to several challenges of approval quality such as inconsistent with due process, weak error correction mechanism of algorithmic decision-making and lagged supervisory regime, which hinder the service-oriented transformation. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the quality of intelligent approval using rigorous, rational, and universally applicable methods, which may not only enhance the service standards of digital government and advance smart cities development toward maturity, but also contribute to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. In the stage of evaluation indicator system construction, determining first-level indicators including legality, rationality, satisfaction and supervision by Delphi Method. Then the corresponding 10 secondary indicators and 38 tertiary indicators are progressively expanded based on value guidance, institutional norms, literature research and cases. In the stage of applying, Taiyuan in China is taken as the evaluation object and implemented through Analytic Hierarchy Process and Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation. The evaluation results indicated that although the overall quality shows good, there are several potential and prominent problems, including insufficient specific modes, inaccessible the right to a hearing, inadequate staff service, ineffective public supervision and the lack of transparency, and the targeted strategies are proposed for improving the approval quality. Additionally, future research will establish a dedicated evaluation committee, leverage digital platforms more extensively, and strengthen relevant legislation and theoretical support.

items.title: Strategic Convergence without Alignment: Vietnam–U.S. Relations amid a Changing Regional Order
items.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
items.abstract: Vietnam–U.S. relations have undergone a remarkable transformation from diplomatic normalization in 1995 to the establishment of a Comprehensive Partnership in 2013 and a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2023. Yet the rapid deepening of economic, technological, maritime security, and institutional cooperation has not led Vietnam to an alliance or formal strategic alignment with the United States. This article explains this apparent paradox through the concept of “strategic convergence without alignment,” defined as a condition in which the overlap of strategic interests and the scope of functional cooperation between two states expand substantially, while the weaker party deliberately limits security and strategic commitments to preserve its autonomy and room for strategic maneuver. Using a multi-level analytical framework, historical process tracing from 1995 to the present, this study illuminates the dynamics of "strategic convergence without alignment" in Vietnam–U.S. relations. The findings reveal four primary drivers of convergence: the changing regional security environment; economic complementarity and supply chain restructuring; the emergence of semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), and technology as a new strategic pillar; and institutionalized bilateral engagement accompanied by trust-building over three decades of normalized relations. Conversely, five structural constraints continue to preclude formal alignment: Vietnam's geopolitical proximity and power asymmetry vis-à-vis China; Vietnam's foreign policy of independence, self-reliance, and its "Four Noes" defense policy; domestic institutional differences; bilateral trade frictions; and the inherent volatility of U.S. politico-economic commitments The article argues that over the short to medium term, the most likely trajectory for Vietnam–U.S. relations is the continued deepening of a “selective strategic partnership”, characterized by “high functional cooperation but low alliance commitme

items.title: Daylighting and Ventilation Strategies for Educational Buildings in the Hot and Dry Climate of Lothal, Gujarat
items.venue: International Journal of Innovations in Science Engineering and Management.
items.abstract: Educational buildings in hot–dry climates such as Lothal, Gujarat face critical challenges in achieving thermal and visual comfort due to high solar radiation, extreme temperatures, and low humidity. While these conditions increase dependence on mechanical cooling and artificial lighting, they also present strong potential for passive environmental control through daylighting and natural ventilation. This study aims to evaluate climate-responsive design strategies that enhance indoor environmental quality in educational buildings while reducing energy consumption. The research addresses the gap in the application of quantified passive design strategies for educational environments in hot–dry regions. The methodology includes climatic data analysis, literature review of passive design principles, and comparative case studies of educational institutions in similar climatic contexts. Simulation tools such as Climate Consultant, Design Builder, and Radiance are used to assess daylight performance Daylight Factor and Useful Daylight Illuminance and airflow patterns by CFD analysis under varying window to wall ratios of 20%, 40%, and 60%. The results indicate that a 40% WWR ratio achieves optimal daylight distribution DF: 1.5 to 2.5% and maintains useful daylight illuminance of 100–2000 lux across a majority of the classroom area, while higher ratios lead to glare and thermal discomfort. Cross ventilation strategies aligned with prevailing wind directions significantly improve air movement of 5–9 ACH, enhancing thermal comfort. The study concludes with design guidelines for climate-responsive educational buildings, focusing on orientation, shading, material selection, and spatial planning. Future research can extend to performance-based optimization and application at larger campus scales.

items.title: Framework for user-centred design and pre-occupancy design evaluation of higher education buildings
items.abstract: Purpose Higher education (HE) buildings often exhibit persistent performance gaps that compromise user comfort, health and satisfaction. These adverse outcomes are frequently linked to inadequate end-user engagement in the design phase. This study develops and validates a holistic framework for end-user engagement that systematically integrates user inputs throughout the design process to enable user-centred design and pre-occupancy evaluation, proactively mitigating performance gaps. Design/methodology/approach The framework was formulated through an integrative review and idea mapping from three knowledge areas: user engagement theories, functional performance specification and design elements. The framework was validated through 70 structured interviews: 35 with end-users, 17 with HE building professionals, and 18 with industry architects. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn tests. Qualitative insights were examined through content analysis. Findings The study presents a novel framework featuring a process-flow model and modules for user-requirements acquisition and design evaluation to engage end-users throughout HE building design. The framework’s overall effectiveness for end-user involvement across pre-design, schematic and detailed design was rated 8.4 out of 10. Study participants identified many benefits of the framework, including comprehensiveness, facilitation of end-user engagement across all design stages, adaptability, quantifiable scoring, stimulation of user reflection, ease of distribution and robustness. Originality/value The systemised framework addresses longstanding barriers to end-user engagement in HE building design. Its modular and traceable structure enables those with limited experience to implement structured engagement practices. By facilitating early, evidence-based user input, the framework promotes people-centred design, minimises post-occupancy modifications and enhances building pe

items.title: Building quality systems through teacher-led evidence: participatory micro-RCTs as a model for improvement in education
items.abstract: Dr Emma Dobson and Dr Wayne Harrison in this chapter argue that education quality systems are improved most effectively when teachers help generate evidence themselves, using participatory action research (PAR) and small-scale micro-randomised controlled trials (micro-RCTs) to test strategies in real classrooms. It shows how combining these teacher-led trials with cumulative meta-analysis and Delphi consensus-building creates feedback loops that connect classroom learning to school-, regional- and policy-level improvement. For education advisers, the key implication is to support systems that balance rigour with professional agency, treating variation as a source of learning and building cultures of trust, collaboration and continuous improvement.

items.title: Identification and Evaluation of Risk in Sustainable Construction Projects: Application of a Hybrid BWM–COCOSO Approach
items.abstract: Uncertainty and risk are inherent characteristics of construction projects, particularly in large and complex upstream oil and gas developments. Effective identification and prioritization of risks are therefore essential for improving project decision making and achieving sustainable outcomes. This study aims to identify and evaluate the key risks affecting sustainable construction projects in the upstream oil and gas industry of Iran using a hybrid Best–Worst Method (BWM) and Combined Compromise Solution (COCOSO) approach. Initially, 40 potential risks were identified from literature and expert opinions and validated through the Fuzzy Delphi method (FDM). Subsequently, BWM was applied to determine the weights of the risk evaluation criteria, where “impact on quality” emerged as the most influential criterion. The COCOSO method was then employed to prioritize the identified risks. The results indicate that insufficient technical information, inefficient project management, and exchange rate fluctuations are the most critical risks. Sensitivity analysis using the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), Multi-Attributive Border Approximation Area Comparison (MABAC), and Evaluation based on Distance from Average Solution (EDAS) was conducted to examine the stability of the obtained risk rankings. The results showed a high degree of consistency across the alternative ranking methods and the examined sensitivity scenarios. These findings provide practical insights for improving risk management and supporting the prioritization of critical risks in sustainable construction projects within the upstream oil and gas sector.

items.title: Building Institutional Integrity Through Service Failure-recovery: Accountability and Cultural Transformation in Public Bureaucracy
items.abstract: Institutional integrity in public bureaucracy is often pursued through formal compliance mechanisms, yet growing scholarship suggests that integrity also emerges from everyday administrative practices that embed accountability, transparency, and ethical responsiveness. This study examines how service failure recovery functions as an internal mechanism for strengthening institutional integrity through cultural transformation in a public organization. The research focuses on the National Institute of Public Administration regional office in Makassar, Indonesia (Pusjar SKMP LAN), where a structured service failure recovery system has been implemented since 2014 and has contributed to the organization receiving the Wilayah Birokrasi Bersih dan Melayani (WBBM) recognition for clean and service-oriented bureaucracy. Using a longitudinal case study design, the research employs mixed methods including process tracing, semi-structured interviews with managers and frontline staff, document analysis of service records and organizational reports, and examination of service performance indicators over time. The findings indicate that systematic service failure recovery practices strengthened internal accountability, increased psychological safety among civil servants, and encouraged learning-oriented responses to service complaints. Repeated engagement in complaint handling gradually shifted organizational norms from blame avoidance toward ethical responsiveness and citizen-centred service values. The study concludes that routinized service recovery practices can function as a practical integrity-building mechanism that complements formal compliance and oversight systems. By showing how accountability is embedded in daily service routines, the research contributes to understanding how public organizations can strengthen integrity and legitimacy through culturally embedded administrative practices.

items.title: Literature-derived criteria and expert-perceived influence structure for age-friendly living environments among older adults living with HIV in China: a text-mining, fuzzy Delphi, and fuzzy DEMATEL study
items.abstract: Background Older adults living with HIV (OALHIV) may experience the demands of long-term HIV care together with frailty, stigma, privacy concerns, and barriers in their residential environment. This study developed an exploratory set of age-friendly living-environment criteria and examined how experts perceived influence among the resulting domains. It did not test epidemiological causality or measure regional service performance. Methods An English-language Web of Science corpus covering 2003–2023 was processed with term co-occurrence mapping and clustering. Fuzzy Delphi method (FDM) ratings from 28 experts were used to screen candidate criteria, followed by domain-level fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (FDEMATEL). Sensitivity analyses examined the FDM cutoff and fuzzy-attitude parameter, and FDEMATEL was calculated using the standard zero-diagonal convention. Results The workflow included 1,487 records, 89 cleaned terms, 43 second-round candidates, and 22 retained criteria in five domains. The second-round mean FDM threshold was 0.4729. The same 22 criteria were retained for fixed thresholds from 0.453 to 0.478, for recalculated fuzzy-attitude parameters from 0.40 to 0.60, and under leave-one-criterion-out recalculation. In the zero-diagonal FDEMATEL analysis, healthcare accessibility ( D − R = 0.320), social support network (0.683), and digital inclusion and assistive technology (0.866) occupied net-influencing positions; built-environment adaptation (−1.170) and psychological wellbeing and destigmatization (−0.699) occupied net-influenced positions. The sign classification matched the originally reported calculation, although magnitudes changed. Conclusions The framework is hypothesis-generating and reflects literature-derived concepts and expert judgement, not demonstrated causal effects or the directly reported priorities of OALHIV. Patient and community co-design, field measurement, and external validation are required before the criteria

items.title: Building Capacity in Paediatric Specialty Practice: Educational Priorities for Nigerian Occupational Therapy Practitioners
items.abstract: Background: Although occupational therapy (OT) educational priorities have been studied globally, evidence specific to pediatric practice in Nigeria remains limited, leaving a knowledge gap that may hinder entry-level practitioners' preparation for this specialist practice area. This study aimed to identify educational priorities for paediatric specialty practice among occupational therapy practitioners in Nigeria. Methodology: An exploratory mixed-method design comprising a cross-sectional survey and a two-round Delphi process was used. In Phase 1, 55 occupational therapy practitioners generated paediatric occupational therapy competencies using an online questionnaire. In Phase 2, these competencies were rated by paediatric occupational therapy experts (n = 17 in Round 1; n = 16 in Round 2). Data were analysed using thematic content analysis, descriptive statistics, and the content validity index (CVI). Competencies with CVI ≥ 0.80 were retained, those scoring 0.70–0.79 were revised, and items below 0.70 were excluded. Results: With a response rate of 57.3%, practitioners from diverse practice settings, with a mean professional experience of 4.6 ± 2.8 years, identified 46 competencies that were organised into five educational themes: basic medical and behavioural sciences; assessment and evaluation; professional values, attitudes, and skills; knowledge of paediatrics and occupational therapy; and intervention processes. Following Round 1, two competencies were revised and four were excluded. Consensus was achieved on 41 competencies after Round 2. Fifteen competencies were rated as essential, 17 as important, and 9 as optional. Twenty competencies were reported as met during entry-level training, while 15 were partially met and 11 were unmet. Conclusion: Priority educational needs for paediatric occupational therapy practice in Nigeria span assessment, foundational biomedical and behavioural sciences, paediatric-specific OT knowledge, intervention processes, and p
