items.title: DIGITAL PROCUREMENT GOVERNANCE AND LOCAL SUPPLIER INTEGRATION: A TECHNOLOGY-DRIVEN SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORK FOR SAUDI ARABIAS URBAN DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS
items.abstract: Saudi Arabias urban development programme provides a significant test of whether digital procurement can genuinely advance the participation of domestic suppliers whilst still maintaining commercial rigour. There is a considerable body of literature that looks at construction supply chain integration, e-procurement, digital project records and public procurement accountability but very little that actually explains how these various strands should be governed in conjunction. This critical integrative review draws on thirty DOI identifiable publications from 2020 to 2025 to develop a technologyenabled governance framework appropriate to the context of complex urban projects.

items.title: Parametric Analysis of Baffle External Shading for Sustainable Building Design: Daylighting and Thermal Performance Optimization in Cold Climate Regions of China
items.abstract: Building energy efficiency is critical for achieving sustainable development goals, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where rapid urbanization drives energy demand growth. This study presents a parametric analysis of baffle external shading for a west-facing educational building in Xianyang, a cold climate region of China, integrating daylighting performance and indoor thermal regulation. Using Ladybug and Honeybee plugins in Grasshopper, three key shading parameters—shading characteristic value (x), baffle angle (δ), and baffle arc (θ)—were systematically varied to evaluate their effects on solar radiation distribution, useful daylight illuminance (UDI), and indoor temperature. Results indicate that vertical louvers with x ≥ 0.50 and δ = 45° in the west orientation reduce ground radiation by up to 47% and lower average indoor temperature by approximately 2 °C under free-running conditions, while UDI reaches 81.3% of occupied hours (6.5 h/d) with optimized shading in cold regions. The baffle arc (θ) has negligible impact. These findings provide actionable design guidelines for cost-effective passive cooling, requiring less than 2% of total building investment with simulated annual energy savings of 10.5% for the case-study classroom (cooling and heating terms only), supporting China’s “Dual Carbon” goals and broader sustainable urban development targets.

Construction of an evaluation index system for emergency response capacity for adverse events following immunisation in secondary and tertiary hospitals across Guangxi
items.abstract: This study aimed to develop an evaluation index system to assess hospitals' emergency response capacity for adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) in secondary and tertiary facilities in Guangxi, China. The findings intend to inform the assessment and systematic improvement of AEFI emergency preparedness within regional hospitals, ultimately safeguarding the overall safety of vaccination programmes.A preliminary framework and draft indicators were established through comprehensive literature review. Two rounds of the Delphi method were implemented, mean expert authority coefficient was 0.91 ± 0.03; all indicators had coefficient of variation < 0.25; Kendall's W concordance coefficients were 0.400 (round 1) and 0.503 (round 2), both with P < 0.01. With indicators screened and revised iteratively based on expert feedback and group discussion.The analytic hierarchy process (AHP) was subsequently adopted to refine the index system. A hierarchical structure and pairwise comparison matrices were constructed, and SPSS AU software was used to calculate the weight of each indicator, conduct hierarchical ranking and consistency tests. Combined weights for tertiary indicators were computed via multiplicative probability.The weights of primary indicators, ranked in descending order, were as follows: First aid knowledge (0.11338), first aid command and coordination (0.1129), first aid personnel (0.11241), first aid techniques and equipment (0.11241), emergency medicine reserves (0.11241), emergency aid plan (0.11192), emergency disposal informatisation (0.10949), first aid site (0.10803), and monitoring early warning and reporting (0.10706). Consensus was achieved among participating experts after two rounds of consultation. items.title: Digital Transformation of Construction Supply Chains through SAP S/4HANA and SAP Ariba: An Integrated Procurement Management Framework for Saudi Vision 2030 Megaprojects
items.venue: Global Academic Journal of Economics and Business
items.abstract: Saudi Arabia's megaproject programme is placing ever greater pressure on the coordination required in construction procurement, with the various demands of design changes, a multitude of dispersed suppliers, complex contractual interfaces and long delivery times all coming into play. While research into digitalisation has identified the potential for improved visibility and collaboration, it is rarely clear from that research how enterprise transaction controls and engagement with external suppliers should be arranged as one integrated process. This integrative review critically reviews 30 publications identified via DOI search between 2020 and 2025 in the areas of construction supply chain management, e-procurement, enterprise integration, supplier governance and sustainable delivery. The evidence was gathered via targeted literature discovery, a backward search of relevant reference lists and source level bibliographic checks. The review distinguishes between the actual challenges that are documented in the literature and the capabilities which could plausibly be realised through the use of SAP S/4HANA and SAP Ariba. Its key contribution is a six-layer procurement management framework which links project requirements through to performance assurance via a set of common data definitions and controlled decision rights. The framework treats financial commitment validation, material traceability, exception management and supplier accountability as interdependent functions rather than as separate software features. A staged adoption pathway and a set of auditable performance indicators are proposed for use in the Saudi megaproject context. As a conceptual review it makes no claim as to the framework having been experimentally validated or as having delivered any quantifiable savings. The review concludes that the value of integration is as much to do with data stewardship, contractual alignment and cross organisational engagement as it is with the functionality of the

items.title: Engineering Optimization of Natural Ventilation for Thermal Comfort and Energy Efficiency in Institutional Office Buildings in Hot-Humid Ede, Nigeria: A Field Evidence-Based Four-Stage Framework
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Code This preprint presents field evidence-based engineering optimization of natural ventilation for thermal comfort and energy efficiency in institutional office buildings in hot-humid Ede, Nigeria (7°44'12"N, 4°26'10"E, 269m, Tropical rainforest Af climate). CONTEXT AND FUNDING:This research was funded by Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund), Abuja, Nigeria under Institution Based Research (IBR) Grant Reference No. FPE/DRD/IBR/17-21/B6/2025/10 at Federal Polytechnic, Ede, Osun State, Nigeria. Tenure: January 2025 - October 2026. This preprint is submitted to Journal of Building Engineering (Elsevier, Q1, Impact Factor 8.1, ISSN 2352-7102) under review (Manuscript ID JBE-XXXX). It is distinct from concurrent Journal of Building Physics (SAGE, Q3, IF 2.3) submission focusing on performance and diurnal collapse per COPE guidelines - this paper focuses on engineering optimization and energy efficiency. METHODOLOGY:Triangulated approach: (i) 10-year climatic analysis (2013-2023) from Nigeria Meteorological Agency (NIMET) and Osun State Ministry of Environment, (ii) indoor environmental monitoring of 34 institutional offices per ASHRAE 55-2020 and ISO 7726 standards (air temperature Ta via Testo 176 H1 ±0.2°C, relative humidity RH ±2%, air velocity Vi via Testo 405i hot-wire ±0.01 m/s at 1.1m height, mean radiant temperature MRT via black globe Ø150mm, CO2 via Testo 315-3 ±3%, thrice daily 09:00/13:00/16:00 WAT for 14 days hot season 15-28 March 2024), (iii) morphological survey (Window-to-Wall Ratio WWR, depth, orientation, window type, obstruction 30%), (iv) occupant comfort survey n=182 using ASHRAE 7-point thermal sensation vote TSV scale (-3 to +3), thermal preference, acceptability (metabolic 1.2 met, clothing 0.71 clo tropical office), and (v) bioclimatic analysis using Givoni psychrometric chart (1992) and Mahoney Tables (1971), PMV-PPD via CBE Thermal Comfort Tool. Statistical analysis: Pearson correlation, t-test, SPSS v26, p<0.05. Ethics: FPE/REC/2026/04/1

items.abstract: The article examined opportunities for industrial symbiosis in Central Asian agroindustrial clusters through circular economy practices and digitalisation. Comparative analysis, scenario modelling and statistical synthesis were applied. Models addressed waste processing, biogas production and water reuse in livestock and fruit and vegetable production. Scenario estimates indicated opportunities to reduce resource consumption and generate added value. Uzbekistan’s cluster infrastructure and digital development indicators were reviewed. Digital platforms were considered for coordinating resource exchanges between enterprises. Proposals addressed regional cooperation, investment and employment within the regional agricultural context. The need to validate projected economic and environmental outcomes through pilot projects was acknowledged.

items.title: LOCALIZATION OF INDUSTRIAL LUBRICANTS AND PETROLEUM PRODUCT SUPPLY CHAINS IN SAUDI ARABIAS OIL AND GAS SECTOR UNDER VISION 2030
items.abstract: The Saudi initiative to localise its industry is now moving the procurement of oil and gas away from simple import substitution and towards the development of domestic capabilities. Industrial lubricants and other petroleum products serve as a good example since they involve regular demand alongside complex formulations, depend on imported additives, have to meet equipment approval requirements, and also have potential in the area of the circular economy. This study draws on peer-reviewed evidence published between 2020 and 2025 to look at where localisation can generate defensible value throughout the supply chain for lubricants and petroleum products and to identify the capabilities needed to ensure reliability, quality, and cost control. A structured integrative review of thirty studies verified by the DOI was carried out and the studies were coded according to feasibility of localisation, supplier capability, resilience, digitalisation, sustainability, and governance. The findings show that localisation should advance at an uneven rate along the value chain. Activities such as blending, packaging, laboratory testing, warehousing, providing field technical services, collecting used oil, and certain re-refining operations present relatively short-term opportunities, while advanced additive chemistry and special formulations need a much longer period for building up capabilities.

items.title: Toward Sustainable Industrial Spatial Planning: Integrating Supply Chain Management and Environmental–Economic Assessment for the Proposed Al-Kuraymat Industrial Zone, Egypt
items.venue: SVU-International Journal of Engineering Sciences and Applications
items.abstract: Industrial zones play a vital role in economic growth and regional development; however, they are increasingly challenged by inefficient resource utilization, environmental degradation, and fragmented industrial development. These challenges highlight the need for integrated planning approaches that improve industrial performance while supporting environmental sustainability. This study develops an integrated framework that combines Supply Chain Management (SCM), Material Flow Analysis (MFA), Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), and environmental–economic assessment to support sustainable industrial spatial planning. The framework is applied to the proposed Al-Kuraymat Industrial Zone in Egypt, where resource availability, material flows, industrial linkages, transportation networks, environmental conditions, and existing infrastructure are systematically assessed to identify opportunities for industrial integration and sustainable development. Based on this assessment, a spatial planning model is developed to optimize industrial zoning, strengthen logistics connectivity, promote industrial symbiosis, and enhance circular resource flows. Three alternative development scenarios are also evaluated to examine the environmental and economic implications of different levels of supply chain integration. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework identifies practical opportunities to improve resource efficiency, reduce industrial waste, enhance environmental performance, support renewable energy utilization, and strengthen spatial integration among industrial activities. By integrating supply chain principles with environmental and spatial planning, the framework provides a practical decision-support tool for sustainable industrial development and offers a planning approach that supports circular economy principles and the objectives of Egypt Vision 2030.

items.title: Developing Light Engineering Industry from Repurposing E-Waste in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Electronic waste (e-waste) refers to disposed electrical and electronic equipment. In Bangladesh, e-waste offers resource potential as well as environmental concern. The growing prominence of e-waste has the potential for contributing to resource recovery and industrial development in the context of the light engineering industry. There is still a large research gap in establishing connections among the existing literature in these aspects, which are available and relevant to the Bangladeshi context. To manage these challenges, an approach is required that links sustainability with the development of formalized, safe, and regionally appropriate industries. A qualitative approach that combines secondary statistical data analysis with spatial evaluation is adopted for this research. An indexing framework assesses existing facilities based on spatial efficiency, environmental performance, and worker safety, drawing from comparative case studies and theoretical grounding in circular economy principles and sustainable design guidelines. To bridge these gaps, the research investigates how context-responsive architectural strategies might enhance sustainability, efficiency, and safety. This will help Bangladesh to explore a potential to establish integrated light engineering industries by formally managing e-waste within a new multidisciplinary framework.

items.title: Europe
items.abstract: This chapter examines the contradictory state of mobility and related policy landscape in Europe, where progress towards sustainable transport coexists with deepening carbon-intensive travel. Drawing on empirical evidence across long-distance and urban mobility, the chapter documents both encouraging trends – the growth of high-speed rail, cycling gains in major cities, and the proliferation of low-emission zones – and persistent structural challenges, including rising aviation demand, continued highway expansion, and growing vehicle size. The chapter analyses the multi-level governance landscape shaping these trends, from EU infrastructure policy and market liberalisation to urban demand management and land-use planning. It identifies five political priorities for the coming decades: improving cross-level policy coherence; prioritising the performance of existing infrastructure over new construction; targeting accessibility rather than mobility alone; steering technological innovation deliberately; and deploying stronger transport demand management. The chapter concludes that lasting transition requires democratic engagement and attention to transport justice, as decarbonisation without equity risks reinforcing both inequality and political resistance.

items.title: RURACTIVE D7.5 Policy recommendations and guidance
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This deliverable presents the final policy recommendations and implementation guidance developed through the RURACTIVE project to support more just, sustainable, resilient and inclusive rural development across Europe. Based on evidence from twelve Rural Innovation Ecosystems (RIEs), territorial experimentation, policy analysis, stakeholder engagement and policy co-creation, the report translates project findings into practical recommendations for European, national, regional and local policymakers. Rather than proposing a new rural policy framework, it identifies how existing policy instruments can be better coordinated through integrated, place-based and participatory territorial governance. The recommendations cover eight horizontal priorities and six Rural Development Drivers: local services, health and wellbeing; sustainable multimodal mobility; culture and cultural innovation; sustainable agrifood systems and ecosystem management; energy transition and climate neutrality; and nature-based and cultural tourism. Key areas of focus include strengthening Rural Innovation Ecosystems and multi-level governance, advancing the Right to Stay, reinforcing intermediary organisations and local capacity, improving coherence across European policy instruments, strengthening the territorial dimension of National and Regional Partnership Plans, and developing outcome-oriented monitoring frameworks centred on accessibility, affordability, resilience, participation, wellbeing, demographic sustainability and territorial attractiveness. The recommendations are grounded in a participatory and evidence-based policy development process involving the twelve RURACTIVE Dynamos and their Local Action Plans, four RURACTIVE Forums, validation with the Multi-Stakeholder Advisory Board and external experts, and benchmarking against other Horizon Europe projects and wider European policy debates. In total, 79 proto-policy recommendations were progressively refined and consolidated into the f

items.title: Circular Modality in Construction
items.abstract: A general consensus is that conventional linear modalities guarantee no industrial sustenance in the long run for many obvious reasons. This is where the topicality of circularity has been accentuated for the last two decades or so in the socio-political arena. However, anecdotal evidence suggests that the emphasis given to circularity in the construction industry is relatively low. Tackling this issue essentially warrants a rigorous co-production of integrated know-how, preferably beyond sectoral boundaries. The present study sheds light on interdisciplinary approaches taken to deal with the slowness of transmuting circularity into the construction sector. A comprehensive literature survey was undertaken to understand this phenomenon at the policy, firm, and site levels. The analysis included 128 articles published in high-impact journals between 2003 and 2024. Eighty-seven gaps in terms of theory, knowledge, practice, method, empiricism, and policy were observed. Forty-four thematic sub-clusters have the potential for empirical research. A new framework was finally proposed to scaffold the systemic transition towards a circular construction sector. On a practical level, the study offers valuable insights and instruments for industry personnel to gauge the efficacy of their own circular approaches and initiatives.

items.title: Architectural practice and the circular built environment transition: empirical insights from Australia
items.abstract: The transition towards a Circular Economy (CE) offers a key pathway to decarbonize the built environment. However, uptake is slow and empirical research on CE adoption in the building industry remains limited, particularly in Australia, where circularity rates are below the global average.This study examines Australian architectural professionals as key actors in the transition towards a circular built environment. It investigates perceptions of CE and the barriers and enablers shaping its implementation through the lived experiences of architectural professionals in navigating CE policies, industry agendas, professional aspirations, and the realities of everyday practice.In-depth, semi-structured interviews with architectural professionals (n = 12) are thematically analysed, revealing fragmented CE perceptions and practices and systemic barriers such as regulatory misalignment, knowledge gaps, limited organizational capacity, market immaturity, and cultural inertia. The study concludes that circular built environment transition requires coordinated action across policy, markets, educational, professional and cultural domains to strengthen the agency and leadership of architectural professionals and enable them to deliver circular outcomes. Identified enablers of CE adoption include collaborative delivery, education, legal instruments, and demonstration projects. The study contributes empirical evidence on Australian architectural engagement with CE and practice-based insights into how architectural practice can accelerate the circular built environment transition.

items.title: Accelerating plastic pollution mitigation in Vietnam: A circular economy policy and implementation roadmap
items.venue: Waste Management & Research The Journal for a Sustainable Circular Economy
items.abstract: Plastic pollution poses significant environmental and public health risks in Vietnam, driven by rising consumption and inadequate waste management. As one of the leading contributors to marine plastic leakage, the country faces challenges linked to linear economic practices and weak recycling systems. This study applies a structured narrative review protocol to synthesize evidence from policy, scientific, and institutional sources in the manuscript corpus. The analysis examines circular economy strategies and evaluates them using a comparative prioritization framework based on impact potential, implementation feasibility, and time-to-effect. The article identifies high-priority interventions for Vietnam (extended producer responsibility enforcement, source segregation, and reuse systems), highlights major barriers (fragmented governance, informal-system exclusion, and weak data systems), and proposes an actionable research and policy agenda for the transition to a circular plastics economy.

items.title: Gouvernance participative et planification du transport ferroviaire : quels enjeux pour les SERM ?
items.abstract: Participatory governance, seen as a key lever to guide and legitimize public action in urban planning and mobility, is at the heart of French Metropolitan Regional Express Services (SERM) projects. However, their specificities - service-oriented, multimodal, multiscale and multistakeholder - make their planning more complex, without a theoretical or operational framework being clearly established. This article sheds light on these issues through a critical review of participatory approaches in railway transport planning, whether mandatory or voluntary. It also relies on an in-depth analysis of the Clermont-Auvergne SERM, where focus groups and mapping tools are evaluated for their contribution to co-design. Our review shows that participatory approaches for infrastructure planning, whether mandatory or voluntary, often remain limited to top-down information sharing, with weak integration into project engineering. Voluntary approaches to service planning seem better suited but are rare. For SERM-type projects, despite tools better suited to capture service dynamics and territorial complexity, participation remains uneven and poorly integrated into decision-making. The case study highlights the value of an anticipated, progressive and visual approach, promoting iteration, understanding of the issues, and co-construction of proposals. It also reveals the persistent limitations of innovative geo-governance approaches that hinder co-design: lack of inclusion, weak appropriation, and absence of methodological framework. The proposed recommendations aim to structure an active, reproducible participatory method tailored to multicriteria criteria planning of complex services like SERM, within a dynamic of cross-fertilization between research and action to realize the participatory ambition. items.title: Comprendre les effets rebonds circulaires et innover pour les atténuer
items.abstract: Malgré des réussites locales, l’économie circulaire ne parvient pas encore à réduire significativement les consommations de matières premières vierges ou les impacts environnementaux à l’échelle planétaire. Parmi de nombreuses autres causes, la notion d’effet rebond circulaire a été mobilisée récemment pour expliquer ce constat, mais elle demeure peu connue. Cela amène deux questions : « Comment les effets rebonds se manifestent-ils en économie circulaire ? » et « Comment atténuer ces effets rebonds pour tendre vers une soutenabilité forte ? ». Cet article présente, au terme d’une revue de littérature métanarrative, une synthèse actualisée des travaux théoriques pour mieux comprendre le phénomène des effets rebonds circulaires. En croisant des études critiques sur l’économie circulaire, des travaux préconisant diverses formes d’innovation et des principes visant une soutenabilité forte, l’article propose également cinq pistes pratiques pour les atténuer à plusieurs niveaux systémiques.

items.title: Green Entrepreneurship as a Catalyst for Local Environmental Management in South Africa: Opportunities, Barriers, and Policy Implications
items.abstract: Building on the question of how environmental management can be addressed at the local level, the transition from a linear “take–make–dispose” model to a circular economy ( CE ) has become central to sustainable development, particularly in emerging economies facing intertwined environmental and socioeconomic challenges. In South Africa, high unemployment, energy security, and escalating waste generation intensify the urgency for systemic restructuring. This study examines green entrepreneurship (GE) as a catalyst for CE development within environmental management, focusing on Limpopo Province as a contextually rich case of resource potential and developmental vulnerability. Using a qualitative design grounded in thematic analysis, data were collected from 40 green entrepreneurs and 10 policymakers across recycling, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, green manufacturing, and governance sectors. Findings reveal a layered circular ecosystem comprising downstream resource recovery (recycling and waste management), midstream production transformation (renewable energy and regenerative agriculture), and upstream systemic enablers (consultancy and ecodesign services). These activities represent distinct circular business model innovations through which firms create environmental value by recovering resources, extending product life cycles, substituting fossil‐based inputs, and redesigning production processes. Findings indicate that green entrepreneurs implement a range of CE practices, including resource recovery, renewable‐energy provision, composting, and environmentally oriented manufacturing. Participants reported that these activities contributed to waste reduction, resource efficiency, and environmental sustainability. However, these reported outcomes reflect participant experiences and perceptions rather than independently verified environmental performance measures. items.title: Sustainability in Jordan’s municipal solid waste management system: reduction of methane emissions and benefits to public health
items.venue: Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management
items.abstract: Municipal solid waste management (MSWM) in Jordan faces significant challenges. Jordan's primary waste management strategy relies heavily on final disposal, with up to 80% of all generated solid waste ultimately being landfilled. These unsustainable practices lead to environmental degradation and public health risks. Increased methane emissions have harmed air quality: methane can lead to the formation of ground-level ozone, which in turn causes respiratory problems including asthma and pneumonia. The main objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of improved solid waste management strategies on methane emissions in the period from 2020 to 2050. The Low Emissions Analysis Platform (LEAP) is used for the analysis, and current methane emissions from municipal solid waste are estimated using data obtained from the Ministry of Local Administration, the Greater Amman Municipality, the Department of Statistics, and the World Health Organization. These datasets, which include information on waste quantities and landfill boundaries, are integrated into the LEAP software to facilitate estimation of methane emissions. Our analysis finds that, without intervention, methane emissions will rise from 4.3 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2020 to 7.8 million tons by 2050 due to increasing population and economic expansion. In addition to the serious environmental consequences, we estimate public health damages of $41 billion per year by 2050, linked to excess mortality. In the short-term, methane emissions can be mitigated by following a “circular economy” strategy of reuse and recycling. This could reduce methane emissions by 12% by 2030. Medium-term strategies, including the establishment of sanitary landfills and recycling facilities, combined with the short-term projects can reduce methane emissions 34% below baseline by 2040. items.title: An early-stage, multi-lifecycle assessment framework for sustainable material selection in automotive industry
items.abstract: The transition toward low-carbon mobility requires material-selection approaches that account for extended use cycles and cross-sector reuse pathways. However, early-stage automotive design decisions are typically informed by single-life cradle-to-grave assessments, which do not explicitly integrate reuse-induced substitution effects or multi-stage emission accounting within development timelines. This study operationalizes an integrated cradle-to-reuse-to-grave (C2R2G) assessment approach by combining established life cycle assessment (LCA), system expansion, and substitution modeling principles into an automotive-specific decision-support structure. The framework formalizes emission accounting across primary use, reuse preparation, secondary application, and end-of-life treatment, including explicit system expansion, substitution, and circular scenario modeling parameters. A bio-based laminated veneer lumber (LVL) seat-shell is evaluated as a demonstrative case within passenger vehicle applications. Scenario modeling compares single-life, recycling, and open-loop reuse pathways under varying lifetime and energy-intensity assumptions. Results indicate that reuse-driven substitution effects can significantly alter cumulative carbon footprints compared to single-life configurations, though outcomes remain highly sensitive to assumed service lifetimes, displaced material emission factors, and energy mixes in second-life sectors. Sensitivity analysis highlights key parameters influencing ranking stability and identifies boundary conditions under which reuse advantages diminish. Rather than proposing a new LCA methodology, this work demonstrates how established analytical components can be systematically integrated to support early-stage automotive material pathway evaluation. The approach enhances transparency in allocation choices and trade-off identification, contributing to more informed low-carbon design decisions in circular mobility systems. Graphical Abstract

items.title: Governing Cross-Border Nuclear Partnerships: A Q-NPT Framework Analysis of the Egypt–Russia El Dabaa Nuclear Power Project
items.abstract: Large-scale nuclear energy projects depend on credible governance arrangements to support international cooperation and address institutional and societal concerns surrounding nuclear energy development. This study applies the Qudrat-Ullah Nuclear Peace and Trust (Q-NPT) framework to examine the governance of the Egypt–Russia El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant (ERENPP). The framework comprises four pillars—Trust, Equity, Transparency, and Inclusion—with institutional alignment treated as a cross-cutting dimension. Using a qualitative single-case study design and deductive content analysis, the study examines documentary evidence from intergovernmental agreements, financing arrangements, regulatory and international review documents, official project statements, media reports, civil-society publications, and relevant academic literature. The analysis distinguishes formal commitments and reported activities from implementation, stakeholder perceptions, and demonstrated outcomes. The findings identify formal bilateral and institutional arrangements relevant to trust and coordination, alongside governance questions concerning the disclosure of project information, the distribution of costs and benefits, and the scope and influence of stakeholder participation. Although documented consultation activities and regulatory milestones provide evidence of governance processes, they do not independently establish public confidence, equitable outcomes, or the effectiveness of stakeholder engagement. The study demonstrates how Q-NPT can structure documentary evidence across the four pillars, identify cross-pillar relationships, and make evidence gaps explicit without assigning an unsupported overall governance rating or inferring causal effects. items.title: From Symbolic to Systemic Sustainability in Higher Education: A Readiness-Gated Framework for Governance, Monitoring, and Institutional Change
items.abstract: Universities’ sustainability commitments frequently outpace their systemic implementation. This paper addresses that gap by proposing the Sustainability Integration Framework (SIF), a mechanism-based, readiness-gated model for verifiable progression from symbolic adoption to institutionalized practice. Using a design science research approach, the study integrates institutional theory, resource-based theory, and responsible leadership to explain how external pressures, leadership interpretation, and internal capabilities shape sustainability integration. The framework is operationalized through a six-component institutional architecture, an Input–Process–Output logic model with auditable indicators, and a five-domain Readiness and Maturity Index (RMI). A six-stage mechanism—pressure, interpretation, resource reconfiguration, routinization, feedback closure, and coupling or decoupling—is supported by PDCA-gated progression, with Institutional Equity and data/AI Governance as cross-cutting levers. A dual-rater protocol, reliability thresholds, and an External Composite Readiness Index support transparent, comparable assessment across institutions. A single-rater demonstration at the American University of Beirut returns a domain profile of three defined domains (Leadership and Governance, Curriculum and Pedagogy, Operations) and two ad hoc domains (Strategy, Metrics and Data), summarized as an indicative RMI of 1.60 at the lower edge of the Intermediate stratum, indicating substantial external visibility alongside partial internal embedding. The contribution is a design proposal in the design science sense: an integrated theorized mechanism and an evidence-gated maturity model aligned with leading sustainability standards, intended to give administrators a replicable, audit-ready pathway for coordinating governance, curriculum, operations, and data systems once validated. items.title: Planning operational costs and CO2 emissions of municipal solid waste collection: A case study in Italy
items.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate and compare the environmental and economic performance of street-bin and door-to-door waste collection systems under different territorial conditions using field-derived data in a context-sensitive modelling framework. A field campaign in central Tuscany (Italy) monitored 238 collection routes operated with different vehicle types and fuels. Measured total fuel consumption was used to derive collection-phase consumption and estimate associated CO 2 emissions. These data were integrated into a predictive model applied to 116 collection areas, using linear population density (LPD) and per capita waste generation as territorial variables. Monitoring results showed that collection-phase fuel consumption and CO 2 emissions were systematically higher than standard transport inventory values across the six vehicle categories considered, with heavy-duty vehicles showing values two to three times higher. Modelling results revealed an inverse relationship between LPD and both operational costs and CO 2 emissions per tonne of collected waste. Under study-area reference conditions, street-bin collection became more carbon-efficient above 76 inhabitants · k m ⁻ 1 , with CO 2 emissions up to 17% lower than door-to-door, whereas door-to-door was economically competitive only below 8 inhabitants · k m ⁻ 1 . Sensitivity analyses placed the environmental and economic crossovers at 53–100 inhabitants · k m ⁻ 1 and 4–12 inhabitants · k m ⁻ 1 , respectively, without altering the overall LPD-dependent performance trends. Updated 2026 fuel prices slightly shifted the reference economic crossover to 9 inhabitants · k m ⁻ 1 and widened the sensitivity range to 4–14 inhabitants · k m ⁻ 1 . Overall, LPD emerged as a key spatial driver of collection-system performance, highlighting the importance of considering local territorial conditions when planning collection strategies to reduce operational costs and carbon emissions.

items.title: So Close, but Different: Uncovering the Different Determinants of Eco-Innovation in Central Europe
items.abstract: Central European countries face lower environmental awareness, reflected in the limited number of studies on eco-innovation in this area. This study contributes to research on environmental innovation in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, which have been among the major European polluters in the past. In contrast to previous studies, we focus on indicators such as energy management, waste minimisation and recycling, and air pollution control measures. The results show that despite the geographical and historical proximity of the Czech Republic and Slovakia, environmental innovation is influenced by different determinants in different areas. In the Czech Republic, the presence of a manager responsible for the environment and climate change was confirmed as a key determinant of firms’ environmental initiatives. In Czech and Slovak firms, environmental regulations trigger environmental innovation, specifically those measures focused on reducing emissions, directly impacting public health and environmental protection. At the same time the Environmental and CO2 Emission goals are an incentive for eco-innovation in the Czech Republic and Slovakia. This paper serves several practical implications, both for policymakers and practitioners. First, we suggest introducing tax incentives or low-interest loan programmes that could encourage businesses to invest in renewable energy and improve energy efficiency within analysed countries. Companies should set measurable targets in energy and waste management, as clear goals and renewable adoption enhance efficiency and foster eco-innovation. JEL CODES: Q56, Q55

items.title: Exploring the Human Capital Underpinnings on Adoption of Green Production Processes: Evidence from the Manufacturing Sector
items.abstract: This study examines the relationship between the adoption of green production processes and green behavior intention and explores how demographic characteristics influence this relationship. The adoption of green production process dimension includes life cycle assessment, green purchasing, and the reduce, reuse, recycle, while green behavior intention is examined through eco-initiative, eco-helping, and eco-civic behaviors. Such relations still needed to be investigated in developing countries such as Türkiye. Data was collected through a structured survey with participation of 385 employees working in textile manufacturing firms located in the Gaziantep region which has a significant impact on the machine-made carpet sector. Structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed relationships. Results reveal that green production process adoption significantly predicts green behavior intention. The study also finds that demographic factors serve as moderators in the link between institutional sustainability practices and individual behavioral intentions. This relationship is stronger among older and more experienced employees. This research contributes to literature by providing empirical evidence on the human-originated factors that shape the effectiveness of organizational green endeavors. The findings offer practical guidance for organizations seeking to align environmental strategies with human resource policies to enhance employee contribution to sustainable practices.

items.title: Risk-constrained adaptive Von Thünen zoning for post-mining educational geotourism: Stakeholder feasibility and community legitimacy evidence from the Martabe Gold Mine, Indonesia
items.abstract: Post-closure land use at large open-pit mines located near settlements is a bounded environmental-management challenge: residual geotechnical, hydrological, and contamination risks must be reconciled with ecological restoration and community expectations. This study develops and evaluates a risk-constrained zoning framework for educational geotourism at the Martabe Gold Mine, South Tapanuli, Indonesia. Geographic information system (GIS)-assisted interpretation of topography, lowland–highland morphology, land cover, inherited infrastructure, accessibility, ecological sensitivity, and technical risk was used to translate Von Thünen's ring logic into explicit decision rules. Two partial least squares structural equation models (PLS-SEM) then evaluated the feasibility and social legitimacy of the functions assigned to each zone, using 80 purposively selected stakeholders and 313 adult residents of 15 mine-ring villages. Reclamation-planning quality was strongly associated with spatial-use suitability (β = 0.729, p < 0.001; R² = 0.531). Ecological readiness and industrial-heritage transformation explained 73.3% of the variance in education and interpretation readiness, which, together with collaborative governance, explained 77.7% of the variance in destination-management sustainability. In the community model, perception was associated with destination image and participation, while attraction (β = 0.397) and participation (β = 0.340) were associated with perceived socio-economic sustainability (R² = 0.451). The resulting Martabe Education Mining and Ecologies Tourism Development (MEMETD) framework assigns controlled public services to Ring 1, research-restoration and restricted interpretation to Ring 2, and ecological protection to Ring 3, with a risk overlay that can override use in any ring. Its decision rules offer a transferable, staged alternative to immediate tourism conversion at near-settlement mines.

items.title: Circular design strategies in the post-consumption journey: a systematic literature review of service design for circular fashion SMEs
items.abstract: Purpose Post-consumption processes are increasingly acknowledged as a critical component of facilitating circular fashion systems within small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Nonetheless, research in this area often remains fragmented and dispersed across disciplinary domains. There is a limited understanding of how service design supports sustainable consumption and what challenges consumers encounter throughout the post-consumption journey. This study aims to systematically map and synthesise the fragmented research concerning post-consumption processes by critically analysing key service touchpoints, consumer pain points and service design strategies to develop an integrated framework for circular fashion SMEs. Design/methodology/approach This study systematically reviews 96 peer-reviewed articles selected from an initial pool of 997 publications using PRISMA guidelines. The data are analysed through inductive thematic analysis supported by NVivo to identify recurring post-consumption stages, consumer interactions and challenges and literature-discussed service design strategies. This is complemented by bibliometric analysis using CiteSpace. Findings Post-consumption functions as an interconnected, multi-stage service journey shaped by recurring touchpoints, consumer pain points and strategic interventions across usage, evaluation, after-sales service and disposal. Three key service design dimensions emerge, as follows: service optimisation, consumer engagement and ecosystem cooperation. Based on these findings, this study develops an integrated analytical framework linking post-consumption challenges with nine major service design strategies and highlights priorities for future research and practice. items.title: Urgensi Tahapan Konsultasi Publik Dalam Penyusunan Rancangan Peraturan Daerah: Studi Kasus Di Dprd Kota Mojokerto
items.abstract: Abstract—The formulation of regional regulations (Peraturan Daerah/Perda) is not merely a formal legislative activity, but a democrati c process that determines the legitimacy, effectiveness, and fairness of local legal products. This article examines the urgency of public consultation stages in drafting regional regulations at the Regional People's Representative Council (DPRD) of Mojokerto City . The study is derived from juridical-empirical research using a case-study approach, with statutory, conceptual, and socio-legal analysis. The research focuses on the gap between formal compliance with the stages of regional lawmaking and the substantive quality of public part icipation. The findings show that public consultation in Mojokerto City tends to remain at the tokenism level in Arnstein's ladder of participation. Citizens may be heard, yet there is no adequate mechanism to ensure that their inputs are considered and explained in the final draft. This weakness is reflected in the resistance to the waste-service retribution arrangement under Regional Regulation No. 7 of 2023 and in the limited documentation of consultation minutes. The article argues that meaningful public consultation must begin at the planning stag e, continue during drafting and deliberation, and be supported by clear standards of representation, information access, documentation, a nd follow-up. Such consultation is urgent to ensure legal certainty, legal utility, and justice in regional regulation.

items.title: Participatory Design of AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems: Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background: AI-based clinical decision support systems (CDSS) can improve diagnostics and treatment decisions, but they are rarely implemented in practice. Barriers include limited integration into clinical workflows, lack of transparency, and insufficient involvement of end users in system design. Participatory and user-centered approaches offer ways to address these challenges by aligning development processes with the needs and routines of clinical staff. However, systematic evidence on how such approaches are applied in the development of AI-based CDSS remains limited. Objective: Our study examined how participatory approaches are used in the development, piloting, and implementation of AI-based CDSS. We analyzed which user perspectives were included, which participatory methods were applied, how they contributed to technical design, and which ethical, legal, and social implications were addressed. Methods: This scoping review followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guideline, with a protocol published in advance. A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE, ACM Digital Library, CINAHL, and PsycInfo for studies published from 2012 onward, complemented by snowballing and manual searches. Primary studies in English or German were included if they involved clinical staff in the development, piloting, implementation, or evaluation of AI-based CDSS. Moreover, 3 independent reviewers conducted screening and data extraction, resolving disagreements by consensus. Data analysis followed JBI methodology and focused on the scope of participation, theoretical and methodological foundations, and reported impacts of participatory approaches. items.title: Circular economy: a growing market for sustainable innovations
items.venue: Journal of Entrepreneurship and Sustainability Issues
items.abstract: As a paradigm shift in sustainable development, a circular economy enabled by innovative business models ensures a competitive advantage by prioritising and improving resource efficiency, reducing waste and costs, creating value, and meeting sustainable demands.This paper explores the circular economy as a growing market for sustainable innovations, analysing key drivers, economic opportunities, and challenges for businesses and economies.The information base for the research is the Eurostat and World Bank panel data for the European Union (EU) countries covering the period from 2014 to 2020.The research aims to examine the impact of circular economy indicators (Private investment and gross added value in circular economy sectors; patents related to recycling and secondary raw materials; persons employed in circular economy sectors) on gross domestic product (GDP) per capita in the selected countries.The research results, obtained through descriptive statistics, correlation, and regression analysis, indicate a positive association between circular economy indicators and GDP per capita.By examining the circular economy indicators in the EU, the authors emphasise how economies and businesses can leverage circular strategies to enhance competitiveness and resilience.The research findings suggest that businesses embracing circular economy models benefit from increased profitability, reduced environmental impact, and enhanced consumer engagement, positioning sustainability as a core driver of long-term economic growth.

items.title: Mapping Gaps in Solid Waste, Wastewater, and Biosolids Education: A National Curriculum Audit of Greek Primary Teacher Education
items.abstract: Primary teachers shape early environmental understanding, yet their formal preparation in waste management remains poorly documented. This study audited all nine Greek public undergraduate primary-teacher programmes. Official study guides and course descriptions available by 29 August 2026 were screened for explicit content on solid waste, wastewater, sludge, and biosolids. Generic environmental references and undifferentiated mentions of waste were excluded unless a target domain or qualifying management operation was explicit. Five programmes (55.6%) contained at least one relevant course. Solid waste appeared in four programmes (44.4%), wastewater in three (33.3%), and sludge or biosolids in none. Of the five retained courses, one was compulsory and four compulsory-choice; only one programme (11.1%) guaranteed relevant exposure. Four courses provided substantive coverage and one incidental exposure. Independent auditing produced agreement on 40 of 45 programme-level decisions (88.9%; pooled Cohen’s kappa = 0.72), with discrepancies resolved by consensus. These results establish a reproducible national baseline for the intended curriculum and distinguish course availability from guaranteed exposure and explicit pedagogical preparation. They do not measure enacted teaching or learning, but identify where formal provision is absent, optional, or pedagogically unspecified, supporting targeted curriculum review and subsequent interview-, enrolment-, and outcome-based research.

items.title: Community Participation in a Protected Area Amid Human—Wildlife Coexistence Challenges: The Case of Kaeng Krung National Park, Thailand
items.abstract: Achieving sustainable coexistence between communities and wildlife in the rapidly changing socio-ecological landscapes of the Global South increasingly challenges protected-area governance. Although participation in long-established protected areas has been widely studied, the dynamics of newly declared parks—where in-migration, insecure tenure, and livelihood dependence persist after designation—remain poorly understood. In this study, a mixed-methods design was employed, comprising a household survey (n = 345) and in-depth interviews (n = 20), to explore factors associated with community participation and coexistence in Kaeng Krung National Park, Thailand. Descriptive statistics were used to assess participation in four dimensions, and the interviews were thematically analyzed. The results indicate a high overall willingness to participate (mean = 3.50); qualitative results show that participation was influenced by the following factors: duration of residence, land tenure security, perceived benefits and disadvantages (including livelihood losses from human–elephant conflict, which were reported to have increased since the COVID-19 pandemic), and access to communication and training. Willingness to pay was much lower (26.3%) than willingness to comply with regulations or engage in activities, indicating that financial constraints, rather than lack of commitment, limit monetary participation. This study advances an empirically grounded model of participation based on livelihood security, institutional trust, and skill-related constraints, providing policy-relevant guidance for protected-area governance in Thailand and similar contexts.

items.title: Waste Management Governance In Muara Satu District, Lhokseumawe City
items.abstract: Waste management remains a critical environmental challenge in Indonesian urban areas, with governance failures contributing to persistent issues including illegal dumping and inadequate infrastructure. This study examines waste management governance in Muara Satu District, Lhokseumawe City, analyzing implementation through five principles of good governance: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, and accountability, while identifying obstacles to effective management. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed, utilizing observation, in-depth interviews with eight purposively and accidentally selected informants, and documentation. Data analysis followed the Miles and Huberman interactive model, with data validity ensured through source and technique triangulation. The findings reveal that waste management governance has not achieved optimal implementation. Community participation remains transactional and limited to economic incentives. Rule of law enforcement is weak despite existing Qanun Number 9 of 2015, with inconsistent sanctions and persistent illegal waste sites. Transparency is partial, with program information available but budget information undisclosed. Responsiveness shows mixed results: while the Environmental Agency has developed innovative processing technologies, operational constraints limit timely service delivery. Accountability operates predominantly through vertical mechanisms, with limited horizontal accountability to communities. Two categories of obstacles were identified: structural constraints including inadequate fleet capacity (39 vehicles serving 133 tons daily waste), damaged equipment, limited storage sites, and insufficient human resources; and cultural constraints including low community awareness, limited participation, and entrenched habits. items.title: De nouveaux types d’innovation frugale analysés par le trade-off qualité écologique/prix
items.abstract: L’article met en lumière la nature, les caractéristiques et les propriétés économiques de deux nouveaux types d’innovation frugale durable. L’analyse s’appuie sur le trade-off qualité écologique/prix récemment apparu dans la littérature et sur une étude de cas. Le premier type concerne la vente de produits imparfaits sans aucune remise en état, que nous considérons comme une forme d’innovation frugale durable en marketing. Le second vise à frugaliser la conception d’un produit afin de rendre le processus de recyclage plus simple, moins coûteux, et donc plus accessible ; il s’agit d’une innovation frugale durable en matière de recyclage. Nous montrons comment et pourquoi ces deux innovations se positionnent à des endroits spécifiques du trade-off qualité écologique/prix. Nous contribuons à élargir la notion standard d’innovation frugale, traditionnellement fondée sur le changement technologique à d’autres formes d’innovation. Ce cadre offre ainsi un terrain pour repenser le management de l’innovation sous l’angle de la durabilité. Codes JEL : D4, O31, O32, O35

items.title: Walking with plastic waste: resonant practices for working with presence-as-absence
items.abstract: Plastic waste in cities creates a paradox: it is everywhere in daily life yet often escapes notice. While previous studies have highlighted plastic’s persistence and visibility as pollution, less attention has been given to its subtle, everyday disappearances in Nordic urban settings. This article develops resonant practices for studying this contradiction. Resonant practices emerged from walking-with plastic waste, extending attention to urban atmospheres in Turku, Finland. These practices focus on subtle signals such as flicker, tang, shimmer, or silence, and documents them as vignettes, composed through writing, drawing, photography, video, and sound recording. I argue that these practices make the hidden presence of plastic workable for research. The research is made possible by treating small atmospheric and bodily traces as evidence, especially when they recur across senses and connect to urban systems that organize disappearance. Examples from fieldwork show how plastic becomes affectively present in ordinary spaces and how careful use of measurement can connect with sensory noticing. Resonant practices condense into what I name as the microplastic gaze: an embodied attentiveness to cultivated absences of plastics that extends fieldwork toward situated resonance. The article concludes by emphasising the importance of methodological approaches, remaining attentive to forms of loss, disappearance, and attenuation, and offering new ways to document the elusive materialities of urban plastic waste.

items.title: Closing the Loop: A Circular Approach to Sustainable Heavy Metal Remediation and Metal Recovery from Soil Leachates Using Tailor-Made Advanced Adsorbents
items.abstract: This study investigates the remediation of natural soil samples from diverse locations, which exhibit varying degrees of copper contamination. To further elucidate the mechanisms of contaminant retention and desorption, similar extraction studies were conducted on representative soils. Finally, the resulting metal-rich leachates were treated using advanced organomodified adsorbents. This step aimed to reduce the volume of contaminated solutions and assess the potential for partial Cu recovery, thereby supporting a circular remediation concept.

items.title: Evaluating Public Health Interventions
items.abstract: Public health interventions include any effort or policy that attempts to improve the health among individuals or an entire population. They can be run by governmental health departments or non-governmental organisations and can include educational programmes, screening programmes, vaccination programmes, environmental improvements and health promotion campaigns. Evaluating and predicting the efficacy of any public health intervention, as well as calculating the cost effectiveness is essential. Using examples from multiple published studies conducted around the world, this textbook shows readers how to evaluate public health interventions in real world settings. It will enable readers to understand how to investigate whether a public health intervention works, for whom, when, where, how and why. It provides a comprehensive introduction to key areas of evaluation including understanding complex interventions, developing programme theories, community engagement in evaluation and the main methods used in process, impact and economic evaluation. It explains how methods can be used individually and in combination to answer different kinds of evaluation question at various phases in an evaluation cycle and considers how the results of evaluations can be brought together to inform action. This textbook is the ideal guide for students, practitioners and policymakers in the field of health policy and evaluation.

items.title: Direct upcycling of unrecyclable household waste into biodegradable high‑performance biocomposites
items.abstract: In the UK, post-consumer waste is sent to materials recovery facilities (MRFs) to separate the metals, plastics, paper and cardboard for subsequent recycling. However, a significant portion of materials sent to MRFs are rejected. Here, we demonstrate a pathway that directly transforms the recovered lignocellulosic pulp (herein termed recovered solids, RS) from MRF rejects and its enzymatic post-hydrolysis solids (PHS) into biodegradable poly(L‑lactide) (PLLA) composites. We found that both RS and PHS act as effective nucleating and reinforcing agents, increasing the crystallinity of PLLA and its tensile modulus to ~6 GPa while maintaining comparable strength ( ~ 60 MPa). By comparison, unreinforced PLLA at a comparable crystallinity possessed only a tensile modulus and strength of 2.5 GPa and 42 MPa, respectively. The resulting biocomposites also show accelerated biodegradation under simulated industrial composting compared to PLLA, achieving complete disintegration within 30 days. This work provides the first demonstration of directly upcycling unrecyclable MRF reject streams into structural, fully compostable materials, revealing a viable, low‑carbon route to integrate post‑consumer and secondary wastes into a closed‑loop circular economy.

items.title: Retrofitting residential septic infrastructure for decentralised biogas production: a scenario-based circular waste-to-energy assessment in Lagos
items.abstract: Purpose Rapid urbanisation in cities such as Lagos requires decentralised solutions that address energy insecurity, inadequate sanitation and environmental sustainability. This study evaluates the feasibility of retrofitting septic infrastructure within an ageing residential estate in Lagos to support decentralised sanitation-to-energy systems within a circular sanitation–energy framework. Design/methodology/approach A case study-based, engineering-calibrated methodology integrates infrastructure characterisation, wastewater estimation, organic loading analysis, infrastructure-constrained methane modelling and techno-economic evaluation. Real septic tank design data (˜20 m3) were used to estimate hydraulic retention time under operating conditions. Alternative retrofit configurations were assessed using multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), supported by sensitivity analysis and multi-layer validation incorporating parameter, structural, benchmarking and sensitivity-based checks. Findings The estate generates 43.2 m3/day of wastewater and 38.88 kg COD/day from 432 residents. The calibrated model estimates methane production of 10.89 m3/day, yielding 92 kWh/day and avoiding approximately 106 tonnes CO2-equivalent emissions annually. A hydraulic retention time of 0.46 days identifies reactor hydraulics as the principal technical constraint despite adequate organic loading. Sensitivity analysis identifies methane yield and capital cost as the principal determinants of economic performance. Although centralised digestion maximises energy output, MCDA results identify cluster-scale systems as the preferred retrofit option. Originality/value The study presents a unified retrofit assessment framework integrating infrastructure characterisation, infrastructure-constrained methane modelling, uncertainty assessment, techno-economic evaluation and multi-criteria decision support. items.title: Digital technologies and the circular economy: charting a shared journey toward sustainable development
items.venue: International Journal of Productivity and Performance Management
items.abstract: Purpose The research aims to identify the practical benefits of implementing Digital Technologies (DTs) and the Circular Economy (CE) for Sustainable Development (SD) by enabling informed decision-making. Design/methodology/approach The research consists of 148 articles, including quantitative (61), qualitative (52) and literature review studies (35), covering various fields such as ecology, supply chain management, marketing and circular business models, sourced from WOS, Scopus and Direct Science. Science-mapping techniques have been employed to analyse citations in published articles, measure their impact and identify leading and emerging trends in the literature. Findings The study demonstrates that artificial intelligence (AI) is developing intelligent devices and processes that analyse large datasets to identify patterns, verify and report on organisational activity, enabling real-time decision-making. Furthermore, companies that excel in CE principles – a system focused on minimising waste and making the most of resources – are more likely to engage with Industry 4.0, which refers to the integration of DTs such as the Internet of Things (IoT), automation and data exchange in manufacturing. This subsequently results in improved financial outcomes and more rational decision-making. In addition, the research highlights limited connections within Industry 5.0 – an industry phase emphasising collaboration between humans and machines – with a particular focus on CE and SD. Originality/value This research provides a unique overview in exploring DTs and CE across environmental performance, financial metrics, accounting relationships and the impact of computer-based analysis on decision-making, thus highlighting significant gaps in the literature. Moreover, this study offers practitioners interesting insights to improve financial outcomes, resource use, DT and CE adoption and decision-making processes.

items.title: Managing co-curation as care-based commoning: Care, commons, and cultural participation in the visual arts
items.abstract: Background Co-curation has increasingly challenged traditional curatorial models by involving citizens and communities directly in cultural production and decision-making. While research has examined co-curation, cultural commons, and care ethics separately, little is known about how collaborative artistic projects are collectively governed and sustained in practice. This paper addresses this gap by conceptualising co-curation as a form of care-based communing. Methods Drawing on commons theory and the ethics of care, particularly the work of Tronto ( 2013a, 2013b, 1993) and Puig de la Bellacasa (2017, 2011), the study investigates collaborative relationships among artists, mediators, and citizen patrons within the New Patrons (Les Nouveaux Commanditaires) initiative using qualitative content analysis on 24 semi-structured interviews conducted in France and Italy. Results The findings show that co-curation operates as a dialogical and adaptive process through which participants construct shared intentions, negotiate diverse perspectives, and collectively steward artistic projects. Conclusion The study highlights the pivotal role of mediators as relational infrastructures that facilitate collaboration and sustain active participation over time. It further demonstrates that collaborative cultural production depends not only on shared governance arrangements but also on care-centered practices of attentiveness, responsiveness, and relationship maintenance. The paper contributes to the literature by integrating co-curation, commons theory, and care ethics into a unified framework of care-based commoning.

items.title: When second-hand markets confront their ghosts: Insights from psychological reactance theory in Douala-Cameroon
items.abstract: The consumption of second-hand products in Douala (Cameroon) unfolds within a fragile equilibrium shaped by informal market dynamics, social norms, and culturally embedded representations. Drawing on participant observations and semi-structured interviews, this study shows that second-hand purchasing extends far beyond an economic decision. Technical uncertainty, social stigma, culturally rooted beliefs about the prior use of objects, and the lack of clear legal protections structure consumers’ hesitations. These barriers do not merely generate avoidance: they activate psychological reactance when individuals perceive that their freedom of choice is constrained whether by economic necessity, social expectations, or moral judgments and seek to restore autonomy while navigating community norms and symbolic risks. The findings extend psychological reactance theory by demonstrating that, in the informal markets of Douala, reactance arises not only from prescriptive messages but also from structural constraints, status-based evaluations, and culturally grounded interpretations of risk. Reactance is simultaneously shaped by spiritual beliefs, tensions between modern and traditional consumption norms, and collective narratives circulating within peer groups. Trust in sellers, products, and informal guarantees, as well as perceived value economic, social, and symbolic emerge as key levers for reducing reactance. The study offers context-specific managerial implications, including reframing second-hand purchasing as a competent and legitimate choice, strengthening local trust-building practices, developing non-prescriptive and culturally sensitive communication, and supporting informal markets through proportionate mechanisms that reduce risk without limiting consumer autonomy.

items.title: How can we meaningfully involve older adults in aged care research? Insights from establishing a consumer research advisory group
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES AND IMPORTANCE OF STUDY: With the global population ageing rapidly, the voices of older persons must be integrated into healthcare research. Consumer involvement can enhance the relevance, quality and policy impact of research. However, there is limited practical guidance on how to meaningfully involve older adults. This study describes the establishment of a consumer research advisory group within an aged care education research program, and explores consumer perspectives on the recruitment, support and involvement of older people in healthcare research. STUDY TYPE: A qualitative descriptive study design was used. METHODS: Data sources included meeting minutes and the research officer logbook documenting the consumer research advisory group's establishment, as well as an online survey of group members exploring their motivations and experiences. RESULTS: Recruitment involved an inclusive expression of interest process, followed by interviews to support diverse representation. Barriers were addressed through remuneration, accessibility adjustments and personalised communication. Members (N = 8) reported positive experiences, and highlighted the importance of a supportive environment, clear orientation and provision of training. Most participants were motivated by a desire to use their lived experience to benefit others. CONCLUSIONS: Establishing the consumer research advisory group demonstrated the feasibility of involving older persons and carers in research. Key enablers included addressing logistical challenges, planning for sensory and cognitive needs, fostering inclusivity, and building trust. These findings provide practical guidance for strengthening consumer involvement in healthcare research in the context of global ageing.

items.title: Supporting participatory PhDs: a call to action
items.abstract: There has been sustained and growing interest in public policy, professional practice, and research, in what has come to be called patient and public, or service user, involvement. Requirements for such involvement are now embedded within health and care legislation, professional education, and training, and the expectations of many research funders and commissioners. There has also been an increasing interest in public involvement in research, learning, and specifically in the undertaking and assessment of PhDs. However, provisions and requirements for PhDs have not caught up with these developments, despite them being offered as providing advanced research training. Consequently, obstacles to fulfilling such involvement are present in existing arrangements concerning the authorship, regulations, funding, and assessment of PhDs, which seek to be participatory and collaborative. This article reports on this issue and the emergence of an international Participatory PhD Network to support this developing field as a result, and the ways forward it suggests. Our paper aims to support the empowerment of people undertaking participatory research, inspire those who may like to approach their PhD through participatory methodologies, advocate for innovative methods of collaboration, and provide evidence for updating PhD processes and procedures in line with increasing participation. Within the paper, we explore both the possibilities and constraints of participatory PhD research. The Participatory PhD Network aims to instil inspiration and confidence in members of institutions, researchers, research participants and others involved, offering support and validation for PhD students preparing for their study design through to examination and subsequent research.

items.title: Forest residue biochars: feedstock, pyrolysis, and properties
items.abstract: The European Union (EU) is fostering the bioeconomy as a strategy to achieve a climate-neutral and circular economy. In this context, valorization of forest wastes as pine sawdust into biochar is a key opportunity in Galicia (NW Spain), one of the most forested areas of the EU. Moreover, two abundant Galician shrubs, Erica cinerea L. and Ulex europaeus L. have not yet been explored as biochar feedstock, although these shrubs are associated with high biomass accumulation and an increase of forest fires in the region. Therefore, their conversion into biochar offers a sustainable waste management pathway. This study aims to characterize biochar produced from different Galician feedstocks (pine sawdust, Erica cinerea L., and Ulex europaeus L.). The biochar was produced under three pyrolysis temperatures (300, 400 and 500°C) and three pyrolysis times (30, 60 and 120 minutes). The results showed that nitrogen, carbon concentration, and C/N ratio in the biochar were greatly affected by feedstock initial composition and operating conditions during pyrolysis. Carbon concentration varied significantly among feedstocks, with all materials showing increased carbon concentration at higher pyrolysis temperatures. Sawdust consistently had the highest nitrogen concentration: up to 8% at 300 °C, after 120 min due to the preprocessing with ammonium polyphosphate (APP). The C/N ratio demonstrated distinct patterns, with sawdust maintaining a lower C/N ratio at lower temperatures, while Erica cinerea and Ulex europaeus showed a higher C/N ratio that varied with temperature and pyrolysis time. The results indicate that biochar derived from Erica cinerea L. and Ulex europaeus L. are suitable for soil carbon sequestration due to its higher and more stable C/N ratios, whereas APP processed pine sawdust biochar shows particular potential as a long-term source of nitrogen due to its consistently higher nitrogen concentration and lower C/N ratio under lower pyrolysis temperatures. items.title: Waste Management in Azerbaijan's Green Economy Transition: A Sectoral Analysis of Generation, Utilization and Neutralization, 2010-2024
items.abstract: The growth of production and consumption has made waste management an increasingly important economic and environmental issue in Azerbaijan.This study examines changes in waste generation, utilization and neutralization in the country between 2010 and 2024, with particular attention to differences across economic activities.The analysis is based on official data obtained from the State Statistical Committee of the Republic of Azerbaijan.Descriptive statistics, growth rates, trend analysis and sectoral comparisons are applied.The findings show that the total volume of production and consumption waste increased from 2,281.5 thousand tons in 2010 to 4,365.0 thousand tons in 2024.During the same period, utilized and neutralized waste rose from 476.1 thousand tons to 1,148.4 thousand tons.Nevertheless, its ratio to generated waste increased only from 20.9% to 26.3% and fluctuated considerably over the period.The sectoral results reveal substantial differences.In 2024, manufacturing generated 856.2 thousand tons of waste, of which 807.5 thousand tons were utilized or neutralized.By contrast, the corresponding ratio remained considerably lower in agriculture and mining.Municipal solid waste accounted for the largest share of total waste generation and continued to increase.The results indicate that growth in waste treatment has not been sufficient to offset the overall expansion of waste generation.The study highlights the need for sector-specific waste reduction, recovery and recycling measures in Azerbaijan.
