items.title: Stabilizing Multi-Metal(loid)s in red mud with multi-waste amendments: Synergistic mechanisms and environmental benefits
items.abstract: Red mud (RM), a highly alkaline byproduct of alumina production, poses significant environmental risks due to its elevated pH and potentially toxic metal(loid)s. This study evaluated sustainable stabilization methods using multi-waste amendments (coal mining soil (CS), distiller’s grains (DG), acid-modified biochar (AB)) supplemented with natural garden soil (GS) to immobilize metal(loid)s and mitigate RM’s environmental impacts. Systematic incubation experiments comparing single-, two combined-, three combined-, and four combined-amendment systems demonstrated that the four combined-amendment system (RM + 1%CS + 1%DG + 1%AB + 1%GS) achieved the most effective metal(loid) stabilization. It reduced water-extractable metal(loid)s in RM by 99.0% (Pb), 86.2% (Cr), 85.2% (Cd), 68.8% (Sb), 60.9% (As), 56.6% (Zn), 32.7% (Ni), and 21.4% (Al), while maintaining low leachability under the Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure (TCLP). However, this treatment mobilized certain cationic elements (Cu, Fe, Mg, and Mn). Despite this mobilization, the concentrations of these elements remained within Chinese groundwater Class II standards (GB/T14848-2017). The four combined-amendment system exhibited significant synergistic effects: 205% increase in organic matter content, 39% reduction in pH, 12% decrease in electrical conductivity, and reduced phytotoxicity (germination index >90%). Economically, it reduced costs by 8.1–68.5% relative to conventional treatments (lime stabilization and phosphate treatment), with a net present value advantage of $3.85 million over 10 years for a 100,000-ton annual capacity facility. This strategy, integrating multi-waste amendments and natural soil, embodies circular economy principles, transforming waste streams into valuable remediation resources and addressing RM management challenges, though its trade-offs warrant consideration for site-specific applications.

items.title: Agriparcs d’Alger face à la transition urbaine : planification et usages à Chéraga et Khraïssia
items.abstract: À la croisée de l’urbanisme, de l’écologie et de la gouvernance territoriale, les agriparcs s’affirment comme de nouvelles aménités urbaines susceptibles de refaire le lien entre la ville et la nature. Cette étude présente les dimensions théoriques, méthodologiques et opérationnelles de ces dispositifs à travers l’analyse appliquée aux communes de Chéraga et de Khraïssia, situées en périphérie d’Alger. En partant d’une grille d’analyse multicritère couvrant les dimensions paysagères, écologiques, sociales et institutionnelles, l’étude révèle les défis liés à la mise en œuvre des agriparcs dans un espace urbain disjoint et en pleine mutation. La méthodologie repose sur une approche croisée, associant analyse documentaire, observations de terrain, cartographie SIG (système d’information géographique), enquêtes qualitatives et entretiens semi-directifs avec les acteurs locaux. Au-delà de l’évaluation des projets pilotes, l’objectif est d’identifier les conditions favorables à l’ancrage territorial et à une gouvernance partagée de ces espaces multifonctionnels, à la fois productifs et écologiques. Les résultats ouvrent des perspectives pour une stratégie globale de planification des agriparcs dans la métropole algéroise, à l’intersection des politiques de biodiversité, d’agriculture urbaine et de résilience territoriale.

items.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine the impact of sustainable development-oriented eco-friendly product design on purchase intention and consumer acceptance, and to reveal the mediating roles of perceived value, perceived quality, and perceived cost in this relationship. Within the proposed research model, the direct effects of eco-friendly product design on perceptual evaluations were tested, as well as the effects of these perceptual variables on purchase intention and consumer acceptance. In addition, the mediating role of purchase intention in the relationship between eco-friendly product design and consumer acceptance was analyzed. Within the scope of the quantitative research method, data were collected from 405 respondents, and the obtained data were analyzed using the SPSS and AMOS statistical software. The findings indicate that eco-friendly product design has a positive and significant effect on perceived value and perceived quality, while it has a negative and significant effect on perceived cost. Furthermore, perceived value and perceived quality positively influence purchase intention, whereas perceived cost has a negative effect. Mediation analyses reveal that perceived value, perceived quality, and perceived cost play partial mediating roles in the relationships between eco-friendly product design and both purchase intention and consumer acceptance. Finally, purchase intention was found to partially mediate the relationship between eco-friendly product design and consumer acceptance. Overall, the results demonstrate that eco-friendly product design influences consumer behavior through multidimensional perceptual and behavioral mechanisms.

items.title: Rethinking Sustainability in Circular Tourism: A Multi‐Theoretical Pathway to Empowerment, Regeneration, Synergy, and Resilience
items.abstract: This study aims to develop a comprehensive conceptual framework for circular tourism that supports the transition from linear consumption models to circular and sustainable systems in the tourism sector. The study employs a systematic meta‐synthesis approach, drawing on 129 peer‐reviewed articles. Through an abductive process of thematic analysis, combining inductive coding with deductive, theory‐guided grouping, 50 implementation practices were identified and then organized according to semantic similarities into 10 organizing themes and ultimately 4 global themes. The proposed framework integrates four complementary theories, Empowerment Theory, Cradle‐to‐Cradle Theory, Social Capital Theory, and Social‐Ecological Resilience Theory, to build a theoretically grounded model. The meta‐synthesis resulted in a three‐layered conceptual framework consisting of 50 implementation practices, 10 organizing themes, and 4 global themes: Empowerment, Regeneration, Synergy, and Resilience. Empowerment establishes the social and human foundation; Regeneration transforms resource and material interaction patterns; Synergy creates the institutional basis for collective action; and Resilience ensures the system's capacity to absorb disruptions and maintain long‐term viability. By combining Empowerment Theory, Cradle‐to‐Cradle Theory, Social Capital Theory, and Social‐Ecological Resilience Theory, it provides a holistic perspective emphasizing synergistic interactions among social, material, institutional, and adaptive dimensions. The framework contributes theoretically by offering researchers and practitioners a structured foundation for implementing circular practices in tourism.

items.title: Exploring Drivers and Mitigation Strategies for Food Manufacturing Wastes in the Circular Economy Using Rich Pictures
items.abstract: This study aims to identify the main types, drivers, and solutions for food loss and waste (FLW) as reported by stakeholders within the UK food manufacturing sector from a Circular Economy perspective. Based on insights from diagramming‐based workshops involving 35 participants working in an organisation in the sector, FLW occurs primarily as a result of it either being unwanted by the primary consumer or due to it being unsafe to consume. Drivers relating to internal considerations include machinery faults, human errors, and miscoordination across business functions, while external factors include sensitive product standards, uncertainties in demand forecasting, and constraints in raw material acquisition. Participants describe potential solutions including actions from across the Circular Economy playbook, including redistribution of surpluses, recovery and re‐use of wastes and a particular focus on narrowing existing material flows through waste prevention. Of interest to parties seeking to understand the systemic drivers of FLW in the manufacturing sector, the results provide evidence for cross‐sectoral collaboration in the design of interventions moving towards increased FLW reduction and productive use.

items.title: Transformative Purpose
items.abstract: The chapter deals with Transformative Purpose in Ecosystems. Purpose can take the form of environmental sustainability, that is, the commitment to managing natural resources responsibly, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and contributing to ecological transitions. items.abstract: Urban communities face interconnected challenges related to livelihoods, waste management, social inclusion, and access to productive resources. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has increasingly moved beyond short-term assistance toward approaches that seek to generate shared social, economic, and environmental value. This study examines the Eco Superstar Program implemented by PT Pertamina Patra Niaga Integrated Terminal Jakarta as a CSR-based social innovation initiative in Sunter Jaya, North Jakarta, Indonesia. The study aims to explore how CSR can enable the reconfiguration of community resources, relationships, and activities into an integrated urban circular system. A qualitative case study approach was employed, using program documentation, field observations, interviews, community-related records, and supporting secondary data. The findings indicate that the social innovation of Eco Superstar lies not primarily in the individual activities or technologies introduced, but in the way previously separate community actors and resources are connected through circular value creation. Furthermore, the gradual strengthening of organizational capacity, productive assets, market access, and community responsibilities indicates a shift from beneficiary-oriented assistance toward greater community agency. items.title: Beyond Remediation: Evaluating the Economic Potential of Recovering REEs and High-Value Metals from Acidic Mine Drainage
items.abstract: The rising demand for critical raw materials (CRMs) and limited European supply drive the search for alternative sources. Acidic mine waters (AMWs) are promising for metal recovery and water reclamation. Although treatment technologies exist, large-scale use is hindered by economic uncertainties. This study evaluates the technoeconomic feasibility of recovering CRMs from AMWs via an integrated process with selective precipitation, ion exchange, nanofiltration, and electrodialysis with bipolar membranes (EDBM). Five scenarios explore different recovery, regeneration, and purification setups. Under these conditions, approximately 1242 t/year of ZnS(s), 5147 t/year of Mg(OH)2(s), 6.65 t/year of heavy rare earth element (HREE) oxides, and 14.23 t/year of light rare earth element (LREE) oxides can be recovered. The results indicate that none of the recovery schemes can be economically viable, with annual net costs ranging from 6.6 million €/year to 12.7 million €/year. Metal precipitation (as hydroxide and sulfide) is the costliest stage, followed by reagent regeneration, where chemical use accounts for 23–90% of costs. Including EDBM increases electricity costs by up to 23%. Although the results highlight that AMW valorization as a circular approach can be useful for obtaining valuable raw materials, reducing supply risks, and reducing EU dependency, the economic results show the need for public subsidies or targeted policy incentives to bridge the viability gap.

items.title: From Agricultural Waste to Community Value: The Prakarsa Bagja Juara Program as A Circular CSR Initiative in Karawang, Indonesia
items.venue: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
items.abstract: Agricultural communities in rural areas face increasing challenges in managing agricultural residues while maintaining productive and sustainable livelihoods. In Pasirtanjung Village, Karawang, Indonesia, agricultural waste, particularly rice straw, had been largely underutilized and was commonly treated as a disposal problem. The Prakarsa Bagja Juara Program, implemented through the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiative of PT Pertamina Patra Niaga Fuel Terminal Cikampek, seeks to address this condition by connecting agricultural waste management with community empowerment and local economic activities. This study aims to examine how the program transforms agricultural residues into community resources through a circular CSR approach. A qualitative case study was employed using interviews, participatory observation, group discussions, and program documentation. The analysis focused on three interconnected processes: resource transformation, community collaboration, and value creation. The findings indicate that the program has encouraged the utilization of rice straw, water hyacinth, field snails, and other organic materials as inputs for compost, planting media, mushroom cultivation, and other community-based activities. These practices have contributed to the development of new linkages among farmer groups, women's groups, waste management initiatives, water service activities, and local micro-enterprises. Beyond waste reduction, the program has created opportunities for skills development, resource sharing, product development, and income diversification. The findings suggest that CSR can function not only as a mechanism for delivering community assistance but also as a platform for connecting previously fragmented local resources, actors, and economic activities. items.title: Patient Participation in Organ Transplant Selection Meetings: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Importance: Organ transplant selection committee meetings determine patient eligibility for life-saving organs, yet their deliberations remain largely inaccessible to patients. Limited transparency contributes to patient-reported mistrust and disengagement. Patient engagement in these processes may improve understanding and trust, but its impact on deliberation, logistics, and patient-clinician relationships remains unclear. Objective: To examine perspectives of patients and clinicians regarding patient participation in transplant selection committee meetings. Design, Setting, and Participants: This qualitative study used semistructured interviews with a purposive sample of patients and clinicians nationally between November 16, 2023, and April 21, 2025. Interviews were conducted via video or telephone. Transcripts were analyzed using iterative thematic analysis. Participant demographics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Main Outcomes and Measures: Key themes reflecting patient and clinician perspectives on patient engagement in transplant selection committee meetings, including perceived benefits, risks, and strategies to support safe and effective implementation. Results: Interviews were conducted with 41 participants (mean [SD] age, 48 [7] years; 22 [53.7%] male), including 19 patients (46.3%), 13 clinicians (31.7%), and 9 patient-clinicians (21.9%). Four interrelated themes emerged: (1) rebalancing power and autonomy, (2) process understanding as empowerment, (3) mutual vulnerability, and (4) navigating uncertainty. Across themes, participants emphasized that meaningful participation depends on addressing these interdependent challenges and proposed strategies, including structured roles, facilitated participation, meeting summaries, and standardized communication frameworks. items.title: Planting Microforests: Practical Guidance, Monitoring Methods, and Lessons Learned from Two Case Studies in the Northeastern United States
items.abstract: Microforests (also called mini forests or tiny forests) are increasingly recognized as a promising nature-based solution for mitigating urban challenges such as flooding, biodiversity loss, air pollution, and the heat island effect. Despite their rapid global adoption, practitioners have limited access to practical, evidence-based guidance for planning, implementing, and monitoring these projects. This article presents an adaptable framework for community-based microforest establishment and long-term monitoring based on lessons learned from two contrasting case studies in the northeastern United States: a demonstration microforest at the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation’s Five Rivers Environmental Education Center and a series of urban microforests established by Groundwork Elizabeth in New Jersey. We describe practical approaches to site selection, soil assessment and preparation, native species selection, volunteer engagement, planting, and maintenance that can be adapted to diverse environmental and social contexts. We also introduce a standardized yet flexible monitoring framework encompassing five complementary components: forest development, soil recovery, biodiversity recovery, microclimate regulation, and community stewardship. The framework incorporates monitoring methods ranging from accessible citizen science protocols to more advanced ecological techniques, enabling organizations with varying levels of technical capacity to document ecological change and compare outcomes across projects. Rather than prescribing a single implementation model, we provide communities, nonprofit organizations, government agencies, and researchers with practical guidance to establish, evaluate, and adapt microforests while promoting standardized monitoring, long-term stewardship, and evidence-based urban ecological restoration.

items.title: Government–Industry–University Collaboration and Perceived Zero-Carbon Community Performance: The Mediating Role of Alliance Mechanisms from a Triple Helix Perspective
items.abstract: The development of zero-carbon communities has become an important pathway for advancing urban carbon neutrality. However, the transition toward zero-carbon development is no longer a process driven solely by technological innovation; rather, it has evolved into a complex governance process involving the collaborative participation of multiple stakeholders. Grounded in Triple Helix theory, this study develops an integrated analytical framework to examine the associations between government–industry–university (GIU) collaboration and perceived zero-carbon community performance with particular attention to the mediating roles of strategic alliance, organizational alliance, and knowledge alliance. Based on survey data from 350 stakeholders in China, covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) was employed to systematically examine the direct and indirect statistical associations among GIU collaboration, alliance mechanisms, and perceived zero-carbon community performance (PZCP). The results indicate that government support and industry participation are not significantly associated with perceived zero-carbon community performance through direct paths but show significant indirect associations through strategic alliance, suggesting an indirect-only mediation pattern. In contrast, university engagement shows a significant positive direct association with perceived zero-carbon community performance and also shows a significant indirect association through strategic alliance, indicating a complementary mediation pattern. Among the three alliance mechanisms examined, only strategic alliance exhibits a significant indirect association, suggesting that shared strategic objectives, strategic alignment, and long-term collaborative relationships are particularly important in linking GIU collaboration with PZCP. items.title: Measuring Human-Capital Performance upon SDGs: A Data-Driven Index for Strategic Management in Airport Operators
items.abstract: Human capital represents the core asset upon which the social dimension of the transition towards the circular economy is based, as the strategies for transition depend on people and their skills, safety, development and inclusion that ultimately determine the success in meeting the human-capital-related Sustainable Development Goals. Human capital, however, represents the least measured dimension of corporate sustainability, since the existing practices of measuring human capital involve either its monetary evaluation or subjective weight allocation within the firm-specific sustainability scorecard or aggregation at the national level without the ability to create an objective firm-level benchmark of human capital performance. In this study, human capital represents a management object, and the question is about the extent to which the standardized public disclosure of data about employment, occupational health and safety, training and education, and diversity and equal opportunity according to the Global Reporting Initiative standards could be transformed into a composite index that would discriminate managerial performance of organizations in managing the human capital-related SDGs. For this purpose, the Managerial Performance Index, a composite indicator based on a data-driven approach to creating a benchmark, where indicators are normalized, weighted objectively by means of Shannon entropy for their discriminating capacity and aggregated into four sub-indexes and one overall score, is created. The framework is applied to the cross-sectional sample of the leading European airport operators—an industry characterized by intensive capital, safety and labor intensity but never benchmarked in terms of human capital before.

items.title: Sagari Berdikari as a Community-Based Social Innovation: Integrating Sustainable Mango Agriculture, Circular Economy, And Women Empowerment in Indramayu, Indonesia
items.venue: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
items.abstract: Rural agricultural communities face interconnected challenges related to limited market access, unmanaged agricultural residues, environmental pressures, and limited livelihood opportunities. These challenges require community development approaches that can connect local resources with economic, social, and environmental solutions. This study examines the implementation of Sagari Berdikari, a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)-based community development program implemented by PT Pertamina Patra Niaga Integrated Terminal Balongan in Sliyeg Lor Village, Indramayu, West Java, Indonesia. The study aims to examine how Sagari Berdikari develops local mango potential through an integrated approach to sustainable agriculture, circular economy, and community empowerment. A qualitative case study approach was employed using program documentation, implementation records, beneficiary information, and documented program outcomes. The findings indicate that Sagari Berdikari has developed three interconnected components: Griya Mangga, Griya Kreasi, and Griya Rasa. These components connect conventional and millennial mango farmers with modern cultivation practices, climate-resilient agricultural innovation, market development, and mango-based product processing involving women former migrant workers. The program also introduces circular practices by utilizing mango skin waste as a bioactivator and harvest residues as compost, while renewable energy is incorporated through a solar photovoltaic system to support agricultural activities. The documented outcomes include increased reported income among farmer and women groups, greenhouse gas emission reduction through mango waste utilization, and electricity cost savings through solar energy utilization. The program also developed intellectual property related to mango-waste bioactivator, greenhouse design, and climate-resilient mango cultivation. items.title: Research through Co-Design
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the early concept of RTC as a novel application of Control Systems Theory (CST) within Research through Design (RTD) and co-design. It embeds the participatory paradigm through collaborative design practice, transforming research into a collective learning process for all participants. The chapter specifically explores the origins and significance of RTC, explaining why RTD, co-design, and CST have been adopted to construct its theoretical framework. It then discusses various perspectives on co-design, outlining its historical development to clarify how co-design is interpreted within RTC. Finally, the chapter explains how this book was conceived and introduces the key questions guiding the discussions throughout. A few challenges are presented to provide readers with essential concepts to support their engagement with the subsequent chapters. These challenges and questions will be revisited in the final chapter to facilitate a concluding discussion.

items.title: Selected physical and mechanical properties and circular reuse potential of driftwood and fire-affected wood in Mediterranean ecosystems
items.abstract: Wildfires and extreme hydrological events in Mediterranean regions generate significant quantities of environmentally exposed wood biomass that is often classified as waste due to presumed structural degradation. However, quantitative evidence regarding its retained mechanical performance remains limited. This study presents a comparative evaluation of marine and riverine driftwood and fire-affected wood collected in southern Croatia. Seven Mediterranean wood species were identified and tested under controlled laboratory conditions. Physical properties (moisture content, density, porosity) and mechanical properties (compressive strength parallel to the grain, bending strength, and modulus of elasticity in bending) were determined. The results show that poplar, hackberry, cypress, oak, pine, and olive retained 75–100% of reference mechanical properties (compressive strength, bending strength, and modulus of elasticity), suggesting potential suitability for controlled non-structural applications. Strength reductions were primarily associated with biological defects and grain deviations, resulting in increased variability rather than uniform degradation. Wood that retains a substantial portion of its reference mechanical properties may be considered suitable for controlled non-structural and value-added applications, although further validation is required. These findings indicate the potential for incorporating environmentally exposed wood into the circular bioeconomy systems and highlight opportunities for improved resource efficiency in Mediterranean ecosystems.

items.title: A perspective from the future: How scenarios can inform blockchain investment and implementation decisions
items.abstract: Conflicting predictions about the prospects of blockchain adoption make it difficult for strategists to decide whether to invest in blockchain applications and undertake the associated business process innovations. This challenge is intensified by a temporal dilemma: while such decisions are made with a long-term horizon in mind, the available information largely reflects present-day conditions and assumptions. To address this problem, this paper introduces the concept of aligning the timeframe of decision-making with the timeframe from which strategic information is derived through the use of far-future scenarios. The paper contributes to blockchain decision-making research by introducing a scenario-based perspective (from the future) that complements the dominant reliance on forecasting approaches and predictive models (on the future). Empirically, we analyse scenarios of far-future life-worlds with blockchain applications developed by 83 young future strategists. The analysis identifies ten ideal types of future life-worlds and demonstrates how far-future scenarios can support present-day decision-making regarding blockchain investment and implementation. The findings reveal four ways in which far-future scenarios contribute to strategic decision-making: (1) by identifying critical conditions for blockchain adoption, (2) broadening perspectives and revealing blind spots, (3) supporting backcasting from desirable futures, and (4) generating novel ideas for innovation. Thereby, the paper contributes to the strategic decision-making and foresight literature by demonstrating how far-future scenarios can bridge the temporal gap between present-day decision-making and future-oriented information, enabling decision-makers to adopt a broader perspective that encompasses the full spectrum of opportunities and threats emerging across alternative futures.

items.title: Digital platforms and political participation: from citizen voice to governance data in China
items.abstract: Digital technologies are rapidly transforming the mechanisms through which citizens interact with governments. Although their impact on political participation is evident, the precise nature, mechanisms and implications of this transformation remain uncertain and insufficiently studied. This article examines how digital technologies reshape political participation in China, conceptualising it as algorithmically mediated participation. It develops a 3×2 analytical matrix linking levels of participation (information, consultation, deliberation) with two technological modes of governance (digitalisation and algorithmic governance). Drawing on a purposive set of typical and information-rich cases, including information provision platforms, online consultation platforms and digital deliberation forums, the study shows that digital participation expands channels of citizen input while reinforcing administrative logic over empowerment logic. Algorithmic mediation makes it possible to convert citizen voice into usable governance data, yet this produces large-scale participation without a corresponding expansion of democratic influence.

items.title: Barriers to meaningful citizen participation in Gram Panchayats: evidence from Tripura
items.abstract: This study examines the gap between formal attendance and substantive participation in Gram Panchayats (GPs) in Unakoti District, Tripura, North East India. Using primary data from 240 respondents across four purposively selected GPs, the study adopts a mixed-method approach combining survey analysis with thematic interpretation of open-ended responses. The findings identify multiple barriers to effective participation, including administrative indifference, political clientelism, corruption perceptions, gender-based marginalisation, and socioeconomic constraints. The study suggests that strengthening transparency mechanisms, ensuring inclusivity, and addressing structural inequalities are essential to transform procedural participation into substantive democratic engagement.

items.title: Entropy as a diagnostic for time-related constraints on circular transition: Evidence from plastic waste management in the OECD–EU countries
items.abstract: This study examines time-related constraints on circularity by applying Shannon entropy to measure distributional dispersion across end-of-life fates in plastic waste management. Using OECD data for 1990–2018, end-of-life shares for recycling, incineration, landfill, mismanaged, and littered waste are combined with entropy to assess structural change over time. Entropy makes that structural shift visible and comparable across time. During the early 1990s, plastic waste management was highly predictable due to landfill dominance. From the mid-2010s onward, entropy stabilized at a high level despite continued growth in recycling. That plateau is consistent with persistent dispersion across competing end-of-life routes rather than convergence toward recycling dominance.

items.title: A Participatory Culturally Responsive Model for Redevelopment of Hausa Informal Settlements in Minna, Nigeria
items.abstract: Redevelopment of informal settlements in Nigeria has historically prioritised physical delivery over the socio-cultural patterns structuring residents’ daily lives, a pattern documented across Lagos and other Sub-Saharan African cities but not examined for its Hausa-specific dimension in Minna, Niger State. This study grounds a Participatory Culturally Responsive (PCR) redevelopment decision-making model. A community-engaged sequential exploratory mixed-methods design, incorporating participatory model validation, combined fifteen qualitative interviews with a questionnaire administered to 144 residents and stakeholders across four settlements; exploratory factor analysis supported an eight-factor, 38-item cultural-value structure and a single-factor, five-item participation structure. Respondents endorsed the influence of Hausa socio-cultural values on housing practice (grand mean and median 3.76, 4.00), with traditional authority, religious practice, and gender-based privacy most strongly endorsed, and moderately endorsed community participation in redevelopment (grand mean and median 3.51, 3.60). Qualitative findings identified gendered spatial separation, extended-family lineage, and the courtyard as dominant cultural determinants of housing form, and late-stage consultation and literacy barriers as principal obstacles to participation. Findings were synthesised—through expert content review and a community validation workshop—into the PCR model, a six-feature framework comprising an empirical foundation, a stakeholder governance structure, three strategic pillars of cultural integration, collaborative process, and sustainability, a staged early-and-continuous implementation process, and a continuous feedback mechanism, offering planners a structured, validated redevelopment tool aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 11.

items.title: Design anthropology for transforming power relations in societal transitions
items.abstract: This article makes the argument that design can serve the purpose of transforming power relations in societal transitions. The article discusses diverse theories of power and their relationship to design, whereby it considers aspects of agency, relationality and scale. Using a design anthropology approach, a theoretical framework is defined for the empirical study of power. The framework is operationalized in a local energy transition project in Amsterdam Southeast. In this empirical study, we describe three power relations that were encountered, the design interventions performed, and their transformative outcomes. Finally, the broader implications for design in societal transitions are discussed.

items.title: Orienting Participatory AI for Frontline Care Work: A Conceptual Framework for Technologists
items.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
items.abstract: Technologists increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) to support frontline care workers ( FCWs ), via work-tracking applications, well-being monitoring systems, and other data-driven interventions aimed at improving care quality and working conditions for this vital labor and labor force. Thoughtful application of AI in this dynamic and high-stakes domain requires centering FCWs ’ voices in technology design and development—but doing so challenges existing approaches in participatory design (PD). For example, care work’s relationality defies standardization and quantification. Moreover, it can be difficult to balance all stakeholders’ needs in a hierarchical and high-stakes collaboration environment as FCWs often prioritize patients’ or clients’ needs above their own. This paper draws together scholarship in CSCW and participatory AI, alongside the authors’ extensive experience developing AI systems in frontline care contexts, to present a conceptual framework for meaningfully engaging frontline care workers’ visions of data and AI systems. We illustrate our framework through case studies of two particularly urgent applications: shift matching in home care and identifying burnout in the medical workforce. We discuss tensions in implementing this framework, including how to do equitable PD, and close with a research agenda for CSCW as the design space around AI in frontline care work expands.

items.title: Cultural Civic Engagement and Typologies of Political Participation in the 2024 Gorontalo City Mayoral Election
items.venue: Journal of Asian Multicultural Research for Social Sciences Study
items.abstract: Studies on political participation in Indonesian regional elections generally continue to interpret non-voting as an indicator of political apathy, while local cultural values are treated merely as a social background that complements institutional analysis. This article offers a conceptual correction to both assumptions through a case study of the 2024 Gorontalo City Regional Election. Using a qualitative case study approach and involving in-depth interviews with voters, non-voters, election organizers, and cultural figures, this study formulates the concept of Cultural Civic Engagement: civic engagement mediated by local cultural values (lipu, pohalaa, huyula, adab, tanggomo, and eeya), which shape who is considered a legitimate actor of participation, which arenas are perceived as meaningful, and what goals citizens seek to achieve through political engagement. This framework is manifested in three modes of participation that differ in their cultural motivations: normative (voting as a form of service to the lipu), ambivalent (voting while restraining criticism in order to preserve adab and social harmony), and resistive-reflective (withdrawing from the polling station as an ethical rejection when tanggomo and adab are perceived to have been violated by the political process). The findings indicate that non-voting in the third mode does not represent an absence of political awareness, but rather a conscious ethical assessment of the legitimacy of the electoral process. This article argues that measures of the success of local democracy need to shift from merely considering voter turnout to assessing the extent to which electoral systems are capable of accommodating civic engagement rooted in citizens’ cultural values.

items.title: Membangun Ketangguhan Desa Melalui Program Tempur Berseri: Pemberdayaan Masyarakat Berbasis Bank Sampah
items.abstract: This article shares the experience of community empowerment through a waste bank under the Tempur Berseri Program, a Social and Environmental Responsibility (TJSL) program of PT. PLN (Persero) UIK Tanjung Jati B in Tempur Village, Jepara. The empowerment program was implemented through three stages: awareness-raising, capacity building, and empowerment. The awareness-raising stage was conducted through social mapping and waste-sorting education to encourage changes in community behavior. The capacity-building stage focused on strengthening institutions, enhancing the capacity of program managers, providing supporting facilities, and strengthening disaster preparedness. Subsequently, the empowerment stage involved utilizing waste and village land for productive activities, including organic fertilizer production, hydroponics, fish farming, waste processing into maggot and pellets, and slope conservation. By the first semester of 2026, the Tempur Berseri Waste Bank had served 496 households, with approximately 3 tons of waste collected and 80% of it utilized. The program also produced 1,650 kg of organic fertilizer, fostered new local community activators, and established a Disaster-Resilient Village (Desa Tangguh Bencana) group consisting of 20 trained volunteers. Beneficiary satisfaction and the program's social value assessment indicated a positive community response. Nevertheless, challenges remain in managing low-value residual waste and strengthening market access. This experience provides practical lessons on waste bank-based community empowerment that can be replicated in other villages with similar contexts.

items.title: Evaluación de los procesos participativos en la elaboración de los Planes Generales de Ordenación Urbana: propuesta de indicadores
items.abstract: El objetivo de esta investigación ha sido configurar una herramienta simplificada que permita evaluar y perfeccionar los procesos participativos para incluir a la ciudadanía en la redacción de los Planes de Ordenación Urbana. Partiendo de las limitaciones de los enfoques participativos en el urbanismo, este trabajo plantea la pregunta de cómo puede evaluarse de forma más operativa la calidad de estos procesos para reforzar su eficacia y legitimidad democrática. En base al análisis bibliográfico, se propone una metodología de evaluativos para medir la calidad de los programas de participación, realizar el seguimiento del proceso para detectar desviaciones y en definitiva optimizar los resultados de estos de cara a enriquecer los documentos del planeamiento urbano.

items.title: Electronic Government Enablers of Circular Economy Transitions in the Battery Electric Vehicle Sector: A Semantic Network Analysis
items.venue: International Journal of Electronic Government Research
items.abstract: Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) have become central to sustainable mobility; however, the integration of circular economy principles throughout the BEV life cycle has remained fragmented, and the role of electronic government in enabling the transition to a circular economy has remained poorly understood. Utilizing 400 Scopus-indexed publications (2010–2024) selected through the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol, this study examined the knowledge structure at the intersection of the circular economy, BEV ecosystems, and digital governance. The findings highlighted the growing importance of blockchain, digital and battery passports, artificial intelligence, and interoperable information systems in strengthening transparency, compliance, coordination, and institutional trust. To guide future research and inform policy and practice, this study proposed a four-layer framework linking circular economy strategies, digital enablers, e-government mechanisms, and governance outcomes.

items.title: Recycling Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) Bottle Waste into Sustainable Building Materials: A Systematic Review of Technical Performance, Environmental Safety and Circular-Economy
items.abstract: Waste polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from single-use bottles is generated in rapidly increasing quantities, yet only about 15–35% of PET bottles are recycled. A systematic search of four databases (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Google Scholar and PubMed Central) returned 798 records; after duplicate removal and two-stage screening, 69 studies met the eligibility criteria, of which 28 reported the quantitative performance data that underpin the ranges extracted here. Three recycling routes were compared, namely mechanical recycling, chemical recycling (glycolysis, methanolysis, hydrolysis, pyrolysis and gasification) and enzymatic hydrolysis. PET has been added to concrete, asphalt, bricks, insulation and panels and tested for mechanical strength, physical behaviour and durability under laboratory conditions, and the associated microplastic release, leaching of antimony and phthalate plasticisers, and fire behaviour were also assessed. Costs and market barriers were examined. The evidence indicates that PET is suitable for non-structural and semi-structural applications, and that the reported dosage windows are application-specific rather than reducible to a single range: roughly 5–15% by volume as an aggregate replacement in concrete, 2–10% in asphalt on bases that differ between studies, 25–40% by mass in PET–sand bricks and 0.5–2% fibre volume fraction in fibre-reinforced mortar. Each window is an envelope across studies that differ in PET form, dosage basis, mix design and test standard, and none is a specification. Long-term field testing, standardised leaching and microplastic-release methods, and full life-cycle assessments remain the principal research and application gaps. By linking technical performance to environmental safety, evidence quality and market readiness, this review supports evidence-based decisions for sustainable, circular construction.
